events.text: Your first case. Gu Hyeon, a lesser god of springs under the Green Assembly, let a well run dry below the clouds to punish a town that had stopped praying. Three hundred mortals walked away from their homes. Seo Gyeol, the clerk who came with your chair, dips a brush and waits. "Whatever you say now," they murmur, "the next Arbiter will have to say too."

choices.text: Mercy: Gu Hyeon refills the well and serves it

effects.log: Gu Hyeon kneels and weeps with relief. Seo Gyeol writes "mercy" on the first page of the Book of Precedent.

choices.text: Strict: seal Gu Hyeon from the springs for a thousand years

effects.log: The seal goes on in silence. Heaven notes that the Arbiter does not flinch.

choices.text: Weigh it: let the town below choose the sentence

effects.log: You send the question down to the mortals. They choose to forgive, but to keep the well-rope. Seo Gyeol writes it all.

events.text: Eighty years on, Hwang Seonjae of the Will of Heaven brings you a god of their own hall: a keeper of fire who let a hearth go out below to punish an unfaithful city. It is Gu Hyeon's case again, line for line. Only the pantheon is great this time, and Seo Gyeol has the Book of Precedent open at the first page.

choices.text: Read the first page aloud and give the same sentence

effects.log: You judge the great as you judged the small. The Will of Heaven is silent for a decade, and heaven believes your scales.

choices.text: Judge the case on its own weight

effects.log: You give a different sentence, a careful one. It is fair. Seo Gyeol writes it under the first, and the two pages argue for ever.

choices.text: Send it to the Heavenly Court instead

effects.log: The Court takes the fire-keeper. Hwang Seonjae thanks you warmly, which is how you know you failed.

events.text: The Green Assembly asked you once for help against a neighbour and you stood between, as an Arbiter must. Now their eastern groves are ash, and Na Puleum, their eldest, sits at the foot of your chair with a sapling in a pot. "Neutral," they say. "Tell me what that word cost, Arbiter. I would like to know the price."

choices.text: Tell them the truth: it cost their groves

effects.log: You say it. Na Puleum nods, plants the sapling beside your chair, and goes. It grows every year you sit there.

choices.text: Shelter the Assembly's refugees in your own hall

effects.log: You open your hall. The other pantheons see it and wonder whose Arbiter you are now.

choices.text: Say neutrality is not for sale, at any price

effects.log: Na Puleum takes the sapling home. Heaven says the Arbiter is stone, and some of them mean it well.

events.text: Gu Hyeon comes back. The god you spared has kept the well below for two centuries, and now the town around it worships them, not the god of springs above them. The Green Assembly wants Gu Hyeon judged for stealing worship. Gu Hyeon only asks you, quietly, whether mercy was meant to end here.

choices.text: Rule that faith earned is faith owned

effects.log: Gu Hyeon keeps the town. Seo Gyeol writes it as the second precedent of mercy, and the Assembly sulks for a century.

choices.text: Give the worship back to the springs above

effects.log: Gu Hyeon bows and gives it back. The town below does not understand, and prays a little less to anyone.

events.text: The thousand years of Gu Hyeon's seal are not up, but the springs below have begun to fail without them. Every god of water in heaven has tried and none can make Gu Hyeon's wells run. The seal is yours. Breaking it early would teach heaven that your sentences bend. Keeping it would teach the town below to thirst.

choices.text: Break the seal early

effects.log: The water runs again below. Above, three gods under sentence write to you that very week, asking for the same.

choices.text: Keep it, and carry water down yourself

effects.log: You carry it, a jar a day, for the years that are left. Nobody in heaven quite believes it.

choices.text: Keep it. A sentence is a sentence

effects.log: The seal holds. Below, the town moves away again. Seo Gyeol writes the date without comment.

events.text: Under your chair, in a drawer you never opened, Seo Gyeol finds a scroll in a hand older than any pantheon: a judgement of Jang Murae, the first Arbiter, who faded before the Calendar began. It condemns a god of the Sea by name, "until an Arbiter sits again." Haeryong, Keeper of Tides, is that god's heir, and has just heard.

choices.text: Uphold the first Arbiter's judgement

effects.log: Precedent above precedent. Haeryong pays an old debt of tides with grim courtesy, and the Throne of Storms remembers it.

choices.text: Overturn it: the condemned is long gone

effects.log: You burn the scroll. Seo Gyeol watches it go with an expression you cannot read.

choices.text: Judge it again, from the first word

effects.log: You hear the old case anew, a hundred witnesses long dead read from the Book of Fates. It takes nine years.

events.text: Pyo Ara, an auditor of the Heavenly Court, lays a charge at your feet: inconsistency. The fire-keeper's sentence and Gu Hyeon's sit side by side in your own Book and do not agree. "If the Arbiter may judge each case on its weight," Pyo Ara asks, "who weighs the Arbiter?"

choices.text: Answer the charge before the Court

effects.log: You climb the Court's ladder as a defendant. Heaven has never seen an Arbiter do it.

choices.text: Answer it here, at your own chair

effects.log: You hear the charge against yourself in your own hall. Pyo Ara says it is the strangest trial in heaven, and the fairest.

choices.text: Refuse: no court sits above the scales

effects.log: Pyo Ara files the refusal. It is the only page in the Court's archive written in red.

events.text: Pyo Ara, an auditor of the Heavenly Court, lays a charge at your feet: cruelty by precedent. You judged the great as the small, always, and some of the small were broken by sentences made for the great. "A scale that never moves," Pyo Ara says, "is only a stone with arms."

choices.text: Answer the charge before the Court

effects.log: You climb the Court's ladder as a defendant. Heaven has never seen an Arbiter do it.

choices.text: Answer it here, at your own chair

effects.log: You hear the charge against yourself in your own hall. It is the strangest trial in heaven, and the fairest.

choices.text: Refuse: no court sits above the scales

effects.log: Pyo Ara files the refusal. It is the only page in the Court's archive written in red.

events.text: The trial of the Arbiter. Four envoys sit where litigants sit, and Pyo Ara reads the charge. Then Seo Gyeol stands, with the Book of Precedent in both arms, and asks to be your witness, though every page of it was written in their hand and every judgement in it is yours.

choices.text: Let Seo Gyeol read the whole Book

effects.log: They read for a year. At the end the envoys agree on one thing: nobody else could have kept it. The charge is set aside.

choices.text: Plead guilty to the inconsistency, and mend it

effects.log: You confess, and spend a century reconciling every page. The Book grows thinner and truer.

choices.text: Defend yourself with nothing but the law

ok.log: Your defence becomes a precedent of its own: the Arbiter answers, but no court binds the scales. Even Pyo Ara copies it.

fail.log: The argument fails on one word. The envoys fine you a year of silence, and heaven quarrels all through it.

events.text: Because you refused Pyo Ara, the Heavenly Court has begun to write its own judgements on the cases you hear: a shadow Book, page for page beside yours. Twice now the two Books have disagreed, and the gods judged simply chose the kinder one.

choices.text: Go to the Court and close the shadow Book

effects.log: You stand before the ladder and say what you should have said a century ago. The shadow Book is closed, not burned.

choices.text: Let the two Books compete

effects.log: Heaven now has two scales. It is less stable, and somehow more honest.

events.text: The scales themselves, the old bronze pans that came with your chair, will not settle. A weight sits in the left pan that no one put there. Seo Gyeol weighs it, measures it, and goes very pale: it weighs exactly as much as every judgement you have ever given that you were not sure of.

choices.text: Leave it in the pan

effects.log: The scales hang crooked for the rest of your life. Every litigant sees it. Somehow they trust you more.

choices.text: Take it out with your bare hand

ok.log: It is cold and very heavy. You set it on the floor and the pans come level for the first time in a thousand years.

fail.log: It burns like frost. The pans swing and do not settle; your hand aches for a century.

choices.text: Ask Seo Gyeol to weigh their own doubts

effects.log: Seo Gyeol's doubts, put in the right pan, balance yours almost exactly. Neither of you mentions it again.

events.text: A young god is brought to your chair, newly risen from below, and the town they were born in is the one whose well ran dry in your first case. They do not know it. They have come to accuse a god of springs of the very same crime, and to ask what an Arbiter does.

choices.text: Tell them about your first case

effects.log: You tell them. The young god listens to the whole of it, and then asks for the Book of Precedent, and reads the first page twice.

choices.text: Judge the new case as you judged the old

effects.log: Precedent holds across the ages. The young god thanks you, and you see the old town in their face.

choices.text: Let them judge it, with you beside them

effects.log: They judge it badly, then well, then very well. You say almost nothing. Seo Gyeol writes it under a new heading.

events.text: Seo Gyeol is old now, older than a clerk is meant to be, and the Book of Precedent has no empty page left. They bring it to you closed. "A new Book," they say, "or the end of this one? An Arbiter who has a Book is bound by it. An Arbiter who has none is bound by nothing at all."

choices.text: Begin a second Book, in a new hand

effects.log: You choose a young clerk. Seo Gyeol teaches them for a decade, and the first page of the second Book is a copy of the first page of the first.

choices.text: Close the Book and judge free

effects.log: The Book goes on a high shelf. Your judgements after are cleaner, lonelier, and nobody can cite them.

choices.text: Give the Book to the four pantheons together

effects.log: Each pantheon copies it. For the first time all four halls read the same law.

events.text: Your last judgement. There is no litigant. The four envoys, Pyo Ara, Seo Gyeol's student and Gu Hyeon sit in the empty space between the halls, and the case before the chair is your own long tenure: was the Arbiter just? They have agreed that you alone must give the verdict.

choices.text: "Mostly. Write down where I was not."

effects.log: You list your errors yourself, one by one, and the list becomes the most cited page in heaven.

choices.text: "Ask the ones I judged."

effects.log: You step down and let them speak. It takes a century. The verdict, at the end, is kinder than you would have given.

choices.text: Leave the chair empty, and the scales on it

effects.log: You walk out of the empty space. The scales sit on the chair, crooked, and for an age no god dares to quarrel in front of them.

events.text: Seo Gyeol grinds their own ink from a stone they will not name. Asked, they say only that it was a piece of the first chair, broken off when Jang Murae, the first Arbiter, faded. "It writes what you meant," they say, "which is not always what you said."

choices.text: Ask them to show you

effects.log: They write your last judgement. The ink comes out with a word you did not say and certainly meant. You laugh, and then you do not.

choices.text: Ask them to use plain ink for your judgements

effects.log: Seo Gyeol bows. Your judgements are written as you speak them from then on. Some of them read worse.

events.text: The ink stone is nearly worn away. Seo Gyeol has a decade of writing left in it, perhaps two, and nowhere in heaven is there another piece of the first chair. They ask you, carefully, whether you would allow them to grind a sliver of yours.

choices.text: Break a sliver from your chair

effects.log: The chair is smaller by a fingernail. The ink that comes from it is darker, and writes your doubts as well as your meanings.

choices.text: Tell them to let the stone run out

effects.log: The last judgement in the true ink is a small one, about a boundary stone. Seo Gyeol frames it.

events.text: A god you sentenced long ago brings a suit against Seo Gyeol, not you: the ink wrote "cruel" in the margin of their sentence, in your hand, and they have read it. "If the Arbiter thought it cruel," the god says, "why was it given?"

choices.text: Admit the margin is true

effects.log: You stand and say it. The god is quiet for a long time, and then asks only for the margin, which you give them.

choices.text: Reduce the sentence on the spot

effects.log: You reduce it. The god leaves lighter. Seo Gyeol does not write the reduction in the sliver ink; they use plain.

choices.text: Rule that margins are not judgements

effects.log: You rule it. It is correct. The god goes away and tells everyone what the ink said.

events.text: Seo Gyeol asks, for the first time in a century, for a day away from your chair. You realise you have never asked where they go when you do not need them, or whether they go anywhere at all.

choices.text: Give them the day and ask nothing

effects.log: They come back at dusk with dust on their hem and say nothing. They work better for a year.

choices.text: Ask to walk with them

effects.log: Seo Gyeol hesitates, then nods. They take you down a road of heaven you have never noticed, to a door with no name on it.

events.text: Behind the door is a small archive, one room, and in it every case that was brought to the empty space between the halls before you came: petitions to an empty chair, centuries of them, unanswered. Seo Gyeol has been reading them alone. "Someone should," they say.

choices.text: Hear the oldest of them now

effects.log: You hear a petition nine thousand years late. The petitioner is gone; their descendants are in the Silent Hall, and stunned to be answered.

choices.text: Seal the room: the old griefs should rest

effects.log: Seo Gyeol locks it. They keep the key on a cord at their throat from then on.

events.text: Word has spread that the Arbiter answers petitions to the empty chair, however old. Every pantheon has discovered a grievance from before the Calendar. The little room behind the nameless door is full of envoys, and Seo Gyeol has not slept in a month.

choices.text: Set a limit: nothing older than a thousand years

effects.log: Precedent again. Most envoys go home; a few weep. Seo Gyeol sleeps for a week.

choices.text: Hear them all, however long it takes

effects.log: It takes three centuries. Heaven is less angry at the end of it, and very tired.

events.text: Gu Hyeon's seal is a ring of bronze set over a dry spring at the edge of the Green Assembly. You visit it once, on the hundredth year, and find the god sitting beside it in grey, tending the dust as if it were water.

choices.text: Sit with them a while

effects.log: Gu Hyeon does not speak, but before you go they pour you a cup of the dust, with great ceremony. You drink it.

choices.text: Check the seal and leave

effects.log: The seal is sound. Gu Hyeon watches you check it with an expression that might be approval.

events.text: Mortals below have found the dry spring's twin, a well in their own world that matches it stone for stone, and they pray at it for rain, and are not answered. Gu Hyeon asks you one thing: may they at least hear the prayers, even if they cannot answer?

choices.text: Grant it

effects.log: Gu Hyeon hears every prayer for the rest of the sentence. It is a harder punishment, and they thank you for it.

choices.text: Refuse: the sentence is silence too

effects.log: The prayers go to no one. Gu Hyeon nods, and you notice they have started to count the years on the bronze.

events.text: The thousand years end on a winter morning. You lift the bronze ring yourself. Gu Hyeon stands, steps onto the dry spring, and waits, as if for permission; and when you give none, the water comes on its own, thin and clear.

choices.text: Say their sentence is served, aloud

effects.log: The words go into the Book. Gu Hyeon bows to you, and to the spring, and goes down to the world below to find the town.

choices.text: Offer them a seat as a clerk of your hall

effects.log: Gu Hyeon laughs, the first sound you have heard from them. "Judge me again in a thousand years," they say, and accept.

events.text: Seo Gyeol has built a shelf beside your chair for the Book of Precedent, and on it, one by one, small things the litigants leave behind: a hailstone that never melts, a seed, a feather, a cracked cup. "Evidence," they say. "Of what, I could not tell you."

choices.text: Keep the shelf

effects.log: The shelf grows for a thousand years. Visitors stop to read it as if it were a book.

choices.text: Return each thing to its owner

effects.log: You spend a decade on the errand. Most of the owners have forgotten; one weeps.

events.text: Seo Gyeol has a cold, which you did not know a clerk of heaven could catch. They insist on writing anyway, and sneeze on a judgement of the Throne of Storms. The ink runs into a little storm of its own across the page.

choices.text: Send them to bed and write it yourself

effects.log: Your hand is worse than theirs. The Throne of Storms complains that it cannot read its own sentence.

choices.text: Keep the page as it is

effects.log: The Throne of Storms accepts the smudged page. Their herald says it is the first judgement that ever looked like them.

events.text: A child of a god, small enough to be carried, has wandered into your hall and climbed onto the litigant's bench. They announce that their sibling took their kite and they want it judged. Seo Gyeol has already opened the Book.

choices.text: Judge it properly

effects.log: You hear both siblings. The kite is shared on alternate days. Seo Gyeol writes it in the Book, solemnly, and it is cited for an age.

choices.text: Fly the kite with them yourself

effects.log: You fly it from the steps of the empty space. Four pantheons watch from their windows and are, for an afternoon, not at war.

events.text: The Heavenly Court offers Seo Gyeol a post: Keeper of the Book of Fates' margins, a rank three rungs above any clerk. They bring you the letter unopened and set it on the shelf. "I would like you to tell me not to go," they say, "or to go. I find I cannot."

choices.text: "Stay."

effects.log: Seo Gyeol puts the letter in the drawer with Jang Murae's old scroll and never mentions it again.

choices.text: "Go. The Book will wait."

effects.log: They go. The Book of Precedent is kept badly for fifty years. When they come back, they have learned the Court's secrets.

events.text: In a trial of two water-gods, Gu Hyeon asks to stand as a witness. Every god of the Green Assembly turns to look: the spring-god you judged first, testifying before the chair that judged them. They speak of thirst plainly, and the hall is quiet.

choices.text: Let the testimony shape the sentence

effects.log: The sentence is gentler for the thirst they described. The water-gods both look at Gu Hyeon afterwards.

choices.text: Thank them, and judge on the law alone

effects.log: You thank them. The law decides. Gu Hyeon nods: they expected nothing else of you.

events.text: It rains in the empty space between the halls for the first time anyone remembers. Rain belongs to the Throne of Storms, the ground to the Green Assembly, and the light it falls through to the Will of Heaven. Three envoys arrive at once to ask whose rain it is.

choices.text: "Nobody's. Get wet."

effects.log: They stand in it with you, the three of them, embarrassed and soaked. The rain stops when they start laughing.

choices.text: Open an umbrella and say nothing

effects.log: The envoys argue under the eaves for an hour and leave without a ruling. It rains again next year, and they do not come.

events.text: Hwang Seonjae, herald of the Will of Heaven, stands in your hall in noon light, and behind them on the floor lies a thin grey shadow. The halls of their pantheon cast none. Their gods cast none. Hwang Seonjae sees you notice and goes very still.

choices.text: Say nothing about it

effects.log: You hear their petition as if the floor were bare. At the door, Hwang Seonjae bows lower than a herald needs to.

choices.text: Ask them, gently, when it began

effects.log: "The day I first doubted a decree of my own hall," they say. "It has grown every year since."

events.text: Hwang Seonjae comes back at dusk, when shadows are longest, and theirs now reaches the door. The Will of Heaven has noticed. Mujin of the Thousand Banners wants the herald brought before the Arbiter for doubt, which in their hall is treason.

choices.text: Rule that doubt is no crime under the scales

effects.log: You give it as a judgement, and Seo Gyeol writes it. Every pantheon reads it; the Will of Heaven reads it twice.

choices.text: Refuse the case: it is the Will of Heaven's own matter

effects.log: You send it back. Hwang Seonjae is stripped of their herald's staff, and keeps their shadow.

choices.text: Ask Mujin to show you their own floor

ok.log: Mujin, laughing, stands in the sun. There is the faintest grey at their heel. The case is withdrawn.

fail.log: Mujin refuses with a war-god's pride. The case goes on, and costs everyone something.

events.text: Centuries later, half the heralds of the Will of Heaven walk with shadows, and the hall itself has begun, at dusk, to cast one. Hwang Seonjae, white-haired, comes to tell you that the pantheon is gentler than it was, and that nobody there will say why.

choices.text: Tell them it was their doing

effects.log: Hwang Seonjae looks at their shadow a long time. "It was a small doubt," they say. "It was enough."

choices.text: Say it was the hall's own growing

effects.log: They accept it, kindly, the way one accepts a gift wrapped badly.

events.text: The mirror the Will of Heaven sent when you first set your chair has hung in a corner for a century. Hwang Seonjae asks, casually, whether you have looked in it. In that hall the mirror is how a god learns what heaven sees of them.
events.arc: The Mirror of the Will of Heaven

choices.text: Look in it now

effects.log: In the glass you are not seated but standing, and the chair is behind you, empty. You do not know what it means.

choices.text: Turn it to the wall

effects.log: Hwang Seonjae nods, pleased in a way that surprises you. "My hall said you would look," they say.

events.text: The mirror has cracked across the middle in the night. Hwang Seonjae is frightened: a cracked mirror in their pantheon means a god is about to be judged falsely. They beg you to name the case before it is heard.
events.arc: The Mirror of the Will of Heaven

choices.text: Read the crack like a line in the Book of Fates

ok.log: The crack runs through a case you heard last year. You reopen it; it was wrong. You set it right.

fail.log: The crack tells you nothing. The case it meant is heard and lost, and you only learn later which one it was.

choices.text: Reopen every case of the year

effects.log: You hear the year again. Two judgements change. The Will of Heaven calls it humility; the others call it weakness.

events.text: Hwang Seonjae brings a mirror-smith of their hall to mend the glass. The smith says it can be made whole, but it will show only what heaven wishes to see from then on. Left cracked, it will keep telling the truth, badly.
events.arc: The Mirror of the Will of Heaven

choices.text: Leave it cracked

effects.log: The cracked mirror hangs in your hall for the rest of your life. Heralds of the Will of Heaven come to look into it in secret.

choices.text: Have it mended

effects.log: The mirror is perfect. Your reflection in it is stern and right and someone else.

events.text: Mok Dami of the Silent Hall, whose pantheon sent nothing at all when you set your chair, returns a century later to bring you nothing again: an empty box of black lacquer, presented with both hands. They watch you very closely.

choices.text: Thank them for it, sincerely

effects.log: Mok Dami almost smiles. "You understood," they say. You are not sure you did, but you keep the box beside the Book.

choices.text: Ask what it means

effects.log: "That the Silent Hall asks nothing of you," they say. "It is the rarest gift in heaven. Few take it."

events.text: Mok Dami comes back with the box. This time something is in it: a single grey feather from the boat of Baekun the Pale Ferryman. The Silent Hall is asking for something at last, and is embarrassed, and will not say what until you open the lid.

choices.text: Open it

effects.log: A plea: a soul the Ferryman would not carry, waiting on the near bank for a thousand years. The Hall wants it judged.

choices.text: Return it closed: the Hall's silence was the point

effects.log: Mok Dami bows, relieved and sorry at once. The feather stays in the Hall.

events.text: On the near bank of the river of Death, a soul in mortal clothes sits on a stone. Baekun the Pale Ferryman will not carry it: it swore it would not leave until someone apologised. Nobody remembers who owed the apology, least of all the soul.

choices.text: Apologise to it yourself

effects.log: You kneel and apologise for whatever it was. The soul looks at you, puzzled and then lighter, and steps into the boat.

choices.text: Find in the Book of Fates who owed it

ok.log: It was a god of Dreams, long faded. You read their apology from an old dream, aloud; the soul goes.

fail.log: The page is torn out. The soul stays, and Baekun leaves the boat tied there in case.

events.text: A case that can only be heard in a dream: two gods of the Silent Hall both claim a sleeping mortal's nightmare, and the mortal cannot wake until it is settled. Mok Dami offers to take you into the dream of Mongsa the Sleeper, where the hearing must sit.

choices.text: Go into the dream

effects.log: You sit your chair inside a dream. The hall is the same but the floor is water. The litigants are very small and very loud.

choices.text: Ask Mongsa to bring the dream to you

effects.log: Mongsa sleeps on your steps for a month. Your hall dreams with them; Seo Gyeol writes in their sleep.

events.text: In the dream court, the nightmare itself asks to speak. It is a small grey thing that says it was only ever a warning, and it does not want to belong to either god. It wants to be heard and then to end.

choices.text: Rule that the nightmare is its own

effects.log: It bows and dissolves. Far below, the mortal wakes, and for the rest of their life never has a bad dream.

choices.text: Award it to the god who made it

effects.log: The law holds even in a dream. The god who made it takes it home. The mortal wakes, frightened, and wiser.

events.text: Mok Dami tells you that since the dream-hearing, the Silent Hall has begun to bring its quarrels to your chair instead of settling them in silence. The Hall's elders are uneasy. "We were remembered for keeping our own counsel," Mok Dami says. "What will we be remembered for now?"

choices.text: "For being heard."

effects.log: Mok Dami writes the words on the inside of the black box and closes it.

choices.text: Send the Hall's small quarrels home again

effects.log: You hear only the great ones. The Silent Hall is relieved, and quieter, and a little lonely.

events.text: The seed the Green Assembly sent when your chair was set has split its shell on the shelf, with no soil and no water. Na Puleum, eldest of the Assembly, walks a day to see it. "It is choosing," they say. "A seed of ours chooses where it grows."
events.arc: The Seed of the Green Assembly

choices.text: Plant it beside the chair

effects.log: The sapling roots in the bare floor of the empty space. The other pantheons call it a Grove flag.

choices.text: Plant it outside, on no one's ground

effects.log: You carry it to the edge of the empty space. It roots in the place where four borders meet.

events.text: The tree on the four borders has grown roots into every pantheon's ground at once. The Will of Heaven says it is spying, the Throne of Storms says it is stealing rain, and the Silent Hall says nothing, which means it agrees.
events.arc: The Seed of the Green Assembly

choices.text: Rule that the tree belongs to the border

effects.log: A tree as a party to the law: Seo Gyeol has to invent a new page for it. The quarrels stop at its shade.

choices.text: Prune the roots back to the empty space

effects.log: You prune for a year. Na Puleum watches without a word and leaves before the last cut.

events.text: Under the border tree, envoys of all four pantheons have started to meet in secret, because nobody's ground is safe ground. Na Puleum, older than ever, asks whether you will forbid it.
events.arc: The Seed of the Green Assembly

choices.text: Let them meet

effects.log: They meet under the tree for a thousand years. Three wars end there before you hear of them.

choices.text: Put your chair under the tree with them

effects.log: The envoys go quiet when you sit. They meet somewhere else. The tree misses them.

events.text: Saengmo, Mother of Seeds, and Horang, Lord of the Wild, both of the Green Assembly, have not spoken for nine thousand years. Now they bring their quarrel to you: Horang's beasts graze Saengmo's fields, Saengmo's fields fence Horang's beasts. Na Puleum came with them and looks exhausted.
events.arc: The Oldest Grudge in the Grove

choices.text: Hear the whole nine thousand years

effects.log: It takes a decade. You hear every grazed field and every fence. At the end you understand both of them, which is worse.

choices.text: Hear only this year's grievance

effects.log: You judge the one field and the one fence. Both gods are furious that it worked.

events.text: Your ruling on the old quarrel has been kept for twenty years. Then a herd of Horang's stags is found inside Saengmo's fence, and Saengmo says Horang drove them there. Horang says the stags went on their own, as beasts do.
events.arc: The Oldest Grudge in the Grove

choices.text: Ask the stags

ok.log: The eldest stag walks to your chair and lies down. It went for the grass. Both gods laugh, for the first time in an age.

fail.log: The stags will not be questioned. The quarrel grows a new branch.

choices.text: Rule that the fence moves a hundred paces

effects.log: Saengmo grumbles and moves it. The stags graze the hundred paces and stop.

events.text: Saengmo and Horang come together, not as litigants. They have agreed, for the first time, on something: that the Arbiter should sit for a while in the Green Assembly's fields, so that the grass knows whose law it is. Na Puleum winces at the word "whose".
events.arc: The Oldest Grudge in the Grove

choices.text: Decline: the law is no one's

effects.log: You stay in the empty space. The two gods go home disappointed together, which Na Puleum counts as progress.

choices.text: Visit, once, for a single season

effects.log: You sit in the fields for one summer. The other pantheons send anxious letters every week.

events.text: Cheon Ugeun of the Throne of Storms, who argues in weather like all their pantheon, arrives in a small drizzle and asks after the hailstone their hall sent for your chair. It sits on the shelf, unmelted after a century. They look relieved.
events.arc: The Hailstone That Will Not Melt

choices.text: Ask why it matters

effects.log: "While it lasts, the Throne trusts you," they say. "A hailstone that melts is an Arbiter who has taken a side."

choices.text: Pick it up and hand it back

effects.log: The drizzle around Cheon Ugeun turns to snow. They take the hailstone as if it were an insult, and a gift.

events.text: One morning the hailstone is wet. A single drop has run down the shelf. Cheon Ugeun arrives in a gale before you have finished looking at it, demanding to know which side you have taken, and against whom.
events.arc: The Hailstone That Will Not Melt

choices.text: Search your last judgements for the leaning

effects.log: You find it: a ruling for the Will of Heaven that a better Arbiter would have split. You reopen it.

choices.text: Tell them a hailstone is not a law

effects.log: The gale stops dead. Cheon Ugeun considers it, rain dripping from their sleeves, and leaves without agreeing.

choices.text: Freeze the drop yourself

ok.log: It freezes. Cheon Ugeun sees the trick and, after a moment, laughs like thunder.

fail.log: The drop will not freeze. You have lied to a storm, and the storm knows.

events.text: The hailstone has kept its shape for a thousand years. Cheon Ugeun, very old for a herald, asks if they may take it home: the Throne of Storms would like to set it in the floor of their hall, as a sign that one judge in heaven never leaned.
events.arc: The Hailstone That Will Not Melt

choices.text: Give it to them

effects.log: The hailstone is set into the Throne's floor. Storm gods step around it as if it were a sleeping child.

choices.text: Keep it: the shelf is where it belongs

effects.log: Cheon Ugeun bows. "Then we will send another, when you are gone," they say, "to the next one."

events.text: Noegong of the Nine Drums and Daeak of the Unmoving Peak, both of the Throne of Storms, are suing each other, and the gods of that pantheon testify only in weather. Thunder rolls on one side of your hall and a slow mist sits on the other. Cheon Ugeun offers to translate.

choices.text: Accept the translation

effects.log: Cheon Ugeun translates for a week. You suspect they soften Noegong's thunder, and say nothing.

choices.text: Learn to read the weather yourself

effects.log: You sit through a year of storm and mist. At the end you can hear a lie in a cloud.

events.text: The case turns on one witness: a single day of hail that fell on a mountain in the world below. Noegong says it was a drum-roll of grief; Daeak says it was an avalanche of insult. The mortals beneath the mountain only remember losing their barley.

choices.text: Rule for the mortals below: both gods repay the barley

effects.log: Both storm-gods are outraged to be judged by barley. Both pay. Below, it is a fat year.

choices.text: Rule it grief, and Noegong's fault

effects.log: Noegong drums a long, low apology across the sky. Daeak sits a little taller.

choices.text: Rule it insult, and Daeak's

effects.log: The mountain sulks for a century. Noegong drums all night in victory and nobody below sleeps.

events.text: The Throne of Storms has adopted your weather-reading. Their gods now write their quarrels as forecasts, and send them to your chair a season ahead. Cheon Ugeun brings this year's: a long drought of resentment is expected in the east.

choices.text: Rule on it before it falls

effects.log: You judge a quarrel that has not yet happened. It never does. Seo Gyeol does not know where to file it.

choices.text: Wait for the weather to arrive

effects.log: The drought comes, and you judge it properly. The east is thirsty for a decade.

events.text: Hwang Seonjae, Mok Dami, Na Puleum and Cheon Ugeun have all been to your hall so often that they have begun to wait together on the bench outside. You find them sharing a single pot of tea there, and talking, very carefully, about the weather.

choices.text: Invite them to dine at your table

effects.log: Four envoys at one table, for the first time since the pantheons split. Nobody eats much. Everybody stays.

choices.text: Leave them alone on the bench

effects.log: You let them have their bench. They come early every year after, to have more time on it.

events.text: At the fourth dinner, Cheon Ugeun says something unforgivable about the Will of Heaven, by accident, in weather: a small cold rain falls on Hwang Seonjae's plate. The table goes silent. Every envoy looks at you, because you are the Arbiter, even at dinner.

choices.text: Laugh

effects.log: You laugh first. Then Mok Dami, who never laughs. The rain stops. Hwang Seonjae eats the wet rice to make a point.

choices.text: Judge it, formally, at the table

effects.log: You fine Cheon Ugeun one dessert. The envoys find it so absurd that it becomes the table's law.

events.text: Na Puleum, the eldest, is fading. At the last dinner they sit with a sapling in their lap and ask the other three envoys to promise one thing: that this table keeps meeting after they are gone, with or without the Arbiter.

choices.text: Promise it with them

effects.log: Four hands on the table, one of them very thin. The dinners go on for an age after, and you are always invited.

choices.text: Say it is for them to promise, not you

effects.log: The three envoys promise without you. You find you are glad and a little left out.

events.text: A new bench has appeared outside your hall, carved in four woods, one for each pantheon, joined so well you cannot see the seams. No one admits to carving it. Seo Gyeol says the envoys did it at night, each a quarter, and each thinks the others do not know.

choices.text: Sit on it once, in the middle

effects.log: You sit. It holds. That is all the judgement it needs.

choices.text: Leave a cushion on each quarter

effects.log: Four cushions, four colours. The next morning they have been swapped round, all of them.

events.text: Cheon Ugeun brings their child to your hall, a small storm-god who has just learned to rain. The child is shy and drizzles on the Book of Precedent. Cheon Ugeun is mortified. The child is fascinated by the scales.

choices.text: Let the child try the scales

effects.log: The child sets a raindrop in one pan and a tear in the other. They balance. You are oddly moved.

choices.text: Dry the Book and pretend not to see

effects.log: The child goes home believing the Arbiter can be rained on and not mind. They will remember it for ten thousand years.

events.text: The Silent Hall invites you to a feast at which nothing is served and nothing is said. You sit for a whole night among the gods of Death, Fate and Dreams. Unmyeong the Weaver passes you an empty cup with great ceremony.

choices.text: Drink the nothing

effects.log: You drink the empty cup. The whole Silent Hall relaxes by a hair. They speak of you kindly for an age, silently.

choices.text: Bring your own tea

effects.log: Nobody says anything, of course. But the next feast has a teapot on the table, empty, in your honour.

events.text: The Will of Heaven holds its noon rite, when every god of their pantheon stands in full light so heaven can see them. They invite you to stand among them. Hwang Seonjae, beside the door, shakes their head very slightly.

choices.text: Decline, politely

effects.log: You stay in the empty space. Mujin of the Thousand Banners is offended; Hwang Seonjae is not.

choices.text: Go, but stand at the edge, in the shade

effects.log: You stand in the one patch of shade in the whole rite. Every god of the Will of Heaven notices.

events.text: Pungnyeon of the Golden Field, god of the Harvest, sends you their ledger unasked: every grain they have sent below in a thousand years. They want it audited by someone with no pantheon. "My own hall would lie to be kind," they write.

choices.text: Audit it, every grain

effects.log: The ledger is honest, except one year of famine, which they paid back twice. You write that it is honest.

choices.text: Send it back unread with a seal: trusted

effects.log: Pungnyeon frames your seal in the granary. Below, the barley is a little heavier that year.

events.text: The four envoys quarrel over who should be heard first each morning. The Will of Heaven says the oldest pantheon; the Green Assembly says they are the oldest; the Silent Hall says nothing; the Throne of Storms says it with hail.

choices.text: Rule by lot, drawn every morning

effects.log: Seo Gyeol keeps four stones in a bowl. The quarrel ends; the bowl becomes famous.

choices.text: Hear them all at once

effects.log: Four petitions at once, every morning. Your hall becomes the loudest place in heaven, and the fairest.

events.text: Hyeolsa the Red Comet has answered a question nobody sent: it has written across a whole quarter of the night sky, in burning letters a hundred leagues high, "WHO JUDGED ME?" Every god of heaven can read it. Every god of heaven is looking at your hall.

choices.text: Write back across the sky: "No one. Come and be judged."

effects.log: Your letters burn beside its own for a season. Then, slowly, the comet turns towards the empty space.

choices.text: Answer only in the Book of Precedent

effects.log: You write: "Cast out without hearing." Seo Gyeol makes a copy and leaves it on the edge of heaven where the comet raids.

choices.text: Let the letters burn out unanswered

effects.log: They burn for a decade. When they fade, the comet raids twice as often.

events.text: The comet comes. It does not land; it hangs over the empty space at the height of a mountain, and its tail of red fire curls around your hall like a cat around a cup. A voice, light and amused, asks for the hearing it never had.

choices.text: Hear it, with all four envoys present

effects.log: The envoys come, trembling. Hyeolsa tells its story to the four pantheons that cast it out. Nobody leaves.

choices.text: Hear it alone, at night

effects.log: You sit on your steps and listen until dawn. It was a god of Thresholds, it says: doors, and the moment before you go through.

events.text: Hyeolsa's case, as Seo Gyeol writes it: a god of Thresholds, cast out because every pantheon claimed the doors of its hall and none would share them. The comet has raided for nine thousand years. The raids were real. The casting out was unjust. Both are true.

choices.text: Judge the casting out first: unjust, and say so

effects.log: You rule it. Four pantheons owe a comet an apology, and must decide whether to give it.

choices.text: Judge the raids first: nine thousand years of them

effects.log: You rule it, and the sentence is heavy. Hyeolsa laughs very softly, as if it had expected exactly that.

choices.text: Judge both at once, in one sentence

ok.log: The sentence is long and it balances. Hyeolsa reads it twice and goes still for the first time in an age.

fail.log: The sentence tips. One half swallows the other. Hyeolsa leaves before you finish, burning.

events.text: A century after your sentence, there is a door at the edge of heaven that was not there before: plain wood, half open, with a faint red light behind it. No god built it. Mortals below have started to dream of it the night before they make a choice.

choices.text: Go through it

effects.log: On the other side is nothing but a step down. You stand there for a moment, between, and come back changed a little.

choices.text: Rule that it belongs to no pantheon

effects.log: Seo Gyeol writes a page for a door. The four pantheons sign it, all of them, which they have never done for anything.

events.text: In the Silent Hall's archive of faded gods, Mok Dami finds a box labelled with no name, only a drawing of a door. Inside is the charter of the domain of Thresholds, signed by all four pantheons, and torn four ways.

choices.text: Mend the charter

effects.log: You lay the four pieces on your table and join them with Seo Gyeol's ink. Each tear runs along a pantheon's seal.

choices.text: Send each piece back to its pantheon

effects.log: Four envoys receive a torn quarter of an old crime. None of them write back.

events.text: With the charter whole, the question is plain: should the domain of Thresholds be restored? It would be a thirteenth domain, and every pantheon would want it, and the comet would stop being a comet. Or it would not, and would raid the new hall too.

choices.text: Restore it, under no pantheon

effects.log: A thirteenth domain with no hall. Hyeolsa does not come down to take it. But the raids stop, that year, and the next.

choices.text: Leave it unrestored, but record it

effects.log: The charter goes into the Book. Heaven now knows it once had thirteen. That is a weight of its own.

choices.text: Offer the domain to Hyeolsa, as reparation

effects.log: The comet circles your hall nine times. Then it says it is too late to be a god, and too early to stop being angry.

events.text: The empty domain of Thresholds has drawn a strange kind of worship: mortals below who stand in doorways at dusk and pray for the courage to go through. Nobody answers them. Their prayers pile up at the door on the edge of heaven like leaves.

choices.text: Answer them yourself, for now

effects.log: You answer a hundred prayers a night, small ones. It is not your domain. It is exhausting, and you are good at it.

choices.text: Ask Hyeolsa to come and hear them

effects.log: The comet comes down to the door, close enough to singe it, and listens. Then it goes away again, slower.

events.text: Hyeolsa has landed. For the first time in nine thousand years the comet is not in the sky: it stands in the doorway of the domain of Thresholds, small and red-haired and tired, and it asks you whether a god who raided for an age may keep a door.

choices.text: "Yes. Under sentence, and under watch."

effects.log: Hyeolsa takes the door and the sentence together. Heaven has its thirteenth god, on probation.

choices.text: "Not yet. Raid no one for a thousand years."

effects.log: Hyeolsa nods and goes back up into the sky, burning softly, and raids no one, and counts.

events.text: Hyeolsa demands a Trial of Judgement: its champion against heaven's. Its champion is itself. Heaven's is to be chosen by the four pantheons, who have spent a month refusing to agree on anyone. The comet is enjoying this very much.

choices.text: Name the champion yourself

effects.log: You name Ok Saebyeok, who has fought in more trials than any god alive. The pantheons are relieved not to have to choose.

choices.text: Make the pantheons agree

effects.log: You lock the four envoys in your hall until they choose. It takes nine days. They choose Ok Saebyeok, who was your own thought.

choices.text: Refuse the trial: a raider has no champion's right

effects.log: The comet laughs and raids three domains in a night to show what it thinks of your rule.

events.text: The trial: Ok Saebyeok, a famous champion of heaven's trials, against a red comet that keeps changing size. You sit in the chair between them. By the third day it is clear the comet is not trying to win. It is trying to be seen fighting fair.

choices.text: Stop the trial and say so

effects.log: You stop it. "It has made its point," you say. Ok Saebyeok sheathes their blade, relieved, and bows to the comet.

choices.text: Let it run to the end

effects.log: It runs nine days. Ok Saebyeok wins, barely. Hyeolsa accepts the sentence with a bow so exact it is almost mocking.

events.text: Ok Saebyeok and Hyeolsa have become something like friends, which nobody in heaven knows what to do with. The champion brings you a letter from the comet: an offer to defend heaven's edges against other raiders, for the price of being let alone.

choices.text: Accept it as a sentence: service, not a bargain

effects.log: You write it as a sentence. Hyeolsa serves it. The edges of heaven are quieter than they have been in an age.

choices.text: Refuse: the Arbiter makes no bargains

effects.log: Hyeolsa writes back one word: "Pity." The edges stay as they were.

events.text: Below the clouds, a whole people have begun to worship the red light of Hyeolsa as it crosses their sky. Their prayers rise to no temple and land, unanswered, in the empty space before your chair, because there is nowhere else in heaven they can go.
events.arc: The Mortals Who Pray to the Comet

choices.text: Read the prayers

effects.log: They pray to the comet for change: for doors to open, for the old order to break. Some of them are very young.

choices.text: Sweep them back down unread

effects.log: You send them back. Below, the priests of the comet say the Arbiter of heaven is afraid of them.

events.text: A god of the Will of Heaven wants the comet's mortal worship forbidden: worship of a Calamity Star, they say, feeds it. Hwang Seonjae brings the petition, unhappy. You can feel the prayers still arriving at your feet as they speak.
events.arc: The Mortals Who Pray to the Comet

choices.text: Forbid it

effects.log: The priests below are scattered by dreams sent from heaven. The comet raids in fury, then sulks.

choices.text: Rule that mortals may pray to anything they like

effects.log: Seo Gyeol writes it: faith is the mortals' own. The Will of Heaven is shocked. The comet, oddly, raids less.

events.text: A comet-priest has climbed all the way from below to your hall, which no mortal should be able to do. They are thin and sunburnt and furious. "Our god will not answer," they say. "You are the only judge in heaven. Make it answer."
events.arc: The Mortals Who Pray to the Comet

choices.text: Call Hyeolsa down to answer one prayer

ok.log: The comet comes down and answers the priest, alone, for an hour. The priest goes home and the prayers below grow gentler.

fail.log: The comet will not come. The priest waits a year on your steps, and goes home old.

choices.text: Answer for it, as Arbiter

effects.log: You tell the priest what the comet told you once: it was a god of doors. They go home and teach it.

events.text: The Calamity Star raiding heaven this age is not Hyeolsa. It is Ma Gwangseong, who stood a gate of the Throne of Storms for three thousand years and then walked off it one night and began to tear down other gates. Cheon Ugeun cannot speak of it without hail.

choices.text: Ask Cheon Ugeun what the gate was

effects.log: "The Gate of Last Weather," they say. "Behind it, the storms that are too large to let out." It is open now.

choices.text: Issue a warrant for the Star at once

effects.log: Your warrant goes out under the Arbiter's seal. Every gate-warden of heaven reads it with a cold feeling.

events.text: Through the open Gate of Last Weather, a storm the size of a domain has drifted out and is sitting over the Green Assembly's fields. Ma Gwangseong sends you a message on its wind: they will close the gate if you will hear why they opened it.

choices.text: Hear them

effects.log: Ma Gwangseong opened it because the Throne of Storms was hoarding the great storms to threaten the other three. They have proof.

choices.text: Close the gate yourself

ok.log: You push it shut against a wind like a mountain. The storm is cut off, and dissipates over a decade.

fail.log: The gate will not move. You are blown back to your chair and lose a year of breath.

events.text: Ma Gwangseong's proof is real: the Throne of Storms kept the great storms penned to threaten its neighbours. Ma Gwangseong's raids are real too. Two wrongs before your chair, one by a pantheon and one by its Guardian.

choices.text: Judge the Throne first

effects.log: The Throne of Storms is ordered to release the great storms slowly, as weather, over a thousand years. Below, the rains are strange for an age.

choices.text: Judge the Guardian first

effects.log: Ma Gwangseong is sealed in their own gate, as keeper and prisoner both. The Throne keeps its storms, uneasily.

choices.text: Judge them both the same: the gate stays open, watched

effects.log: An open gate, and a Guardian bound to stand beside it. Neither side can use it now.

events.text: You find a trail of small red embers leading from the edge of heaven to the foot of your steps, as if something had walked there in the night and stood looking at your chair a long time before leaving.

choices.text: Leave a cup of tea on the bottom step

effects.log: In the morning the cup is empty and warm, and there is a tiny scorch on the rim.

choices.text: Have the embers swept up

effects.log: Seo Gyeol sweeps them up and keeps them in a jar. They glow for a century.

events.text: A Calamity Star has raided the border between two pantheons, and each says the other let it through. Their armies are already standing at the line, facing each other, while the Star sits behind them both, burning.

choices.text: Ride to the border and turn both armies round

ok.log: Both armies turn, and see the Star, and remember who the enemy is. It flees.

fail.log: Neither army turns. The Star is gone before they finish arguing, and so is a domain's worth of temples.

choices.text: Issue a decree: the border is the Star's, not theirs

effects.log: Both armies stand down to save face. The Star raids somewhere else.

events.text: A band of Righteous Immortals climbs to your hall asking for a warrant: they would hunt the Calamity Star raiding heaven, if the Arbiter would make their hunt lawful. Their captain is very young, and very sure.

choices.text: Grant the warrant, with limits

effects.log: You write a warrant that forbids them to burn any domain to catch the Star. They are disappointed and obey.

choices.text: Refuse: a hunt is not a judgement

effects.log: The captain goes away angry. You hear later they went anyway, and came back fewer.

events.text: The keepers of the Heavenly Calendar complain that the Calamity Star has crossed three festivals in a year, and each time the festival had to be held again. They want the Arbiter to rule on whether a festival a comet interrupted still counts.

choices.text: Rule that it counts

effects.log: The festivals count. The Calendar keepers are relieved; the gods who wanted a second feast are not.

choices.text: Rule that it does not, and hold the next one in your hall

effects.log: Your hall hosts a festival for the first time. All four pantheons come, to watch the sky.

events.text: A small red stone arrives on your shelf. It is warm. On it, scorched very carefully, is a single word in an old script that Seo Gyeol has to look up: "Thank you." No one in heaven admits to sending it.

choices.text: Put it beside the hailstone

effects.log: A warm stone beside a cold one. The hailstone does not melt. The envoys stare at both.

choices.text: Write back across the sky

effects.log: Your letters burn for one night: "You are welcome." Every god of heaven reads it and wonders.

events.text: A widow of a domain the Calamity Star burned brings no petition. They want only to sit in your hall while the Star's case is heard, so that someone who lost something is present when the scales move.

choices.text: Give them a seat beside the chair

effects.log: They sit through every hearing of the age. Your sentences on the Star are not softer for it, but they are slower.

choices.text: Give them the litigant's bench

effects.log: You make them a party to the case. The Star's sentence becomes partly theirs to shape.

events.text: A small shower of falling stars has begun to land in the empty space between the halls, each one a fragment of some raid. The pantheons argue over who owns the fallen pieces, which are, after all, bits of their own broken domains.

choices.text: Return each piece to the domain it came from

effects.log: It takes a decade to sort them. Every pantheon is grudgingly grateful.

choices.text: Build a wall of them around your chair

effects.log: A wall of fallen stars. Litigants approach it nervously; it reminds them of what quarrels cost.

events.text: Ok Saebyeok arrives with a scorch-mark on their armour in the shape of a hand. They will not say whose. They only ask whether a champion of heaven's trials may, outside a trial, shake a Calamity Star's hand.

choices.text: "A champion may do as they like outside a trial."

effects.log: Ok Saebyeok nods, relieved, and keeps the scorch-mark unpolished.

choices.text: "Not while the Star's case is open."

effects.log: They nod. You hear they sent a polite letter instead.

events.text: The War in Heaven between {sov_war_a} and {sov_war_b} has reached your chair as two scrolls, each the length of a hall, each a list of the other side's crimes. Seo Gyeol has read both overnight and found something: the first crime on each list is the same night, the same domain, the same fire.

choices.text: Hear that night first

effects.log: You set both scrolls aside and hear one night. Both sides came to the same burning domain, each to save it, each thinking the other lit it.

choices.text: Read both lists aloud, in full

effects.log: You read for a month, alternating. By the end the envoys of both sides are staring at the floor.

choices.text: Judge the war by its latest crime only

effects.log: Precedent says the last wrong is the live one. You judge it swiftly. Both sides call it unfair, which is a balance of sorts.

events.text: The night of the fire, heard properly: the domain was lit by neither side. A lesser god of Fire, in the service of neither, set it to start the war and profit from both. They have been selling weapons of flame to {sov_war_a} and {sov_war_b} for a century.

choices.text: Summon the lesser god before both armies

effects.log: They come in chains of light and confess in front of both hosts. The war does not end. But it falters, for a year.

choices.text: Tell both sides privately, separately

effects.log: Each side thinks only it knows. Each slows its war out of shame. Neither admits to slowing.

events.text: Hwarin of the First Hearth, god of Fire, comes to your chair in person: the lesser god who lit the war was of their domain. They ask to be judged too. "I did not watch my own fire," they say. "That is a crime in the oldest law there is."

choices.text: Judge them: a century of watching every hearth below

effects.log: Hwarin accepts. For a century no hearth below goes out untended, and none burns what it should not.

choices.text: Refuse: a domain is not guilty of its servant

effects.log: Seo Gyeol writes it as a precedent. Hwarin bows and goes home relieved and ashamed.

events.text: Long after, {sov_war_a} and {sov_war_b} send you the same gift on the same day: a burnt beam from the domain of the first fire, with both their seals on it. There is no letter. It is the closest either will come to saying the war began with a lie.

choices.text: Hang the beam over your chair

effects.log: The beam hangs there for the rest of your life. New litigants ask about it, and are told.

choices.text: Send it below, to a temple of peace

effects.log: Mortals below build a small shrine around a burnt beam from heaven, and pray there before they quarrel.

events.text: Between the two pantheons at war, the stars have gone out one by one, as each side breaks the other's lamps. Cheonho, Who Hangs the Stars, comes weeping to your chair: those were their stars, and they belong to neither army.

choices.text: Order both armies to stop breaking stars

effects.log: The order goes out. One army obeys. The other says the first is lying, and keeps breaking.

choices.text: Help Cheonho hang new stars yourself

effects.log: You hang stars all night with the god of the Sky. Below, the mortals see new constellations and do not know why.

events.text: The new stars are being broken as fast as you hang them. Below the clouds, sailors and herders have lost the night: there is a dark patch in the sky where the stars of their grandparents were. Their prayers come up confused and frightened.

choices.text: Hang one star that cannot be broken

ok.log: It takes all you know of the law. The star hangs; no blade of either side will touch it. Sailors steer by it for an age.

fail.log: The star breaks in your hands. Both armies see it and fight harder.

choices.text: Decree the dark patch neutral ground

effects.log: No army may stand in the dark. The fighting moves aside, and in the dark a few stars come back on their own.

events.text: Cheonho names the unbreakable star after you, and you have to sit and listen while the god of the Sky explains to four pantheons why. The armies at war have begun to use it as the place where envoys meet.

choices.text: Accept the name

effects.log: There is a star with your name on it. Below, a child points at it and asks who you are. Nobody knows.

choices.text: Ask Cheonho to name it after the sailors

effects.log: Cheonho names it the Sailors' Lamp. Below, it is the brightest thing in the night for a thousand years.

events.text: A soldier-god of {sov_war_a}, young, still in war-silk, has run from the front and is sitting on the litigant's bench. They ask for asylum in the empty space. Behind them, two captains of their own side wait at the door, very politely.

choices.text: Grant asylum

effects.log: The soldier stays. The captains go, and {sov_war_a} writes you a cold letter that ends, "We will remember this."

choices.text: Hear their reason first

effects.log: The soldier was ordered to burn a temple full of mortals below. They would not. They ran.

choices.text: Return them: the empty space shelters no side's soldiers

effects.log: You return them. The captains bow. Seo Gyeol does not look up from the Book for a day.

events.text: The soldier's reason is now a case: {sov_war_a} gave an order to burn a temple below, and {sov_war_b} wants it judged as a crime of the war. The soldier is the only witness. If they testify, they can never go home.

choices.text: Ask them to testify

effects.log: They testify. {sov_war_a} is fined a thousand years of temple-building below. The soldier stays in your hall as a clerk.

choices.text: Judge it without their testimony

effects.log: Without a witness the case is weaker. You rule what you can. The soldier is grateful, and goes home in secret.

events.text: The deserter, now a clerk of your hall, has been writing letters to their old comrades at the front, telling them about the empty space and the chair. A dozen more have run. {sov_war_a} accuses you of hollowing out their army.

choices.text: Close the door to deserters

effects.log: You rule that the empty space shelters no more of them. The clerk weeps, and keeps writing, and the letters stop arriving.

choices.text: Keep the door open, for both sides

effects.log: You take in deserters of {sov_war_b} too. Both armies shrink. The war slows.

events.text: You ended the war by decree. The two armies have gone home. Now the generals of both sides come to your hall together, which they have never done, and ask what they are for, in a heaven where the Arbiter can end a war with a page.

choices.text: Give them the borders to keep, together

effects.log: Two generals who fought for a century now walk the same border as wardens. They hate it, and do it well.

choices.text: Tell them: you are for the next war, if my scales fail

effects.log: They nod grimly. You have made them the price of your failing.

choices.text: Ask them to teach their soldiers to build

effects.log: The armies are set to mend what they burned. It takes a thousand years. Some of them come to like it.

events.text: The losing side of the decreed peace, if a decree can have a loser, holds a festival of mourning every year on the day you sealed it. This year they have invited you. Their gods wear grey. Their children have been told you are the reason.

choices.text: Go, and wear grey

effects.log: You stand among them in grey. Nobody speaks to you. At the end a child brings you a cup of water, and that is all.

choices.text: Go, and explain the decree

effects.log: You explain it. It is just. It changes nobody's grief. They listen out of courtesy.

choices.text: Do not go

effects.log: The festival goes on without you. Its songs about you grow worse each year.

events.text: A god of the losing side has found a flaw in your decree: a single clause that, read strictly, gave the winning side one more domain than it should have had. They bring it to you with shaking hands. They expect to be laughed at.

choices.text: Admit the flaw and return the domain

effects.log: You admit it before both sides. The domain goes back. The festival of mourning becomes, slowly, a festival.

choices.text: Rule that the clause, read rightly, was fair

ok.log: Your reading holds and both sides accept it. The god who brought it bows, half-convinced.

fail.log: Your reading fails. Heaven sees the Arbiter defend their own error. It costs you.

events.text: A thousand years of peace by your decree. The two sides who fought hold a joint feast in the empty space, and set a cup at the head of the table for you. The generals, old now, give a toast to the page that stopped them.

choices.text: Raise your cup to the page

effects.log: You raise your cup. The generals drink. It is a good feast; it is not quite forgiveness.

choices.text: Raise your cup to the dead of both sides

effects.log: The hall goes silent and everyone drinks. Afterwards, they speak of the dead by name for the first time.

events.text: Mujin of the Thousand Banners, god of War, brings a suit against you. War is their domain; every war you end takes worship from them; the Arbiter is stealing a god's domain by decree. It is, Seo Gyeol says nervously, a fair point of law.

choices.text: Hear it as you would any suit

effects.log: You hear Mujin as a litigant at your own bench. The god of War is visibly startled to be taken seriously.

choices.text: Dismiss it: no god owns the suffering of others

effects.log: Mujin leaves in a fury of banners. Three small wars break out that year, and you know whose they are.

events.text: Your ruling on War: Mujin may keep the worship of courage, of the guard at the gate and the hand that shields, but not of slaughter. Mujin listens with their banners furled. They ask one question: "And when there is no war at all, Arbiter, what is left of me?"

choices.text: "The guard at the gate."

effects.log: Mujin is quiet for a long time. Then they unfurl one banner, plain white, and take it home.

choices.text: "That is for War to discover."

effects.log: Mujin bows like a soldier. For a century they hold drills with no enemy, and are uneasy.

events.text: Below the clouds, temples of the god of War have begun to change: the statues hold shields, not swords, and soldiers pray there before they stand guard, not before they march. Mujin sends you one of the new statues, small, carved by a mortal.

choices.text: Put it on the shelf of evidence

effects.log: A shield-bearing war-god beside the hailstone and the seed. Hwang Seonjae stands looking at it for an hour.

choices.text: Send it back with thanks

effects.log: Mujin puts it in the middle of their hall, among the thousand banners. It is the smallest thing there.

events.text: {sov_war_a} and {sov_war_b} hold each other's gods as prisoners, a hundred on each side, bound in light. Both want to exchange them and neither trusts the other to let go first. They ask the Arbiter to hold all two hundred, for one night, in the empty space.

choices.text: Hold them

effects.log: Two hundred bound gods sleep in your hall for a night. Nobody escapes. Nobody sleeps much, either.

choices.text: Refuse: you hold no side's prisoners

effects.log: The exchange fails. Both sides keep their hundred another decade.

events.text: In the night, two prisoners from opposite sides ask to speak to you. They were lovers before the war. Each was captured trying to reach the other. In the morning, each will be sent home to their own side, and the border will be between them again.

choices.text: Send them both to the same side, by their choice

effects.log: They choose {sov_war_b}. {sov_war_a} protests and is ignored. Seo Gyeol writes it as a precedent of the heart.

choices.text: Send them home as agreed

effects.log: They go to their sides. They write. You see the letters pass through your hall for a hundred years.

choices.text: Keep them both in the empty space

effects.log: They stay as clerks. Neither side can claim them. Neither side can quite object.

events.text: Because the exchange in your hall worked, {sov_war_a} and {sov_war_b} send all their prisoners through the empty space now, every season. Your hall has become the hinge of the war. Some say it keeps the war going, by making it bearable.

choices.text: Keep the exchanges

effects.log: The war goes on, more gently. Fewer gods are lost in it than in any war before.

choices.text: Stop them: let the war bear its own weight

effects.log: Without exchanges, both sides feel the cost in full. Within a decade they are talking peace.

events.text: Both sides of the war have agreed to an armistice, if the Arbiter will draw the line. Each has sent you a map; each map puts the line in the other side's domain. You have a brush of light and a hundred leagues of disputed sky.

choices.text: Draw the line where the armies stand now

effects.log: You draw it down the front. It is ugly and exact. Both sides hate it and keep to it.

choices.text: Draw it where the old pantheon borders were

effects.log: You draw the old line. One side loses a decade's gains. They keep the armistice, grimly.

choices.text: Draw it through the middle of your own hall

effects.log: The line runs under your chair. Neither side can cross it without crossing you.

events.text: A mortal city below lies directly under your line. Half its streets now pray to one pantheon and half to the other, and the priests of each have built a wall down the market. The city sends one prayer up for the Arbiter: please, move the line.

choices.text: Move it, by one city's width

effects.log: Both pantheons object to a mortal city bending a heavenly line. You move it anyway. The wall comes down.

choices.text: Leave it: a line moved once is moved for ever

effects.log: The city keeps its wall. Its two halves trade across it, and in time marry across it.

events.text: The armistice has held so long that both pantheons have forgotten it was ever meant to be temporary. Your line of light is still there, a little faded, and young gods on either side of it think it is a law of heaven, like the turning of the Calendar.

choices.text: Let them think so

effects.log: The line becomes old law. Nobody remembers the war it ended. That may be the point.

choices.text: Tell them what it was

effects.log: You teach the young gods of both sides the history. Some of them start to resent the line; some start to cross it, visiting.

events.text: Soldiers of both sides of the war have begun to sing the same song at night across the front, a song about the Arbiter's chair: how it is empty, and cold, and always there. You are not sure whether it is a complaint or a prayer.

choices.text: Learn the song

effects.log: You sing it to yourself on the steps. Seo Gyeol pretends not to hear, and hums along.

choices.text: Send them a second verse

effects.log: Your verse goes down the front by a herald: the chair is cold so that their hearths need not be. Both sides sing it.

events.text: One side of the war has sent a child as its envoy, on purpose, to shame you. The child does not know this. They recite their petition perfectly, then ask whether the Arbiter has a garden, because the child's own was burned.

choices.text: Show them your garden, and hear the petition fairly

effects.log: You show the child the border tree. You hear the petition on its merits. Their side is ashamed, as it should be.

choices.text: Send the child home with a rebuke for their elders

effects.log: The rebuke is read aloud in their pantheon's hall. They do not send a child again.

events.text: Seo Gyeol has counted the dead of the War in Heaven between {sov_war_a} and {sov_war_b}, gods and immortals and the mortals below who were in the way. They bring you the number on a single slip of paper and set it on your chair without a word.

choices.text: Read it aloud to both envoys

effects.log: The envoys listen to the number. Neither argues with it. The next battle is smaller.

choices.text: Keep it in your sleeve

effects.log: You carry the slip of paper through every hearing of the war. Your sentences grow shorter, and harder.

events.text: A delegate of {sov_war_b} leaves a casket of starlight on your shelf of evidence, carefully, as if it were evidence. It is a bribe. They know you know. It is meant to see what you do.

choices.text: Return it publicly, before {sov_war_a}

effects.log: Both sides watch you return it. Neither believes you could be bought, now. It is worth more than the casket.

choices.text: Give it to the mortals below whom the war has burned

effects.log: The starlight goes down as rain over a burned country. Both sides are furious, and the country is not.

events.text: On the night of the Heavenly Calendar's great turning, both armies of the war light lamps along the front and do not fight. It is an old custom. This year each side sends you a lamp, and asks you to say which side's burned longer.

choices.text: Burn both on your chair, together

effects.log: Both lamps go out at the same breath. You report it. Nobody believes you, and everybody likes it.

choices.text: Refuse to measure lamps

effects.log: You say a truce is not a contest. Both sides grumble, and light more lamps next year.

events.text: Veterans of the war you ended by decree have nowhere to go: a god who fought for a century does not know how to stop. Several of them have taken to standing guard outside your hall, unasked, in full armour, against no one.

choices.text: Let them stand

effects.log: Your hall has an honour guard of former enemies. They stand back to back. Litigants are very polite.

choices.text: Give them work as couriers of the Court

effects.log: They carry decrees now, not swords. Some are good at it. A few are very fast.

events.text: A god has lost one child on each side of the war: the children chose different pantheons long ago. The parent brings no petition, only asks the Arbiter to say aloud that both children were right.

choices.text: Say it

effects.log: You say it before your chair. The parent goes home. Both pantheons hear what you said, and neither can object.

choices.text: Say only that both were brave

effects.log: It is less, and it is true. The parent nods, and you see it is not enough, and it is all you could give.

events.text: You walk an old battlefield of heaven from before your time, where two forgotten pantheons fought until both faded. Nothing grows. The ground still remembers which side each stone was on.

choices.text: Sit and hear the stones

effects.log: You hear an old quarrel nobody alive remembers. You judge it, aloud, alone. The ground is a little quieter after.

choices.text: Plant a seed from the border tree

effects.log: It grows, slowly, and its roots go to both sides of the old line. Na Puleum hears of it and comes to see.

events.text: {sov_corrupt} has written a price list for their domain and nailed it to the gate of their hall: so much faith for a season, so much for a miracle, so much to be left alone. A copy has been nailed to your chair as well, by someone who wanted you to see it.

choices.text: Go and read the original at their gate

effects.log: The list is real and in their own hand. Under it, the gate is worn smooth by petitioners.

choices.text: Summon {sov_corrupt} to your chair

effects.log: They come, smiling, with gifts for every clerk. Seo Gyeol refuses theirs very loudly.

choices.text: Ask the mortals below what they have paid

effects.log: The answer rises in a hundred thousand prayers at once. Some of them have paid with their harvests, some with their children's names.

events.text: {sov_corrupt}'s defence is simple and terrible: every god sells. Worship for blessings is the oldest trade in heaven; they have only written the prices down. "Judge me," they say, "and you judge every temple in the four pantheons."

choices.text: Rule the difference: a gift is not a price

effects.log: Seo Gyeol writes the distinction in a page that every god in heaven reads that year. Many of them are uncomfortable.

choices.text: Accept the challenge: audit every temple

effects.log: It takes three centuries. You find a little of {sov_corrupt} in every pantheon, and a great deal in one.

choices.text: Turn their own ledger against them

ok.log: Their ledger shows they raised the price of rain in drought. That is not a trade. It is extortion, and you say so.

fail.log: Their ledger is cleverer than you are. The case stalls, and {sov_corrupt} leaves still smiling.

events.text: Below, a river has stopped in the middle of a valley because nobody paid for it to run. Its water stands like a wall of glass. Children throw stones at it and the stones stick. The valley's people are leaving.

choices.text: Start the river yourself, and bill {sov_corrupt}

effects.log: You put your hand to the water and it moves. Above, {sov_corrupt} receives an Arbiter's bill and does not laugh.

choices.text: Leave it standing as evidence until the sentence

effects.log: The glass river stands for a year. The gods of all four pantheons come to look at it. It is the best witness you have.

events.text: Sentence day for {sov_corrupt}. The four envoys are present; so are a thousand mortal prayers, which Seo Gyeol has written out and stacked on the bench beside the god. {sov_corrupt} has stopped smiling and is watching you, finally, as an equal.

choices.text: Strip the price list and bind them to give freely for an age

effects.log: They must answer every prayer of their domain for a thousand years, unpaid. It is a strange sentence, and it holds.

choices.text: Take their domain into the Arbiter's keeping

effects.log: Their domain is held by the empty space, unworshipped, while a new god is found. Heaven is uneasy at the precedent.

choices.text: Seal them, as the oldest law allows

effects.log: The seal is laid in silence. The four envoys rise together, which they do not often do.

events.text: A clerk of {sov_corrupt}'s hall, a small grey god named Baek Narae, comes to your door in the middle of the night. They have kept their master's accounts for four hundred years, two books of them: one for heaven, one true. They have brought the true one.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Kept Two Books

choices.text: Take the book and shelter the clerk

effects.log: Baek Narae sleeps on a bench in your hall for the first time in years without fear. The book is heavy.

choices.text: Ask why now, after four hundred years

effects.log: "Because there is an Arbiter now," they say simply. "Before, there was no one to bring it to."

events.text: {sov_corrupt} accuses Baek Narae of theft. The true book is their master's property, the corrupt god says, and a clerk who steals it is a thief whatever is written inside. It is, again, a fair point of law.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Kept Two Books

choices.text: Rule that a true account belongs to all it touches

effects.log: Seo Gyeol writes it with a certain satisfaction. A clerk's duty to the truth is above their duty to a master.

choices.text: Rule it theft, but pardon the thief

effects.log: Baek Narae is a thief and is pardoned. The book is evidence. It is untidy, and it works.

events.text: Baek Narae has become famous. Clerks of a dozen halls now come to your door at night with second books. Most are honest; a few are forgeries, made to ruin a rival. Seo Gyeol cannot tell them apart fast enough.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Kept Two Books

choices.text: Make Baek Narae the examiner of second books

effects.log: The grey clerk reads every second book in heaven. They can smell a forgery. They are, at last, happy.

choices.text: Stop taking second books at night

effects.log: You hear only books brought in daylight, with the clerk's name on them. Fewer come. Those that do are true.
