events.text: The god you sealed sits behind your seal, in a hall of grey light at the edge of heaven. Seo Gyeol reports that visitors have begun to come: lesser gods, and one immortal, who stand at the seal and talk to the god inside. It is not forbidden.

choices.text: Let them come

effects.log: You let them. Seo Gyeol keeps a list of names. Some are surprising.

choices.text: Forbid it: a seal is silence

effects.log: The visitors are turned back. One of them, an immortal, weeps at the gate and goes home.

events.text: Among the visitors is the sealed god's child, small and serious, who comes every year on the same day and sits with their back against your seal, reading aloud. Seo Gyeol has checked what they read. It is your judgement. All of it. Every year.

choices.text: Go and sit with the child

effects.log: The child stops reading when you come. Then, without a word, they hand you the page and you read the next line aloud.

choices.text: Leave them to it

effects.log: You do not interfere. The child grows up reading your judgement, and in time knows it better than you.

events.text: The sealed god's child, grown, petitions you for parole for their parent: not freedom, only one day a century outside the seal. They argue from your own judgement, line by line. They are very good.

choices.text: Grant it: one day a century

effects.log: Once a century the sealed god walks the edge of heaven for a day, and goes back without being told.

choices.text: Refuse, and argue back from the same lines

ok.log: You win. The child bows and says, "Next century, then." They mean it kindly.

fail.log: You lose the argument and refuse anyway. The child sees it. So does Seo Gyeol.

events.text: On the sealed god's day outside, they come to your chair. They are thinner than when you sealed them, and quieter. They say their child turned out better than they deserved, and that they would like you to know they know it.

choices.text: Tell them their child is the best advocate in heaven

effects.log: The sealed god nods and smiles and goes back behind the seal an hour early.

choices.text: Say nothing, and offer them a seat

effects.log: You sit together for the rest of the day without speaking. At dusk they rise, bow, and go back.

events.text: Below the clouds, a high priest of {sov_corrupt} grew rich collecting their god's prices from the faithful. Now that heaven is judging their god, the mortal is terrified and has sent up a prayer to you, of all gods, begging mercy.
events.arc: The Priest Who Kept the Price

choices.text: Answer the prayer

effects.log: You answer: give it back. The priest stares at the sky for a long time.

choices.text: Leave mortal priests to the mortal world

effects.log: The prayer is not answered. The priest flees their temple in the night with what they can carry.

events.text: The priest is giving it back. Town by town below, they walk barefoot, returning coin and grain and the names of children that families gave to the temple in pawn. Mortals follow them. Some throw stones. More, by now, walk with them.
events.arc: The Priest Who Kept the Price

choices.text: Send rain ahead of them on the road

effects.log: A soft rain falls a day ahead of the priest wherever they go. It is not your domain. Nobody complains.

choices.text: Do nothing: penance is theirs alone

effects.log: The priest walks for nine years. When they finish, they build a small shrine with no god in it.

events.text: The priest has died, old, below. The Silent Hall sends word: their soul will not get in the Ferryman's boat until it has asked the Arbiter one thing. Mok Dami brings it. "Did I give back enough?"
events.arc: The Priest Who Kept the Price

choices.text: "Yes."

effects.log: Mok Dami carries the word down to the river. Baekun reports the soul crossed without looking back.

choices.text: "Nobody gives back enough. You gave back what you could."

effects.log: The soul takes a long time with that. Then it gets in the boat.

events.text: Your seal on {sov_corrupt} is thinning. Seo Gyeol can see light through it at dawn. It is not that the god is stronger: it is that fewer and fewer gods believe the seal is right, and a seal of the Arbiter holds only on heaven's belief.

choices.text: Find out who has stopped believing

effects.log: You walk the four pantheons for a decade, asking. The answers are uncomfortable and honest.

choices.text: Pour your own will into the seal

ok.log: It holds, and you are tired for a century.

fail.log: It holds, barely, and costs you.

events.text: What you learned: the sealed god's worshippers below never stopped praying to them, and their prayers wear the seal thin from the inside. They are not wicked. They simply loved their god, prices and all.

choices.text: Go below and speak to the worshippers

effects.log: You appear in their temple as a stranger and listen. You come back understanding why the seal is thin.

choices.text: Turn their prayers to the god who holds the domain now

effects.log: The prayers go elsewhere. The seal thickens. The worshippers below feel something has been taken from them.

events.text: You have a choice now that the seal cannot make for you: renew it with a new judgement, open it with one, or leave it to thin out on its own and see what heaven believes.

choices.text: Hear the case again, from the start

effects.log: A second hearing of the sealed god. The sentence is shorter. The seal that follows is thick as stone.

choices.text: Let it thin

effects.log: The seal fades over a century. The god walks out, quiet. Their worshippers below rejoice. You watch it all.

events.text: {sov_corrupt} answers the charge with a charge: the god who first brought them before you, a god of Fate under Unmyeong the Weaver, is the worse offender, they say, selling glimpses of the Book of Fates to the highest bidder. They have proof.

choices.text: Hear both cases at once

effects.log: Two corrupt gods at one bench. They watch each other more closely than they watch you.

choices.text: Finish the first case before the second

effects.log: Precedent: one case at a time. {sov_corrupt} is furious; their accuser is relieved, too relieved.

events.text: Unmyeong the Weaver comes in person, which Fate does not do. Their servant is guilty, they say, and they would rather you sentence the servant than that the Silent Hall be seen to protect them. Mok Dami stands behind the Weaver, unhappy.

choices.text: Sentence the servant fairly

effects.log: The servant is sentenced. Both corrupt gods are now under your scales. Heaven is shocked at how many there are.

choices.text: Refuse the Weaver's haste

effects.log: You make the Silent Hall wait for the full hearing. Unmyeong is displeased; Mok Dami is grateful.

events.text: After two corrupt gods, every pantheon is quietly cleaning its halls. Gods who sold blessings are buying them back; ledgers are being burned. Seo Gyeol wonders aloud whether you should stop it, since burned ledgers are evidence too.

choices.text: Let them clean

effects.log: Heaven is a little more honest for an age, and has a great deal less paper.

choices.text: Order every ledger brought to you first

effects.log: Ten thousand ledgers arrive. You read some. You burn the rest yourself, so that nobody burns them in secret.

events.text: {sov_corrupt} visits privately, without a petition. They offer you a share of their domain's worship, forever, if the case against them is simply never heard. They are polite about it. They think everyone has a price, even the empty space.

choices.text: Have Seo Gyeol write the offer into the case

effects.log: The offer is now evidence. {sov_corrupt} stops being polite.

choices.text: Laugh, and show them the door

effects.log: They go. You notice later that a clerk of yours was paid to listen at the door. You dismiss them.

events.text: Mortals below the domain of {sov_corrupt} have heard their god is being judged. They are afraid: if the god is sealed, who will bring the rain, even at a price? Their prayers rise up to your chair in a frightened flock.

choices.text: Promise them the rain will come either way

effects.log: You send the promise down in a dream. You will have to keep it. Below, they sleep.

choices.text: Let the god's fate be the god's

effects.log: The mortals go on fearing. The case goes on. Fear is not evidence.

events.text: The keepers of the seals of heaven, a quiet order older than the pantheons, come to inspect your seal. They tap it, listen, and write in a small book. "Firm," they say, "but lonely. A seal works better if someone visits it."

choices.text: Visit it once a decade

effects.log: You visit. The seal grows firmer for it. So, oddly, does the god behind it.

choices.text: Thank them, and change nothing

effects.log: The keepers bow and go. In their book, under your seal, they write "lonely" twice.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has issued a warrant for {sov_corrupt}, and so have you, and the two warrants contradict each other on one point: whether the god may keep their hall while they are judged. Two couriers stand at the hall's gate with two papers.

choices.text: Withdraw yours: one warrant is enough

effects.log: The Court's warrant stands. The Court is pleased. You are a little less than you were.

choices.text: Meet the Court and write one warrant together

effects.log: One warrant, two seals. It is the first such paper in heaven. Seo Gyeol frames a copy.

events.text: You dream of the god behind your seal. In the dream they are not angry; they are explaining their price list to you, patiently, line by line, and every line makes sense, and you wake not knowing which of you was being judged.

choices.text: Write the dream down

effects.log: Seo Gyeol files it under no heading. It is the only page in the Book of Precedent marked "doubt".

choices.text: Tell no one, and visit the seal

effects.log: You stand at the seal in the morning. Behind it, the god is asleep, and smiling.

events.text: A god of a small domain, the wind over one mountain, brings you their accounts unasked. They have never charged for a single breeze. They are poor and they are proud, and they want the Arbiter to say so in writing.

choices.text: Write it

effects.log: One page in the Book: an honest god. They hang it over their mountain. Below, the wind is sweeter that year.

choices.text: Ask them to stand witness in the next case

effects.log: They stand witness against a corrupt god, and the contrast is all the evidence you need.

events.text: Someone has put a coin of heaven in the left pan of your scales in the night. Only one coin. The scales tip, very slightly. Seo Gyeol is horrified. You are, for a moment, curious who thinks so little of you.

choices.text: Leave the coin and judge the next case anyway

effects.log: You judge with the coin in the pan. The judgement is fair. The coin is gone the next morning.

choices.text: Put a coin in the other pan

effects.log: The scales come level. Whoever did it never tries again. Heaven hears, and laughs.

events.text: {sov_pantheon} stands over half of heaven, and the other three pantheons meet in secret to decide what to do about it, each meeting in its own way: one in a dream, one in a storm, one in a field at midnight. All three have invited the Arbiter.

choices.text: Go to none of them, and tell {sov_pantheon} nothing

effects.log: You stay at your chair. All three meetings go on without you; all three wonder what you know.

choices.text: Go to all three, openly, and say so

effects.log: You go to each and tell each that you went to the others. They are horrified, then relieved: at least the Arbiter is honest.

choices.text: Tell {sov_pantheon} the meetings exist

effects.log: It is the truth. {sov_pantheon} thanks you warmly. The other three never invite you again.

events.text: At the meeting in the storm, the three pantheons decide on war. They will strike {sov_pantheon} together in the next century, unless the Arbiter can give them another way to stop being swallowed.

choices.text: Propose a Concord of Domains: no pantheon may hold more than four

effects.log: You write it on the back of a raincloud. The three sign. Now it must be put to the fourth.

choices.text: Promise to judge every domain {sov_pantheon} takes, one by one

effects.log: A hundred cases, each a domain. It will take an age. The three agree to wait for it.

choices.text: Say that war is their right, and you will judge after

effects.log: The three go to war. Heaven shakes for a century. Your scales wait for the end.

events.text: You bring the Concord of Domains to {sov_pantheon}'s great hall, where their gods stand on every stair. They read it. They are strong enough to refuse it and everyone knows it. Their eldest asks what the Arbiter will do if they say no.

choices.text: "Nothing. Heaven will."

ok.log: The eldest looks out at three pantheons waiting under a storm, and signs. The Concord binds heaven.

fail.log: They do not believe you. They refuse. The three pantheons begin to gather.

choices.text: "Judge you, domain by domain, until you sign."

effects.log: It takes three centuries of hearings. Domain by domain they lose, and at last they sign to stop losing.

events.text: The Concord of Domains has held for a long age. {sov_pantheon} keeps its four domains and complains about it in every season. But its gods have started to come to your chair with ordinary quarrels, like any others, as if they were no longer the largest.

choices.text: Treat them as any other

effects.log: You hear {sov_pantheon}'s smallest quarrels as gravely as anyone's. It is the best thing that has happened to them.

choices.text: Remind them, now and then, of what they were

effects.log: They keep the Concord more carefully for it, and like you less.

events.text: {sov_pantheon} has begun to build. Its newest hall reaches out over the empty space between the four pantheons, a roof of gold that will, when finished, cover your chair. They say it is a gift: the Arbiter should not sit in the rain.
events.arc: A Roof Over the Empty Space

choices.text: Refuse the roof

effects.log: You send their architects home. The half-built roof hangs over the empty space like a hand.

choices.text: Let them finish it, and judge under it

effects.log: The roof is finished. You judge under gold. Every litigant from another pantheon looks up before they speak.

events.text: The half-built roof is still hanging over the empty space, and its shadow falls on your chair at noon. Litigants of the other three pantheons have begun to wait until afternoon to bring their cases. {sov_pantheon} says the roof is theirs to leave.
events.arc: A Roof Over the Empty Space

choices.text: Take it down with your own hands

ok.log: Gold beam by gold beam, you take it down over a year and send it back. {sov_pantheon} receives it in silence.

fail.log: The roof is too strong. You manage half. The other half hangs crooked and stays.

choices.text: Move your chair out of its shadow

effects.log: You move the chair three paces. The empty space has a new centre. Seo Gyeol has to redraw every map.

events.text: Under the gold roof, it has been centuries since a litigant of the other three pantheons came before your chair. They go to the Heavenly Court now, or to war, or to no one. Your hall is warm and dry and full of {sov_pantheon}'s quarrels only.
events.arc: A Roof Over the Empty Space

choices.text: Tear the roof down, at last

effects.log: You tear it down in a single night. {sov_pantheon} is furious. In the morning three envoys are waiting on the bench.

choices.text: Go out from under it to the others

effects.log: You take your chair on the road, to each pantheon in turn. It is slow and hard and it brings them back.

events.text: The Throne of {sov_realm} stands empty, and its claimants are at war. Three of them have sent their genealogies to your chair, each a thousand pages long, each proving their own right and the others' bastardy. Seo Gyeol has a headache already.

choices.text: Read all three genealogies

effects.log: You read them all. Two of the three are forged in the same places. The third is real, and its claimant is the weakest.

choices.text: Refuse: the Arbiter does not crown

effects.log: The claimants go back to their war. It is not your throne. It is your heaven it burns.

events.text: The rightful claimant of {sov_realm}, by the genealogies, is Yeo Danbi, a quiet god of the archives who never wanted the throne and is now being hunted by the other two. They come to your hall and ask you not to tell anyone what you found.

choices.text: Keep their secret

effects.log: You keep it. The war goes on between the forgers. Yeo Danbi lives, unknown, in your hall.

choices.text: Publish the truth

effects.log: The forgeries are named. Both false claimants lose half their followers in a day. Yeo Danbi is in more danger than ever.

choices.text: Ask them what they want

effects.log: Yeo Danbi wants the throne to stay empty. They say an empty throne cannot start a war.

events.text: The two false claimants of {sov_realm} come to your chair together, for the first time allies: if the genealogies are true, they say, then neither of them has a right; so let the throne go to whoever wins. They want the Arbiter to bless a duel.

choices.text: Bless no duel: let the throne pass to Yeo Danbi

effects.log: You rule it. Yeo Danbi takes the throne weeping and holds it, badly, gently, for an age.

choices.text: Hold a Trial of Judgement between them

effects.log: They fight before your chair. The winner takes {sov_realm}. The loser lives, which is your one condition.

choices.text: Rule the throne empty, by Yeo Danbi's wish

effects.log: An empty throne of heaven, by law. Nobody can sit it. Strangely, the war stops.

events.text: Long after, Yeo Danbi comes to your hall with the crown of {sov_realm} in a cloth bag. Whatever the throne became, they say, it began at your chair, and they want the Arbiter to keep the crown while heaven decides whether it needs one.

choices.text: Keep it in the drawer with Jang Murae's scroll

effects.log: The crown sits beside the oldest judgement in heaven. It is a very quiet drawer.

choices.text: Give it back: a crown kept by a judge is a crown judged

effects.log: Yeo Danbi takes it home. They put it on a shelf and do not wear it.

events.text: A decree in your hand and under your seal has been read aloud in the war-camps of {sov_realm}: the Arbiter, it says, recognises one claimant as rightful. You never wrote it. Seo Gyeol holds a copy up to the light and says the seal is perfect.

choices.text: Denounce it at once

effects.log: Your denial goes out under your true seal. Now there are two seals of the Arbiter in heaven, and nobody knows which is true.

choices.text: Find the forger first

ok.log: The forger is a clerk of the claimant who benefits. You find them before the denial goes out, and the claimant falls.

fail.log: The trail runs cold in the camps. The forged decree is believed for a year.

events.text: Two seals of the Arbiter: the true one, and one so good that you yourself cannot tell them apart. Every decree you send now will be doubted. The only answer is a seal nobody can forge.

choices.text: Make every decree carry a line only you could write

effects.log: Each decree now holds one sentence of true judgement, in your voice. Forgers can copy a seal. They cannot copy that.

choices.text: Break your seal and carve a new one

effects.log: The old seal is broken before all four envoys. The new one is plainer, and nobody has seen it yet.

events.text: The forger, found at last, is brought before you: a very gifted clerk who copied your seal out of admiration before anyone paid them to. They have copied every judgement in your Book too, by hand, for practice.

choices.text: Sentence them to keep the second Book

effects.log: The forger becomes a clerk of your hall under Seo Gyeol. Their hand is perfect. Seo Gyeol checks every page anyway.

choices.text: Sentence them to the Heavenly Court's justice

effects.log: The Court seals the forger for a century. They go quietly, still copying in the air with one finger.

events.text: Small gods who belong to no pantheon, gods of a single well or a single hill or one kind of moth, have banded together. They call themselves the Lesser Hall and they want the Arbiter to recognise them as a fifth pantheon.

choices.text: Hear their petition properly

effects.log: The Lesser Hall is a thousand gods of almost nothing. Together, Seo Gyeol notes, they hold a tenth of all mortal prayer.

choices.text: Rule that a pantheon is recognised by the four, not you

effects.log: They go to the four. The four laugh. The Lesser Hall comes back to your bench.

events.text: The four pantheons object: a fifth would mean a new seat at every table, and the Concord of heaven would have to be rewritten. The Lesser Hall's speaker, a god of the moths that come to lamps, says they only want to be counted.

choices.text: Recognise them

effects.log: A fifth pantheon, by the Arbiter's judgement. The four are furious for a century. Then they get used to the moths.

choices.text: Count them, but give them no seat

effects.log: Seo Gyeol writes them into the census of heaven. They are counted. They go home not quite satisfied.

events.text: The Lesser Hall has become a voice in heaven. In the last crisis, the four great pantheons were deadlocked, and it was the moths, the wells and the hills that tipped it. The speaker comes to thank you, and to say that they now understand why the four were afraid.

choices.text: "Then you will be careful."

effects.log: The moth-god bows. The Lesser Hall stays small on purpose for an age.

choices.text: "Then you will be heard."

effects.log: The Lesser Hall grows. Heaven has five voices now, and is louder, and more balanced for it.

events.text: Seo Gyeol has noticed something you had not: in every case between {sov_pantheon} and a weaker pantheon this century, you have ruled for the weaker one. Every ruling was fair. Together they lean.

choices.text: Correct it: judge the next cases blind

effects.log: You hear the next ten cases with the pantheons' names hidden. {sov_pantheon} wins four of them.

choices.text: Keep leaning: balance is your office

effects.log: You lean, knowingly. {sov_pantheon} notices. So does the Court.

events.text: {sov_pantheon} brings a formal complaint: the Arbiter leans. They have counted the rulings as Seo Gyeol did. They are not wrong, and they know you know it.

choices.text: Admit it, and explain why

effects.log: You explain balance. {sov_pantheon} listens and says, "Then you are a pantheon too, Arbiter, of one." It stings.

choices.text: Recuse yourself from their cases for a century

effects.log: For a century, {sov_pantheon}'s cases go to the Heavenly Court. They do worse there, and come back.

events.text: Because you leaned, the weaker pantheons have grown. One of them is now nearly as large as {sov_pantheon} was. Its envoy comes to you with a request you have heard before, from the other side: help us against the largest.

choices.text: Lean the other way now

effects.log: You lean back. Balance is a pendulum. Seo Gyeol writes "again" in the margin.

choices.text: Stop leaning at all

effects.log: You judge level from then on. Heaven finds its own balance, roughly.

events.text: {sov_pantheon} sends you a new chair: carved from the heartwood of their oldest hall, padded, beautiful. A note with it says the Arbiter's old chair is shabby, which it is.

choices.text: Keep the old chair

effects.log: You thank them and keep sitting where you sat. The new chair stands in a corner, unused, for an age.

choices.text: Give the new chair to the litigants' bench

effects.log: Litigants of all four pantheons now sit on {sov_pantheon}'s heartwood. They find it very comfortable.

events.text: The census of domains is due, and {sov_pantheon} claims nine of the twelve. Seo Gyeol has found that two of the nine are claimed by a single god of that pantheon who has not been seen for a thousand years.

choices.text: Rule the absent god's domains vacant

effects.log: Two domains vacant. {sov_pantheon} is weaker by two by morning. Heaven exhales.

choices.text: Send to find the absent god

effects.log: The search takes a century. The god is found asleep in a dream, and wakes, and is furious with everyone.

events.text: A god whose hall stood in {sov_realm} has lost it to the war of the Thrones. They do not want to petition anyone. They want to know whether there is a law of heaven that says a god must have a hall at all.

choices.text: "No. There is not."

effects.log: They stay in the empty space, hall-less and content. Others come after them.

choices.text: Give them a corner of your own hall

effects.log: A god of nowhere in particular now keeps your lamps. They are very good at it.

events.text: A herald of one of the claimants of {sov_realm} arrives to announce their master's victory, a little too early. The battle is still going. The herald, realising this, asks if they might wait in your hall until it is over.

choices.text: Let them wait

effects.log: They wait two days, very embarrassed. Their master loses. They ask if they can stay.

choices.text: Send them back to the battle

effects.log: They go, unhappily. You hear they arrived in time to announce the defeat instead.

events.text: A young god of {sov_pantheon} has been sent to study at your chair, to learn the law. They are clever and arrogant and plainly meant to report back. They ask why a pantheon that holds half of heaven should be judged by someone who holds none.

choices.text: Make them judge a case of their own pantheon

effects.log: They judge it. They rule against their own hall, honestly, and go home a different god.

choices.text: Answer: "Because I hold none."

effects.log: They write it down and send it home. {sov_pantheon} reads it and does not reply.

events.text: The gods of the twelve domains gather to renew the Concord of Domains, as they do once an age. It is a dull ceremony of seals. The Arbiter, by custom, sits at the head and says nothing at all.

choices.text: Say nothing, as custom asks

effects.log: It goes by in a day. Twelve seals. Your silence is the thirteenth.

choices.text: Say one thing: thank them

effects.log: The twelve gods are startled. Nobody has ever thanked them for signing. They sign more carefully.

events.text: You dream that the four pantheons are four weights on a single beam, and you are the pin it turns on. It is very quiet in the dream. The pin does not move. Nothing can move without it, and it never goes anywhere.

choices.text: Accept that this is your life

effects.log: You wake rested, oddly. The pin does not need to go anywhere.

choices.text: Resolve to walk somewhere, once

effects.log: You take a day away from the chair and walk to the edge of heaven and back. Nothing falls.

events.text: Pyo Ara, an auditor of the Heavenly Court, arrives with an abacus of black beads and a polite smile. The Court has asked them to audit the stability of heaven, which the Arbiter is said to keep. "I would like to see your figures," they say.

choices.text: Show them everything

effects.log: You open the Book and your own notes. Pyo Ara works through the night, beads clicking, and says "hm" eleven times.

choices.text: Ask what the Court means by stability

effects.log: Pyo Ara stops. "No one has asked that," they admit. They write the question on the first page of their audit.

choices.text: Refuse: the scales are not the Court's to count

effects.log: Pyo Ara bows and leaves. The Court writes that the Arbiter keeps no accounts. It is almost true.

events.text: Pyo Ara's audit is finished. Stability in heaven, by their count, is real; but a third of it, they say, is fear of the Arbiter, not trust in the law. "If you vanished tomorrow," they ask, "how much of it would stay?"

choices.text: Ask them to help you find out

effects.log: Together you design a test: a century in which you judge nothing unless asked twice. Heaven holds, mostly.

choices.text: Thank them, and change how you judge

effects.log: You judge more slowly, explain more. Fewer gods fear you; more of them cite you.

choices.text: Tell them fear is a kind of trust

effects.log: Pyo Ara writes it down without comment. Their next audit is shorter.

events.text: A century later, Pyo Ara audits heaven again, unasked. They bring you one figure only: the part of stability that is fear has fallen by half. They seem, for an auditor, quite moved.

choices.text: Ask them to audit you every century

effects.log: Pyo Ara agrees. The black beads come every century after, like a season.

choices.text: Ask them what the other half is

effects.log: "Habit," they say. "Which is the next best thing to trust, and lasts longer."

events.text: Pyo Ara is in trouble. The Heavenly Court has charged them with exceeding their office: an auditor audits clerks, not Arbiters, and their audit of you embarrassed the Court's higher rungs. They have come to your hall, not to ask for help, but to say goodbye.

choices.text: Offer to stand as their witness

effects.log: Pyo Ara stares at you. "The Arbiter as witness for the auditor of the Arbiter," they say. "The Court will hate it."

choices.text: Offer them a post in your hall instead

effects.log: They refuse gently. "If I leave the Court for you, I prove the Court right."

events.text: At the Court, before a bench of the highest rungs, you testify that the auditor did their duty: that the scales are better for being counted. The highest judge of the Court asks you, with great courtesy, whether the Arbiter is also offering to be audited by the Court.

choices.text: "Yes. By Pyo Ara."

effects.log: The bench murmurs. It is a bargain: they cannot convict an auditor the Arbiter accepts. Pyo Ara is cleared.

choices.text: "No. The scales are counted, not ruled."

ok.log: Your distinction holds. Pyo Ara is cleared on it, and the Court has a new page of law.

fail.log: The bench is not persuaded. Pyo Ara is demoted three rungs, and thanks you anyway.

events.text: Pyo Ara is old now. They bring you the black abacus as a gift: their last audit is done, and they would like the Arbiter to keep the beads, so that someone in heaven still counts the one who counts.

choices.text: Keep it beside the Book

effects.log: You learn to use it, badly. Every century you count yourself, and write the figure down where anyone can read it.

choices.text: Give it to Seo Gyeol's student

effects.log: The young clerk is terrified of it, then devoted to it. The audits go on.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has accused {sov_accused}, and the warrant is already written. They have come to the empty space instead of the Court's ladder, to ask whether the Arbiter will hear an appeal before there is anything to appeal.

choices.text: Hear them, but only to listen

effects.log: You listen. {sov_accused} talks for a whole night. In the morning you send them to the Court, with your notes.

choices.text: Refuse: the Court must judge first

effects.log: They go to the ladder. Seo Gyeol watches them climb it and says nothing.

choices.text: Take the case from the Court

effects.log: You claim it as the Arbiter's. The Court is affronted, and has to yield, and remembers.

events.text: The case of {sov_accused}, as Seo Gyeol has laid it out: the Court's warrant rests on a single line in the Book of Fates, which says the accused will do the crime, not that they have done it. They are accused of their future.

choices.text: Rule that no one is guilty of a fate

effects.log: It is a great precedent. The Court is shaken. Every god under a fate-warrant in heaven writes to you that year.

choices.text: Rule that the warrant may stand, but no sentence

effects.log: {sov_accused} is watched, not punished. The Court accepts it. The accused does not, quite.

events.text: Years after your ruling, {sov_accused} comes back. The fate was right: they did the crime, small, and late, and in anger. They are standing in front of your chair to say so, before anyone else does. They want to know whether your precedent still holds.

choices.text: It holds: now they are guilty of the act, not the fate

effects.log: You judge the act. The sentence is light, because the act was. The precedent stands.

choices.text: Admit the precedent cost something

effects.log: You say it aloud. Pyo Ara, if they hear of it, will write it down. {sov_accused} bows and takes the sentence.

events.text: You hold a post on the Heavenly Court's ladder and you sit the Arbiter's chair. Today the same case has come to both. Seo Gyeol and a clerk of the Court stand at your door with the same file, each waiting for you to say which one of you will hear it.

choices.text: Give it to the Court and step off the bench

effects.log: You recuse yourself from both. The case is heard by others. You are less, and more trusted.

choices.text: Hear it as Arbiter

effects.log: The Court takes it as a slight. Your rung on the ladder grows colder.

events.text: The Court has begun, quietly, to send you the cases it does not want: those that would embarrass a high rung, those where a pantheon would be angry whatever the ruling. Your bench is full of the cases nobody else will touch.

choices.text: Hear them all

effects.log: You hear them. Heaven sees the Arbiter judge what the Court would not. The Court sees it too, and is ashamed, a little.

choices.text: Send them back with a note

effects.log: Your note says: the Court's courage is the Court's. The cases come back up the ladder, and are heard, badly.

events.text: A high judge of the Court comes to your hall at night, without robes, and asks how you bear it: deciding when every side will hate you. They have been on the ladder for ten thousand years and they are tired.

choices.text: Tell them about the crooked scales

effects.log: You show them the weight in the pan. They look at it a long time. "So you are not sure either," they say, comforted.

choices.text: Make them tea and say nothing useful

effects.log: They drink three cups and go home. They come back every century, at night.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has exiled a god from heaven, and the exile is camped at the edge of the empty space, which, being no one's, is not quite heaven. They are within the letter of the sentence and they know it. They ask the Arbiter to let them stay.

choices.text: Let them stay

effects.log: The exile stays in the empty space. The Court protests that you have made a loophole of your hall.

choices.text: Rule that the empty space is heaven, for exiles too

effects.log: The exile is sent on. The precedent closes a gap the Court had not noticed. The exile curses you all the way down.

events.text: The exile in the empty space has been there a century and has begun to teach. Other gods come to hear them, gods of the Court's own ladder among them. What they teach is how the Court judges, and where it is wrong.

choices.text: Hear their teaching yourself

effects.log: You sit with the class. The exile is bitter, and mostly right. You write two of their points into the Book.

choices.text: Ask them to stop, for the peace

effects.log: They stop. The class disperses. The exile sits alone again, and you feel it.

events.text: The exile asks you to carry their appeal to the Court. Not for themselves, they say: for the points you wrote in your Book. If the Arbiter has accepted them, the Court must at least read them.

choices.text: Carry the appeal up the ladder

ok.log: The Court reads the points. Two laws change. The exile's sentence is shortened, which they did not ask for.

fail.log: The Court will not read an exile's words in any hand. You come back down the ladder with the appeal unopened.

choices.text: Carry it as your own judgement

effects.log: You put your name to the points and send them up. The Court reads them as the Arbiter's. The exile is not mentioned.

events.text: Unmyeong the Weaver sends a page from the Book of Fates for your judgement. It holds the fate of a mortal below: in forty years, they will start a war that drowns three kingdoms. The Weaver wants to know whether heaven may change a fate to stop it.
events.arc: A Line in the Book of Fates

choices.text: Rule that it may not

effects.log: The page goes back unchanged. The Weaver, oddly, seems relieved.

choices.text: Rule that it may, if the mortal is asked

effects.log: You send for the mortal's dream. You will ask them, in their sleep, whether they want a different life.

events.text: The mortal in the dream is a child, eight years old, who is building a tower of pebbles on a riverbank. You ask them whether they would like to be something other than what they will be. They do not understand. They want to show you the tower.
events.arc: A Line in the Book of Fates

choices.text: Look at the tower

effects.log: You look. It is a very good tower. You wake, and write to the Weaver that a child cannot consent to a fate.

choices.text: Show them, in the dream, what they will become

ok.log: They look at the war and weep and knock their tower down. When they wake, something in them has turned.

fail.log: They do not understand the war. They wake frightened and remember nothing.

events.text: Forty years on. Unmyeong sends the same page again. The line has changed by itself: the mortal built bridges instead, across the three kingdoms, and no war came. The Weaver wants to know if the Arbiter changed it. You do not know.
events.arc: A Line in the Book of Fates

choices.text: "I asked. They answered."

effects.log: The Weaver files the page under a heading of their own: fates that chose.

choices.text: "Nobody changed it. That is the point."

effects.log: The Weaver laughs, for the first time in your hearing.

events.text: A warrant has been brought to your chair for Mongsa the Sleeper, god of Dreams: in their sleep, which never ends, they walked into the dreams of a god of the Will of Heaven and left a nightmare there. Mongsa cannot be woken to answer.

choices.text: Hear the case in their dream

effects.log: Mok Dami takes you in. Mongsa's dream is very large and very gentle. They do not remember walking anywhere.

choices.text: Rule that the asleep are not liable

effects.log: A short precedent, and a popular one. The Will of Heaven complains that it is too popular.

events.text: In Mongsa's dream you find the path they walked, and at its end, the nightmare: not one they left, but one they took away. The god of the Will of Heaven had a nightmare already, and Mongsa carried part of it off. The warrant is for a kindness.

choices.text: Dismiss the warrant, and say why

effects.log: The Will of Heaven's god is embarrassed, then grateful. They send Mongsa a pillow.

choices.text: Dismiss it quietly, saying nothing

effects.log: The warrant is withdrawn. Only you and Mok Dami know. Mongsa sleeps on.

events.text: A young clerk of the Heavenly Court asks you how you climbed the ladder. You did not; the Arbiter's chair is not on it. They seem to find this more frightening than anything else about you.

choices.text: Tell them the chair is on the ground

effects.log: "So is everyone, at the bottom," you say. They write it down to think about later.

choices.text: Take them to sit in it, once

effects.log: They sit for a breath and jump up as if it were hot. "It is cold," they say, amazed.

events.text: The family of {sov_accused} come to your hall to ask what they should do while the Court judges their kin. They do not want you to interfere. They only want to know how long, and what to tell the children.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: you do not know

effects.log: They thank you for not lying. The eldest asks if they may come back each year to ask again.

choices.text: Ask the Court for a date

effects.log: The Court gives a date, grudgingly. The family keeps it like a feast day.

events.text: A warrant has been issued for the Eternal Arbiter, by a court of a faded pantheon that has had no gods for nine thousand years. It is legally perfect. Its charge is that you sit in their old ground. Seo Gyeol found it in the archive behind the nameless door.

choices.text: Answer it, to the empty court

effects.log: You stand before an empty bench and answer the charge. It takes an afternoon. You find yourself not guilty.

choices.text: Rule it expired

effects.log: The warrant is filed as expired. Seo Gyeol adds a note: "with respect."

events.text: A letter arrives from below the clouds, from a god the Court exiled long ago, now living as a mortal potter. They do not ask for anything. They only want to tell the Arbiter that the pots are good, and that they are happy, and that the Court was right.

choices.text: Write back

effects.log: Your letter goes down. The potter puts it in the kiln with the next firing, and the pots that year are excellent.

choices.text: Send it to the Court

effects.log: The Court reads it, unsure whether to be pleased. It is filed, oddly, under "mercy".

events.text: A blank page has turned up in the Book of Fates, bound between two lives that are full. Unmyeong the Weaver says blank pages appear when the Arbiter is about to make a judgement that no fate has foreseen.

choices.text: Look for the case

effects.log: You hear every case that week as if it were the one. One of them, about two gods and a well, turns out to be.

choices.text: Write "unknown" on it

effects.log: The Weaver is appalled. The page stays as you left it. In a thousand years, nobody has changed it.

events.text: The great bell of the Heavenly Court has rung once, unrung, in the night. By the Court's law, it means a judgement of the Court has been wrong. The Court sends a messenger to ask whether the Arbiter knows which.

choices.text: Find it

effects.log: You go through a decade of the Court's rulings. It is a small one: a god of moths, fined for a lamp. You reverse it.

choices.text: Say the Court must find its own

effects.log: The Court searches for a century. It finds three. The bell is quiet after.

events.text: The Heavenly Court proposes an exchange: one of its clerks to serve a century at your chair, and one of yours at theirs, so each may learn the other's law. Seo Gyeol says it is a fine idea, and plainly hopes they will not be the one sent.

choices.text: Send Seo Gyeol's student

effects.log: The student comes back after a century knowing every rung of the ladder, and a little less sure of the empty space.

choices.text: Accept the Court's clerk only

effects.log: The clerk from the Court is quiet and watchful and, by the end, the hardest worker you have.

events.text: Ok Saebyeok has fought in more Trials of Judgement than any god alive, for any side that asks, and lost only twice. They come to your hall between trials to ask a question that has troubled them for an age: is a champion who fights for anyone a mercenary?

choices.text: "No. You fight for the trial, not the side."

effects.log: Ok Saebyeok sits back, relieved. "Then I am a kind of clerk," they say, "with a sword."

choices.text: "Yes. Choose a side, once, and see."

effects.log: They look troubled for a long time. "I will think on it," they say, and fight their next trial worse.

events.text: Ok Saebyeok has been asked to champion two sides of the same trial: {sov_war_a} and {sov_war_b} both sent for them on the same morning. By custom, the champion goes to whoever asked first. Both asked at dawn exactly.

choices.text: Rule that they champion neither

effects.log: Two lesser champions fight instead. The trial is clumsier, and more honest.

choices.text: Let them fight both sides, alternate rounds

ok.log: The strangest trial in heaven: Ok Saebyeok against themselves, round by round. It ends level. Both sides accept.

fail.log: It is a farce. Both sides walk out. The clash goes on outside the hall.

events.text: Ok Saebyeok's two lost trials haunt them. They ask you to read both judgements again, the ones that went against their side: not to reverse them, they say, but to know whether they lost because they were wrong, or only because they were slower.

choices.text: Read them, and tell the truth

effects.log: One they lost fairly. The other, the side they fought for was right, and lost anyway. You tell them both.

choices.text: Tell them a trial judges the clash, not the champion

effects.log: It is your own law. Ok Saebyeok nods. It is not what they wanted to hear.

events.text: The trial Ok Saebyeok lost unjustly: the side that was right was a small god of a ford below, who lost their river to a larger god. Ok Saebyeok wants to go down and help them now, outside any trial, with their own hands.

choices.text: Let them go

effects.log: They go below and dig a new channel for the ford-god with a champion's strength. It takes a year. Heaven is amazed.

choices.text: Reopen the old case properly instead

effects.log: The case is heard again. The ford-god wins the river back by law. Ok Saebyeok watches from the gallery, satisfied.

events.text: Ok Saebyeok is old and wants one last trial, and they want it to be against you. Not for any clash: only so that the Arbiter of heaven has once, they say, felt the weight a champion carries into the hall.

choices.text: Accept

effects.log: You step down from the chair and take a champion's blade. Seo Gyeol has to judge. Their hands are shaking.

choices.text: Decline, gently

effects.log: Ok Saebyeok bows. "Then let me sit in your chair for one hour," they say. You let them.

events.text: The trial between the Arbiter and the champion lasts a whole day. Neither of you is trying to win, and both of you are trying not to lose, which is a different thing. At sunset Seo Gyeol stands up to judge.

choices.text: Fight to the end

ok.log: You win by a hair. Ok Saebyeok laughs on the floor of the hall and says it was the best trial of their life.

fail.log: You lose by a hair. Ok Saebyeok helps you up and says it was the best trial of their life.

choices.text: Ask Seo Gyeol to call it level

effects.log: Seo Gyeol calls it level. Both of you know it was not, and neither says which way.

events.text: Ok Saebyeok has faded, quietly, in their sleep. Their blade is brought to your hall by the champions of heaven, a hundred of them, who have agreed on one thing for the first time: that it should hang over the Arbiter's chair, beside the burnt beam and the cracked mirror.

choices.text: Hang it there

effects.log: The blade hangs over your chair. In every trial after, both champions bow to it first.

choices.text: Give it to the youngest champion present

effects.log: A young champion who has never fought takes it, terrified. You will see that blade again.

events.text: Heaven is unsteady, and your last decree has come back in a hundred unopened envelopes. Seo Gyeol has laid them in rows across the floor of your hall. One envelope, the hundred and first, has been opened, read, sealed again, and sent back with the rest.

choices.text: Find out who opened it

effects.log: A god of the Harvest. They read it, agreed, and were afraid to be the only one. They send apologies by return.

choices.text: Leave the envelopes where they lie

effects.log: The rows of envelopes stay on your floor for a decade. Litigants step around them, reading the seals.

events.text: The god of the Harvest who opened your decree has written again: if you send it once more, they will read it aloud in their hall, first, so that the others cannot pretend not to have received it. They are frightened, and they mean it.

choices.text: Send it again, to them first

effects.log: The decree is read aloud in the Harvest hall. One by one, other halls open their envelopes. Not all. Enough.

choices.text: Do not make them carry it

effects.log: You write a new decree, smaller, that no hall can refuse. It is less. It holds.

events.text: The halls that refused your decree are now ashamed of it, which is worse than if they had argued. Their envoys avoid your bench. Seo Gyeol says that a refused decree is a debt, and heaven does not like owing the Arbiter.

choices.text: Forgive the debt in writing

effects.log: A decree of forgiveness, which nobody can refuse. The envoys come back to your bench, sheepish.

choices.text: Let them carry it

effects.log: The debt hangs over heaven a century. Your next decree is opened in every hall the day it arrives.

events.text: Your decree was copied by ten thousand clerks and carried down every road of heaven. Now Seo Gyeol has found that one clerk in a far domain copied a single word wrong: "shall" became "may", and in that domain the decree has been treated as advice.

choices.text: Correct the copy at once

effects.log: You send a corrected copy. The far domain obeys, belatedly, and complains it was never told.

choices.text: Go there and see what "may" has done

effects.log: In the far domain, the gods chose to obey anyway, because they were asked and not told. It is the best-kept decree in heaven.

events.text: The clerk who copied the word wrong is brought to you, terrified, expecting to be sealed. They are a minor god of ink in a far domain, and they say they did it on purpose: they thought "shall" was cruel.

choices.text: Pardon them, and write "may" in the next decree

effects.log: Your next decree asks instead of commands. It is obeyed more widely than any before.

choices.text: Sentence them to copy the decree correctly, ten thousand times

effects.log: They copy it, every word, for a century. They come out of it the finest clerk in heaven.

events.text: A whole school of clerks has grown up in the far domain around the ink-god, copying decrees with the wording softened, sending them back to their writers for approval. They call it the Kinder Hand. Two pantheons now ask for their decrees to pass through it.

choices.text: Send all your decrees through the Kinder Hand

effects.log: Your decrees go out softened. A few lose their force. Most gain something better.

choices.text: Keep your own words, plain

effects.log: You thank the school and keep your own words. The Kinder Hand serves others, and is still proud of you.

events.text: At a Trial of Judgement this decade one champion knelt and the other walked out with a wound of yours on their blade, and has not cleaned it. They carry it everywhere, Seo Gyeol hears, as a trophy, and say the Arbiter can be cut.
events.arc: The Champion Who Struck the Chair

choices.text: Summon them

effects.log: They come, swaggering, with the blade. When they see the scar on your arm, they stop swaggering.

choices.text: Let them talk: the Arbiter can be cut

effects.log: You say it aloud in your hall. It is true. Heaven finds it oddly reassuring.

events.text: The champion asks you what they should have felt, walking out of the trial. They expected victory. They felt sick. They have not fought since, and their side has lost three clashes without them.
events.arc: The Champion Who Struck the Chair

choices.text: "What you felt. That is what striking a judge is."

effects.log: They sit on the litigant's bench a long time. At last they unbuckle the blade and leave it.

choices.text: Offer them a second trial, to end it properly

effects.log: They kneel this time. The clash is settled. The blade is cleaned at last.

events.text: The champion who struck the chair has become a teacher of young champions, and the first thing they teach is to bow to the Arbiter before the trial and after it. Their students do not know why. Their teacher does not tell them.
events.arc: The Champion Who Struck the Chair

choices.text: Visit their school, once

effects.log: The students bow in rows. Their teacher stands at the back and does not meet your eye. It is enough.

choices.text: Leave them their reasons

effects.log: You hear of the school and do not visit. Every trial after is a little more careful.

events.text: At a Trial of Judgement this decade both champions beat you, and you rose. Now heaven is talking: if both sides of a clash can stand over the Arbiter, why should either side kneel to the Arbiter's judgement? Envoys have begun to send champions to your trials who are stronger every time.

choices.text: Raise the price of a trial

effects.log: Only clashes the four pantheons agree are grave may come to trial. Fewer champions, fewer falls.

choices.text: Train

effects.log: You train with Ok Saebyeok every morning for a century. You are not a champion. You become hard to stand over.

events.text: The next trial: two champions, both strong, both told by their pantheons to beat the Arbiter as the last ones did. When they kneel to begin, one of them whispers that they have been ordered to fall on purpose instead, so that you can win and be trusted again.

choices.text: Stop the trial and expose the order

effects.log: You stop it. The pantheon that gave the order is shamed before heaven. The clash is judged on the law instead.

choices.text: Fight both honestly, and tell the one to fight

ok.log: You win, honestly, both of them. Heaven sees it. Nobody stands over the Arbiter again.

fail.log: You lose honestly. You rise again. It is still better than a bought win.

events.text: The two who first stood over you come back, old, together. They want to say that they were proud of it then, and are not now, and that watching you rise was the hardest thing they have seen in heaven.

choices.text: Rise from your chair to greet them

effects.log: You stand. They watch you all the way up, as they did then. This time they bow.

choices.text: Tell them they did their office

effects.log: They did. A champion fights. You say it and they look lighter, and older.

events.text: At a Trial of Judgement this decade the two champions knelt to your judgement and left by the same door. Seo Gyeol has learned that they did not part on the other side of it. They walked together as far as the edge of the empty space and sat there for a day, talking.
events.arc: They Left by the Same Door

choices.text: Ask them what they spoke of

effects.log: They tell you, separately, the same thing: the clash. Each had only ever heard their own side.

choices.text: Leave them their day

effects.log: You never ask. Years later you hear they became friends, and are glad you never asked.

events.text: The two champions have proposed something new: that before every trial, the two champions should spend a day together outside your hall, as they did. They think half the trials would never need to happen.
events.arc: They Left by the Same Door

choices.text: Make it the law of the trial

effects.log: A day at the door before every trial. A third of the trials end before they begin.

choices.text: Make it a custom, not a law

effects.log: It is done when both champions wish. Most do. A few refuse, and their trials are the hardest.

events.text: The two champions have died in the same century and asked to be buried on the step outside your door where they sat. The four pantheons argue whose ground the step is. You know the answer: nobody's.
events.arc: They Left by the Same Door

choices.text: Bury them there yourself

effects.log: Two champions of opposite sides lie under your step. Every litigant crosses them going in.

choices.text: Let their pantheons bury them, each at home

effects.log: They are buried in two halls. The step stays bare. You find you sit on it sometimes.

events.text: You have drafted a decree that will end a clash of heaven, and Seo Gyeol has made the fair copy. Reading it over, you find a sentence you do not remember writing, and it is the best sentence in it.

choices.text: Keep it, and ask no questions

effects.log: The decree goes out with the sentence. You suspect the ink. Seo Gyeol does not meet your eye.

choices.text: Strike it out: only your words go out

effects.log: The decree is weaker without it. It is all yours.

events.text: A copy of one of your decrees has fallen below the clouds, by accident, into a mortal city. Its people cannot read the script of heaven, but they have framed it in their market hall, and swear oaths on it.

choices.text: Leave it with them

effects.log: A decree of heaven sits in a mortal market for a thousand years. Its oaths are kept unusually well.

choices.text: Send a dream to tell them what it says

effects.log: They learn it ends a war of gods. They are disappointed it is not about them, and keep it anyway.

events.text: The decree that failed is still on your desk. Seo Gyeol has written it out again in a plainer hand, with shorter words, and set it beside the old. "Perhaps it was the words," they say.

choices.text: Send the plain one

effects.log: It is opened in more halls than the first. Not all. It is a kind of answer.

choices.text: Leave both on the desk

effects.log: You study them side by side for a decade. Your next decree is the plainest thing you have ever written.

events.text: The floor of your hall where champions kneel has two hollows worn into the stone, one on each side of your chair, from every trial ever held. Seo Gyeol measures them: the left is deeper by a finger.

choices.text: Have the floor levelled

effects.log: Masons of the Mountains level it. Champions notice the floor is new, and kneel more carefully.

choices.text: Kneel in the shallow one yourself, a while

effects.log: You kneel there an hour a day for a year. The hollows come level. Nobody saw.

events.text: A champion of heaven's trials sent for their first time is so young they still have the colour of the world below in their face. They kneel at the wrong side of your chair. The other champion, older, quietly moves to let them stay.

choices.text: Let the trial run as they knelt

effects.log: The young champion fights from the wrong side, and wins, and never learns their mistake.

choices.text: Thank the older one, after

effects.log: You thank them. They shrug. "We were all young," they say. You make them a judge of trials.

events.text: The wax for your decrees comes from the bees of Saengmo, Mother of Seeds, who have always given it freely. This year the bees will not give. Saengmo says, apologetically, that the bees disagree with your last decree.

choices.text: Hear the bees' objection

effects.log: You sit with the hives a day. They have a point, about a field. You amend the decree. The wax comes.

choices.text: Seal with plain ink this year

effects.log: Decrees go out unsealed. They are obeyed anyway. The bees, offended, give double next year.

events.text: Crowds have begun to come to your trials, gods of every pantheon packed into the galleries to watch the champions. They cheer. They trade faith on who will win, Seo Gyeol reports, under the benches, where they think the Arbiter cannot see.

choices.text: Close the galleries

effects.log: Trials are private from now on. The champions are relieved. The galleries are dusty and empty.

choices.text: Keep them, but forbid the cheering

effects.log: The crowds watch in silence. It is a far more frightening thing to fight in front of.

events.text: You bent a law of heaven slightly, as an Arbiter may, and in one world below a clock runs a breath slower every day. Nobody noticed. Now, a thousand years on, the breaths have added up: in that world, a whole season has gone missing from the year.

choices.text: Go down and look

effects.log: You walk that world as a stranger. Its people have a season they call the Gap, in which nobody is born and nothing ripens.

choices.text: Unbend the law at once

effects.log: The clock catches up in a single night. Below, a whole season happens between dusk and dawn. It is not gentle.

events.text: In the world of the slow clock, the season called the Gap has become holy. People marry in it, because nothing can go wrong; they make peace in it, because no war can be fought in a season that does not exist. The priests of the Gap pray to whoever made it.

choices.text: Leave it: the Gap is a gift

effects.log: You leave the law bent. The Gap goes on. Seo Gyeol writes the first entry of a new heading: laws bent well.

choices.text: Mend it slowly, over a century

effects.log: You let the Gap shrink by a day a year. The people below have time to grieve it, and do.

events.text: Gods of other worlds have heard about the Gap and want one too. Saengmo, Mother of Seeds, objects: a season with nothing growing is a wound in Life. Pungnyeon of the Golden Field objects louder. You are the only one who can bend the law.

choices.text: Refuse them all: one Gap is enough

effects.log: One world keeps its Gap. Others envy it. Saengmo thanks you, a little coldly.

choices.text: Give the Gap a single seed, for Saengmo

effects.log: One plant, a pale flower, now grows in the Gap. Saengmo is satisfied. The priests of the Gap call it the Arbiter's flower.

events.text: Baekun the Pale Ferryman, god of Death, comes to your chair with an extraordinary request: that the Arbiter bend the law of dying, only once, only for one mortal below, a child whose boat has been called too early by an error in the Book of Fates.
events.arc: The Law That Must Not Bend

choices.text: Hear the case

effects.log: The error is real: a clerk of Fate wrote one life's end on the wrong line. The child below is very ill.

choices.text: Refuse: Death is not yours to bend

effects.log: Baekun nods, as if expecting it. "Then I will take the child gently," they say, and do not leave.

events.text: It is not a matter of bending death. It is a matter of an error. The law of Fate allows an error to be corrected, if the Arbiter and the Weaver both agree. Unmyeong the Weaver is on the far side of heaven and will not be back for a year. The child has a week.
events.arc: The Law That Must Not Bend

choices.text: Find Unmyeong in time

ok.log: You find the Weaver in a dream of Mongsa's, and they sign the correction in their sleep. The child below recovers.

fail.log: You cannot find them in time. Baekun waits with you through the last night, and then takes the child gently.

choices.text: Correct it alone and answer to the Weaver after

effects.log: You correct it. The child lives. A year later the Weaver comes, very calm, and asks you never to do it again.

events.text: Baekun the Pale Ferryman comes to your hall each year on the date the child should have died, and does not say why. They sit on the litigant's bench in grey and watch you work, and leave at sunset.
events.arc: The Law That Must Not Bend

choices.text: Ask, at last, why they come

effects.log: "To remember that the law has a judge," they say. "Even mine."

choices.text: Make them tea, every year

effects.log: You make it. They drink it. It becomes a thing that happens in heaven, like the seasons.

events.text: The keepers of the Heavenly Calendar have found an extra day. It falls between the last festival of the Will of Heaven and the first of the Green Assembly, and it belongs, by every rule they have, to no pantheon. Both want it. So, it turns out, do the other two.

choices.text: Rule it the Arbiter's day

effects.log: A day of the Calendar for the empty space. Nothing is held on it. Heaven, by custom, rests.

choices.text: Give it to the gods of no pantheon

effects.log: The Lesser Hall, the moths and wells and hills, get a festival. It is very small and very loud.

choices.text: Divide it in four, by the hour

effects.log: Six hours each. Every pantheon holds a short, cross feast. The keepers despair.

events.text: Below the clouds, mortals have noticed a day appearing in their own calendars that was not there before, because a day of heaven falls on every world. Their astronomers are frightened. Their priests are excited. Their tax-collectors are confused.

choices.text: Send a dream to explain it

effects.log: Mortals below learn that heaven has found a spare day. Many of them decide to spend it resting too.

choices.text: Leave them to make of it what they will

effects.log: Below, it becomes a dozen different holidays in a dozen countries. In one, it is the day debts are forgiven.

events.text: A thousand years of the extra day, and the keepers of the Calendar have done their sums again: the day was never extra. It was stolen, long ago, by a pantheon that faded, and has only now been returned by the turning of the ages. Its owner is long gone.

choices.text: Keep the ruling you made

effects.log: Precedent holds. Seo Gyeol writes the history beside it. The day goes on as it was.

choices.text: Give the day to the faded pantheon's memory

effects.log: The day becomes a day of remembering a pantheon nobody knew. Mok Dami approves, silently.

events.text: Daeak of the Unmoving Peak, god of the Mountains, has been asked by every other pantheon to move one mountain a little to the east, so a road of heaven can pass. Daeak has refused for nine thousand years. Now the road's builders sue.
events.arc: The Mountain That Will Not Move

choices.text: Hear Daeak's reason

effects.log: Daeak speaks very slowly, over three days: the mountain stands where it stands because once a god promised it would.

choices.text: Rule that a road may go round

effects.log: The road goes round. It takes a hundred years longer. The builders curse the mountain all the way.

events.text: The promise: long ago, a god of the Mountains promised a mortal shepherd below that the peak would always be there for them to find their way home by. The shepherd is long dead. Daeak still keeps the promise. "A mountain does not know when to stop," they say.
events.arc: The Mountain That Will Not Move

choices.text: Rule the promise kept, and released

effects.log: You tell Daeak the shepherd got home every time. The mountain moves a little east, slowly, with something like relief.

choices.text: Rule the promise still binding

effects.log: The mountain stays. The road goes round. Mortals below still find their way home by it, many of them.

events.text: Haeryong, Keeper of Tides, and Pungnyeon of the Golden Field have fallen out over a coast below: the sea floods the fields in the spring, and the fields push the sea back with dikes in the autumn. Their mortal worshippers have begun to fight on the dikes.

choices.text: Go and stand on the dike

effects.log: You stand where the sea meets the field. Both gods arrive, embarrassed, to argue in front of you.

choices.text: Ask each god to judge the other's case

effects.log: Haeryong argues the fields' side. Pungnyeon argues the sea's. They agree with each other halfway through.

events.text: The mortals of the coast have their own idea: let the sea have the fields every seventh year, as a fallow year, and the fields have the shore the other six. Both gods find it insulting to be advised by mortals. Both privately like it.

choices.text: Rule it as the mortals proposed

effects.log: Seo Gyeol writes a judgement whose author is a fishing village below. Both gods sign it, grumbling.

choices.text: Improve on it, and rule your own

effects.log: Your version is more exact. The mortals keep theirs anyway, which the gods also allow.

events.text: A hundred seventh years on, the coast below is the richest in its world: salt-fields every seventh year, grain the other six, and festivals at both turnings. Haeryong and Pungnyeon attend the festivals together, in disguise, and think nobody knows.

choices.text: Attend once yourself, also in disguise

effects.log: You stand between them in a crowd of mortals, all three in disguise. Nobody says anything. Everybody knows.

choices.text: Leave them their secret

effects.log: You hear about it from Seo Gyeol and smile. The two gods are friends by now.

events.text: Horang, Lord of the Wild, held a great hunt in the old way, and the hunt crossed into the domain of the Sky, and a stag of Horang's was shot by a hunter of Cheonho's. Both gods claim the stag. The stag, being a god's beast, is still alive and quite annoyed.
events.arc: The Hunt That Crossed the Line

choices.text: Ask the stag whose it is

effects.log: The stag walks to the middle of your hall and lies down facing neither god. It is its own.

choices.text: Rule by the old law of the hunt: the first arrow

effects.log: Cheonho's hunter fired first. Horang accepts it with a growl, and the stag goes to the Sky.

events.text: Because the stag was ruled its own, every beast of Horang's that wanders across a border now claims it was its own choice. Horang is delighted. The other gods are not.
events.arc: The Hunt That Crossed the Line

choices.text: Limit the precedent to that one stag

effects.log: Seo Gyeol narrows it in the margin. The other beasts sulk back over the borders.

choices.text: Let the beasts choose

effects.log: Heaven's borders become a little wilder. Horang sends you a cub, which grows into an enormous, devoted cat.

events.text: Heaven has been stable for so long that your scales hardly move, and for the first time in an age you have time to sit with the Dao itself. Balance, you find, is not a stillness. It moves all the time, very finely, like a bird holding still in the wind.

choices.text: Sit with it for a century

effects.log: You sit. The scales move a hair this way and that. You learn to feel every hair of it.

choices.text: Go back to work

effects.log: You return to the bench. Your judgements are a little lighter for the glimpse.

events.text: In the depth of your sitting, you understand something about the empty space between the halls: it is not empty because nobody wanted it. It is empty because it is where heaven turns, and the turning needs room.

choices.text: Hold the understanding

ok.log: You hold it. For a moment the four pantheons turn around your chair like the hours around noon.

fail.log: It slips. You keep only the shape of it.

choices.text: Let it go, and write down only one word

effects.log: Seo Gyeol finds the word on your desk in the morning: "room". They file it under the first page.

events.text: Cheonho, Who Hangs the Stars, has lost one. Not broken, not stolen: it simply left its place in the night and went somewhere else. Cheonho wants a warrant. A star of heaven is a servant of the Sky, and a servant may not leave.

choices.text: Issue the warrant

effects.log: The warrant goes out. The star is found sitting in the sky of a small world below, where it was never meant to be.

choices.text: Ask why a star would leave

effects.log: Cheonho has never asked. It takes them a century to find the courage to go and ask it.

events.text: The star went to the sky of a world below that had none, a world under permanent cloud that had never seen a light at night. It pushed the cloud aside. Below, a whole people now have one star, and they have built their calendar around it.

choices.text: Rule that it may stay

effects.log: Cheonho has one star fewer. A world below has one star. Seo Gyeol writes it as the precedent of the runaway.

choices.text: Rule it must go home, and Cheonho hang a new one there

effects.log: The star goes home. Cheonho hangs a new one in the dark world, smaller. The people below never know.

events.text: Seo Gyeol has made a list of every law of heaven you are allowed to bend. It is short. Beside it, in a smaller hand, a second list: the laws they think you will be asked to bend. It is very long.

choices.text: Read the second list

effects.log: You read it. Most of them you would never bend. Two you will, and soon. You can feel it.

choices.text: Burn the second list

effects.log: Seo Gyeol watches it burn with relief. "I did not like having written it," they say.

events.text: A world below has asked, through every one of its gods, for a little more time: its sun is dying, and it needs another thousand years to learn to leave. A small bending of the law of its years would give it them.

choices.text: Bend it

effects.log: The sun dims more slowly. The world learns to build ships. In a thousand years, it leaves.

choices.text: Refuse: a sun's life is a sun's

effects.log: The world below learns faster, from fear. Some of it leaves in time.

events.text: Hwarin of the First Hearth brings you a coal from the first fire ever lit, which they have kept burning since before the pantheons. They want it judged: whether a fire can be so old that it belongs to everyone.

choices.text: Rule that it does

effects.log: A hearth is set beside your chair with the first coal in it. Litigants warm their hands at it.

choices.text: Rule it Hwarin's, and always theirs

effects.log: Hwarin takes the coal home, relieved. "I would have given it," they say. "I did not want to have to."

events.text: There is a queue on the near bank of the river of Death longer than any in memory. Baekun the Pale Ferryman says the War in Heaven has sent down so many that the boat cannot keep up, and asks the Arbiter to say who goes first.

choices.text: The ones who waited longest

effects.log: The oldest souls go first. The queue moves, slowly, fairly.

choices.text: Lend a hand at the oar

effects.log: You row for a year beside the Ferryman. The queue empties. Heaven is astonished.

events.text: Noegong of the Nine Drums has lost one of the drums: the ninth, the one that is struck only when a law of heaven is broken. It has turned up on your doorstep, gently thrumming.

choices.text: Return it to Noegong

effects.log: The god of Thunder takes it home without a word. A week later, it thrums again, quietly, on its own.

choices.text: Keep it until it stops

effects.log: It thrums for a year beside your chair and stops on the day you reverse an old wrong ruling.

events.text: Horang, Lord of the Wild, insists that the beasts of heaven be counted in the census, as gods are. Every other pantheon thinks it absurd. Horang has brought an elephant to your hall to make the point.

choices.text: Count them

effects.log: The census of heaven now includes the beasts. It takes a decade. The elephant is listed first.

choices.text: Count only the elephant

effects.log: One beast in the census. Horang laughs so hard the hall shakes. The point, somehow, is made.

events.text: A mortal scholar below has guessed that the laws of their world can be bent, and by whom, and has written a whole book addressed to the Arbiter, asking for just one change: that ink should never fade.

choices.text: Grant it, in that one world

effects.log: Ink never fades in that world. In a thousand years, it has the best library below the clouds.

choices.text: Send a dream: some things should fade

effects.log: The scholar wakes and writes one more page, which says so, and then burns their book.

events.text: You find, after an age, that a law you bent long ago has bent itself back on its own, gently, the way a branch does. Nothing was harmed. The world below did not notice. Only you did.

choices.text: Leave it as heaven chose

effects.log: You write it down: some laws heal. It is the most comforting entry in the Book.

choices.text: Bend it again

effects.log: You bend it again. It stays bent this time. You are not sure whether that is better.

events.text: A mortal has climbed into heaven. Nobody knows how. Yun Haesol, a ferry-keeper from a river town below, sits on your bottom step with mud on their sandals and a petition written on a piece of sail. The gods of three pantheons have come out of their halls to stare.

choices.text: Hear them, at once, as any litigant

effects.log: You hear a mortal at the Arbiter's chair. The galleries are full. Yun Haesol's voice shakes, then stops shaking.

choices.text: Ask first how they came

effects.log: "I kept walking up," Yun Haesol says. "Nobody told me to stop." Seo Gyeol writes it down very carefully.

choices.text: Send them home gently, with a blessing

effects.log: They go down the steps, looking back. The blessing is real. So, you think later, was the petition.

events.text: Yun Haesol's petition: the god of their river, a small god of the Sea's pantheon, has taken the ferry's toll as worship for three hundred years, and the town is poor for it. They are not asking for the toll back. They want the god to ride the ferry once.

choices.text: Order the river-god to ride the ferry

effects.log: The river-god rides it, hating it. Halfway across they see the town from the water, as the town sees them.

choices.text: Rule on the toll instead

effects.log: The toll is halved by law. The town is less poor. Yun Haesol thanks you and looks, briefly, disappointed.

events.text: Yun Haesol has not gone home. They sleep on your bottom step and help the litigants find the right bench, and translate the prayers of mortals that arrive at your chair into plain words. They are growing old. Mortals do, even in heaven.

choices.text: Offer them a post as clerk of mortal petitions

effects.log: They accept, weeping. Mortal prayers to the Arbiter now come to Yun Haesol first, and are answered faster.

choices.text: Send them home to live out their life

effects.log: They go down. Below, they are a legend before they reach their town. They keep the ferry till they die.

events.text: Yun Haesol is dying, old, on a bench in your hall. They have one last petition. They would like to know whether a mortal who served at the Arbiter's chair goes to the Ferryman like any other, or whether the empty space has a law of its own.

choices.text: Ask Baekun to come for them here

effects.log: The Pale Ferryman comes into your hall. Yun Haesol gets into the boat on the floor of heaven, and waves.

choices.text: Ask the four pantheons to raise them

effects.log: It has been done before, rarely. Four envoys agree. Yun Haesol wakes a god, very confused, of a domain nobody has named yet.

events.text: Yun Haesol, raised a god, has a domain at last: the four pantheons have named it Appeals. Mortals who think heaven has wronged them can pray to Yun Haesol now, and Yun Haesol brings the prayer to you. The first week, there are a hundred thousand.

choices.text: Hear them all

effects.log: It takes a century. Most are small. A few are not. Heaven is a little more careful for it.

choices.text: Ask Yun Haesol to choose the ones that matter

effects.log: They choose well, painfully. The ones they put aside haunt them.

events.text: The gods of all four pantheons dislike the domain of Appeals: every grievance below now has a road to the Arbiter. Mujin of the Thousand Banners proposes that it be dissolved. Yun Haesol stands at your bench, very small and very still.

choices.text: Defend the domain before the four

ok.log: You speak for it. The four pantheons, embarrassed to be seen fearing mortal prayers, let it stand.

fail.log: The four vote to shrink it: appeals from kingdoms only, not from single mortals. Yun Haesol accepts it with grief.

choices.text: Let Yun Haesol speak for it

effects.log: The ferry-keeper speaks. It is not eloquent. It is about a toll, and a river. The domain stands.

events.text: Yun Haesol has an appeal of their own to bring: against you. A judgement you gave long ago went against a mortal town, and the town has been praying to Appeals about it for a century. Yun Haesol is sick with nerves, and brings it anyway.

choices.text: Hear it, and reverse yourself

effects.log: You were wrong. You say it. Yun Haesol goes home and is ill with relief.

choices.text: Hear it, and uphold yourself, and explain

effects.log: You were right, and you explain it to the town below in a dream. They do not like it. They understand it.

events.text: In {sov_world}, the Pocket World you made, the people have heard that their maker is the Arbiter of heaven. So they have made one of their own: a wooden chair in their market square, and a pair of scales from a fishmonger's stall, and nobody sitting in it.
events.arc: The Little Scales of the Pocket World

choices.text: Go down and see

effects.log: You visit as a stranger. People bring their quarrels to the empty chair and argue in front of it, and somehow settle.

choices.text: Leave them their chair
