effects.log: You do not interfere. Seo Gyeol says it is the first time anyone has copied you without asking.

events.text: The empty chair of {sov_world} has a sitter now: an old fishmonger, chosen by lot, who judges the market's quarrels. They are very good, and very frightened, and they pray to you every night to tell them if they are doing it right.
events.arc: The Little Scales of the Pocket World

choices.text: Answer their prayers, every night

effects.log: You talk them through cases in dreams for forty years. They become the best judge in {sov_world}.

choices.text: Answer only once: "Trust the scales."

effects.log: They hear it once, and never pray about it again. They judge more slowly after.

events.text: The fishmonger-judge of {sov_world} has made a ruling you would not have made: a thief allowed to keep what they stole, because they stole it from a famine. The market accepts it. Your scales, above, tip a hair.
events.arc: The Little Scales of the Pocket World

choices.text: Correct it from above

effects.log: You send a dream. The ruling is changed. The fishmonger is hurt, and the market less sure of their chair.

choices.text: Write it into your own Book as a precedent

effects.log: Seo Gyeol writes a ruling of a mortal fishmonger into the Book of heaven. Mok Dami, reading it, nods.

events.text: The fishmonger-judge is dead, and {sov_world} has a whole court now, a hall of mortal judges with a wooden chair at the front, empty, for you. On the day the court opens, they invite their maker to sit in it once.
events.arc: The Little Scales of the Pocket World

choices.text: Sit in it

effects.log: You sit, as a stranger, for one morning. A child brings a case about a goat. You judge it well. Nobody knows who you were.

choices.text: Leave it empty

effects.log: The chair stays empty in {sov_world}'s court. It is the most respected thing in it.

events.text: Two valleys of {sov_world} are at odds over a river that runs between them, and both have prayed to their maker. It is a small quarrel, by heaven's measure. In {sov_world}, it is the biggest thing that has ever happened.
events.arc: Two Valleys of the Pocket World

choices.text: Judge it as gravely as a war of pantheons

effects.log: You hear both valleys for a year, in dreams. They are astonished to be taken so seriously.

choices.text: Let them settle it themselves

effects.log: They fight a little, and then settle. They resent you a little for not helping.

events.text: Your judgement on the river of {sov_world} has been carved on a stone at the border of the two valleys. Pilgrims come to read it. A scholar of one valley has noticed it was written by the same hand as the decrees of heaven, and has started a religion.
events.arc: Two Valleys of the Pocket World

choices.text: Let the religion be

effects.log: The Church of the Stone grows in {sov_world}. Its only teaching is that both sides must be heard. You can live with that.

choices.text: Send a dream to the scholar: worship nothing, hear everyone

effects.log: The scholar writes it down. It becomes the religion anyway.

events.text: A hero of {sov_world} has risen, born in the river-valley, and has come up into heaven to ask the Arbiter one thing: whether their world is allowed to have its own pantheons, and its own wars, and its own Arbiter.
events.arc: Two Valleys of the Pocket World

choices.text: "Yes. And I hope you never need any of them."

effects.log: The hero goes home and tells {sov_world}. It is a hopeful age there.

choices.text: "Yes, but come to me before your first war."

effects.log: The hero promises. In {sov_world}'s history, that promise is kept for ten thousand years.

events.text: Below the clouds, someone has built a temple to the Eternal Arbiter: a plain hall with an empty chair at one end and a pair of scales on it. People come there not to pray but to argue, both sides together, in front of the chair.
events.arc: The Temple of the Empty Chair

choices.text: Answer the first quarrel brought there

effects.log: A dispute over a cow. You send a sign: the scales tip, gently, to one side. Both parties are awed, and accept it.

choices.text: Never answer: let them judge themselves

effects.log: The scales never move. People learn to settle before the empty chair, because it is empty.

events.text: There are now hundreds of temples of the empty chair below, in a dozen countries. Their priests have begun to call themselves judges, and some of them take fees. Others have started to say that the Arbiter of heaven agrees with them, on everything.
events.arc: The Temple of the Empty Chair

choices.text: Send a dream to every priest at once

effects.log: The dream says one thing: the chair is empty. Half the priests understand. The other half claim the dream supports them.

choices.text: Let the temples sort themselves out

effects.log: They split into three schools and argue for a century. It is the most peaceful religious quarrel below.

events.text: A temple of the empty chair below has become a court in all but name: kings bring their disputes there, and abide by them. The priests ask the Arbiter, in a single long prayer, whether this is what you wanted.
events.arc: The Temple of the Empty Chair

choices.text: Send them the first page of the Book of Precedent

effects.log: They copy it into their own book, and Gu Hyeon's well, and the town, become a tale told below.

choices.text: Send them nothing: they did it themselves

effects.log: The silence is the answer they hoped for. Their court grows.

events.text: One prayer comes to your chair every year from the same mortal below, a weaver, and it is always the same: "Let it be fair." No name. No case. Seo Gyeol has kept every one in a box. There are three hundred of them now.

choices.text: Answer it, at last

effects.log: You send a single word down in a dream: "Mostly." The weaver wakes laughing.

choices.text: Keep the box, and the silence

effects.log: The prayers keep coming after the weaver dies: their grandchild has taken it up.

events.text: Mortals below have begun to leave offerings for the Arbiter: two of everything, always exactly matched, two cakes, two candles, two coins. Seo Gyeol is touched. You are a little embarrassed.

choices.text: Accept them, and give one of each away

effects.log: Half of every offering goes back below as rain or luck. The mortals notice, and leave more.

choices.text: Send word to stop

effects.log: They stop. They leave single things instead, which seems worse somehow.

events.text: A judge below, a mortal of some great city, prays to you each night before a hard verdict. Tonight the verdict is death for a young thief, and the judge prays for a sign that they are wrong.

choices.text: Send the sign

effects.log: A lamp in the courtroom goes out at the moment of sentence. The judge changes the verdict. The thief lives to be old.

choices.text: Send nothing: it is their scale

effects.log: The judge decides alone. You will never know which way, and that is right.

events.text: Two kingdoms below have built a single shrine on their border, to you, as a place to sign treaties. Each kingdom built one half. The halves do not quite meet in the middle; there is a crack down the floor exactly where the line runs.

choices.text: Leave the crack

effects.log: Treaty-signers step over it carefully. It reminds them. The treaties hold better for it.

choices.text: Close it with a sign from heaven

effects.log: A seam of gold runs down the crack overnight. Both kingdoms take it as approval, and sign more.

events.text: A child of {sov_world} has written you a letter and burned it, as their grandparents taught them, so that the smoke would carry it to the maker. The letter asks why the maker made a world where people disagree.

choices.text: Answer in a dream

effects.log: You tell the child that a world where nobody disagreed would not need anybody. They wake satisfied.

choices.text: Keep the smoke

effects.log: Seo Gyeol catches the smoke in a jar. It is on the shelf of evidence still.

events.text: Below, a guild of merchants swears its oaths on a little pair of brass scales they call the Arbiter's, and none of them has broken an oath in a hundred years. Their guild-master asks, by prayer, for heaven's blessing on the scales.

choices.text: Bless them

effects.log: The little scales are a little truer. The merchants are a little richer and very honest.

choices.text: Tell them the scales were never the point

effects.log: The guild-master hears it in a dream, and laughs, and keeps the scales anyway.

events.text: A second mortal has climbed into heaven, following the stories of Yun Haesol. This one is young and arrogant and has a list of complaints against every god by name. They are, Seo Gyeol says, mostly correct.

choices.text: Hear the whole list

effects.log: It takes a month. Several gods are summoned. The young mortal goes home stunned to have been taken seriously.

choices.text: Hear one, and send the list to the Court

effects.log: The Court is appalled. The young mortal is pleased. One god is fined.

events.text: Hwang Seonjae reports, a little stiffly, that the Will of Heaven has noticed that mortals pray to the Arbiter more each century, and to them less. "We do not object," the herald says. "We only wonder what you are offering them."

choices.text: "Only that both sides will be heard."

effects.log: Hwang Seonjae carries it home. The Will of Heaven begins, cautiously, to hear its mortals more.

choices.text: "Nothing. That is what they like."

effects.log: Hwang Seonjae laughs despite themselves. The Will of Heaven does not.

events.text: The four Elder Lineages of heaven, older than any pantheon, have never agreed which of them is eldest. Every age it costs a festival, a marriage or a war. Now they bring it to you, each with a scroll of descent going back past the Calendar.

choices.text: Read the scrolls

effects.log: All four scrolls begin with the same name, in four different hands. The lineages are one house that split.

choices.text: Rule that precedence goes by turns, each age

effects.log: A rota of eldership. Every lineage is eldest once in four ages. They hate it equally.

events.text: You tell the four Elder Lineages that they share a single first ancestor. The hall goes very quiet. The eldest of the eldest, a god so old they are mostly light, asks whether the Arbiter is sure. It would mean their quarrel is with themselves.

choices.text: Show them the four first lines side by side

ok.log: The four first lines are the same name. Four old gods stand looking at it, and one of them laughs.

fail.log: One scroll is too faded to read. Three lineages accept it; the fourth walks out.

choices.text: Leave it with them to decide what it means

effects.log: They take it home. It takes them a century to talk about it.

events.text: The four Elder Lineages hold a feast together for the first time in an age: a feast of one house, they call it. They have set a seat at its head for the first ancestor, empty, and a second beside it for the Arbiter.

choices.text: Sit beside the empty seat

effects.log: You sit by the ancestor nobody remembers. The four lineages raise cups to both of you.

choices.text: Decline, and let them be one house alone

effects.log: They understand. Their feast is quieter without you, and more theirs.

events.text: An heir of an Elder Lineage, Yang Seoha, has been disinherited for marrying a god of the Throne of Storms. Their lineage says it is the oldest law of the house. Yang Seoha says the house is older than the law.

choices.text: Hear the house's law

effects.log: It is real and very old: no heir of the lineage may bind themselves to a pantheon. It was written to keep them free.

choices.text: Hear Yang Seoha first

effects.log: They speak simply: they did not bind themselves to a pantheon. They bound themselves to one god.

events.text: The law of the Elder Lineage and Yang Seoha's marriage do not have to collide, if the Arbiter rules that a marriage is not a binding to a pantheon. It would be a new reading of very old words, and every lineage would study it.

choices.text: Rule it: a marriage is not a pantheon

effects.log: Yang Seoha is an heir again. Three other lineages amend their own laws within the century.

choices.text: Rule for the law, and ask the house for mercy

effects.log: The law holds. You ask the house, as a petitioner, to forgive. It does, a little, after a long time.

events.text: Yang Seoha's child is the first of an Elder Lineage with a parent in a pantheon. The child is very gifted and very lonely. Neither house knows what to do with them. Yang Seoha asks if the child may study at your chair.

choices.text: Take them as a pupil

effects.log: The child learns the law at the Arbiter's side. In an age, they are the best mediator heaven has between houses and halls.

choices.text: Send them to both houses in turn

effects.log: A year with each, all their childhood. They grow up belonging to both, and to neither, and they are fine.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun, which sits where light does not reach, has passed a sentence on a god of the Will of Heaven, in absence. Nobody in heaven recognises its right to judge. Its sentence is being carried out anyway, quietly, in the god's dreams.
events.arc: The Court of the Unlit Sun

choices.text: Summon the Court of the Unlit Sun

effects.log: Its envoy comes, hooded, to your bench. They are courteous and very cold, and they have read your whole Book.

choices.text: Rule its sentence void at once

effects.log: Your ruling goes out. The dreams of the sentenced god stop. The Unlit Sun says nothing at all.

events.text: The envoy of the Unlit Sun argues that their court judges what the others will not see: crimes committed in shadow, by gods who are never caught in light. They give a list. Some of the names are of gods you have judged innocent.
events.arc: The Court of the Unlit Sun

choices.text: Reopen those cases

effects.log: You reopen three. Two of the gods were guilty after all, in the dark. You sentence them properly.

choices.text: Refuse: shadow is not evidence

effects.log: The envoy bows and says they expected nothing else of a court that sits in daylight.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun offers a treaty: they will judge nothing that has been brought to your chair, and you will hear any case they bring to it, in the dark if they wish. Two courts of heaven, one in each half of the day.
events.arc: The Court of the Unlit Sun

choices.text: Sign it

effects.log: For an age, the Unlit Sun brings its cases to you at midnight, and you judge them by one lamp. Heaven is safer in the dark.

choices.text: Refuse: there is one law

effects.log: The Unlit Sun withdraws into its shadow. You do not hear from it again for a thousand years.

events.text: At one of the midnight hearings, the hooded envoy of the Unlit Sun brings a case against themselves. They have kept a sentence secret from their own court, out of pity. They want it judged in the only place in heaven they trust.
events.arc: The Court of the Unlit Sun

choices.text: Judge it with mercy

effects.log: You judge it at midnight. The envoy takes their hood off afterwards, for a moment. They are very young.

choices.text: Judge it by their own court's law

effects.log: You rule by the Unlit Sun's law, strictly. The envoy thanks you. It is what they needed.

events.text: A Dao Ancestor has come down into the Divine Realm for a while, as they may, and has walked into the empty space and sat on the litigant's bench. Every god in the galleries has stopped breathing. The Ancestor says they have a complaint.

choices.text: Hear it as any other

effects.log: You hear a Dao Ancestor as you would a ferry-keeper. They are delighted. They had not been treated as anyone for an age.

choices.text: Ask whether the scales may judge an Ancestor

effects.log: The Ancestor thinks about it for a whole day. "Let us find out," they say.

events.text: The Ancestor's complaint: a god of the Throne of Storms has built a hall on a peak where the Ancestor once sat to think, ages ago, and the Ancestor would like to sit there again. It is a very small complaint from a very great being.

choices.text: Rule for the god who built the hall

effects.log: The Ancestor came after the hall, in law, if not in time. You rule it. The galleries gasp. The Ancestor bows.

choices.text: Ask the god to lend the peak for a day

effects.log: The storm-god lends it, terrified and proud. The Ancestor sits there one afternoon and thanks everyone.

events.text: Before the Dao Ancestor goes back up, they visit you once more and ask a question that the gods of heaven have been asking about you: who judges the Arbiter? They do not wait for an answer. They only say, kindly, "Not I."

choices.text: Thank them

effects.log: They go. You sit with the words for a long time. Seo Gyeol says it was the best thing anyone has said to you.

choices.text: Call after them: "Then who?"

effects.log: The Ancestor stops on the stair. "Whoever you let," they say, and are gone.

events.text: A split-soul clone, forged long ago from a god of the Harvest and sent to keep a far field, has come to your chair to sue its original: it wants to be recognised as a god in its own right, with its own name. Its original is outraged.

choices.text: Hear the clone

effects.log: The clone speaks quietly about four hundred years alone in a field. It has thoughts the original never had.

choices.text: Rule that a clone is its maker's

effects.log: The clone bows and goes back to its field. The original is relieved. You are not.

events.text: The original god testifies: the clone was made from a part of their own soul, and if it is a separate god, then that part of them is gone for ever. They do not want to lose themselves. The clone does not want to be lost either.

choices.text: Find a ruling that keeps both whole

ok.log: The clone is its own god, and the original keeps a tie: one dream a year, shared. Both accept, weeping.

fail.log: There is no such ruling. You have to choose, and choose the clone. The original goes home smaller.

choices.text: Rule for the clone, and mourn the original's loss

effects.log: The clone has a name. The original has a hole in them, and a very polite letter from the clone.

events.text: Other forged clones across heaven have heard. A dozen have come to your door with the same petition. Their originals have hired champions for a Trial of Judgement, all at once. The Clone Forge itself has sent an envoy to ask what you are doing to their trade.

choices.text: Hear each case on its own

effects.log: A dozen cases, a dozen outcomes. The Clone Forge revises its contracts. Every clone now has a clause.

choices.text: Rule once, for all forged clones

effects.log: One precedent for every clone in heaven. It is too broad, and it holds, roughly.

events.text: The guardian of one of the Tower's divine floors, a god set there an age ago to test climbers, has stopped testing them and simply lets them through. Climbers below are delighted. The gods who set the guardian are not. They want it judged.

choices.text: Climb to the floor and see

effects.log: The guardian sits cross-legged by the stair. "Everyone who comes this far has been tested enough," they say.

choices.text: Rule that a guardian must guard

effects.log: The ruling goes up the Tower. The guardian returns to testing, with a sigh you can hear from heaven.

events.text: Climbers who passed the guardian unchallenged have reached the higher floors unready, and some have fallen back down. The guardian is grieved. They ask the Arbiter whether a test is a cruelty or a kindness.

choices.text: "A kindness, if it is fair."

effects.log: The guardian goes back to testing, carefully, gently. Fewer fall above them.

choices.text: "Whichever you make it."

effects.log: The guardian designs a new test, one that teaches as it bars. Climbers below call it the Arbiter's floor.

events.text: Your own disciples, raised in your hall, have begun to argue among themselves about the war of two pantheons. Two of them have taken sides. A third says that disciples of the Arbiter may never take a side. All three want you to say who is right.

choices.text: Rule for the third: disciples stand between

effects.log: The two partisans are hurt. One of them leaves your hall that year for the side they chose.

choices.text: Let them choose their own

effects.log: Your disciples are free to take sides. Your hall becomes a place where both sides' young gods argue.

events.text: The disciple who left for a side has come back, older, with a wound and an apology. They do not want to come home. They want to tell you, and the others, what taking a side was like.

choices.text: Let them speak to the hall

effects.log: They speak for a whole night. Afterwards, your other disciples are quieter, and more careful, and kinder.

choices.text: Take them back as a disciple

effects.log: They take their old bench. They never speak of it. You see, now and then, that they know something the others do not.

events.text: Two of the Elder Lineages want to marry their heirs, and ask the Arbiter to witness. A marriage between lineages has not happened in nine thousand years, because each fears the other will become eldest by it.

choices.text: Witness it, and rule it changes no precedence

effects.log: You rule it first and witness it after. The feast lasts a year. Nobody becomes eldest.

choices.text: Witness it, and say nothing of precedence

effects.log: The marriage is beautiful. The quarrel about what it means lasts longer than the feast.

events.text: Someone of the Court of the Unlit Sun has left a lamp on your steps, unlit, with a note: "For the hearings you cannot see." There is no oil in it.

choices.text: Light it anyway, at midnight

effects.log: It burns without oil, a cold blue. In its light you can see who is lying. You use it sparingly.

choices.text: Leave it unlit on the shelf

effects.log: An unlit lamp beside the warm stone and the hailstone. The Unlit Sun seems to approve.

events.text: Your youngest disciple asks whether you have ever been wrong. Every other disciple goes silent and pretends to be reading. Seo Gyeol, at the back, lowers their brush.

choices.text: "Yes. Often. Here is a list."

effects.log: You give them the list. It is long. Your youngest disciple reads it all and says, "Thank you," and means it.

choices.text: "Yes. Find out where yourself."

effects.log: They spend a decade on it and find more than you did. You make them a clerk.

events.text: A mortal-born immortal climbing the Tower has reached a divine floor and found an inscription there in your hand, which you do not remember carving. It reads: both sides. They have climbed down again to ask you what it means.

choices.text: Tell them

effects.log: You explain the scales. They go back up the Tower, slower, and pass the next floor by listening to its guardian.

choices.text: Ask them what they think

effects.log: They think it means the Tower has two ways up. They are not wrong. They find the second.

events.text: The Clone Forge reports that someone has commissioned a split-soul clone of the Arbiter. The commission was refused. They want to know whether you would like to know who asked.

choices.text: Yes

effects.log: It was a pantheon that wanted an Arbiter of its own. You write them a short letter. It is not angry. It is worse.

choices.text: No

effects.log: You never learn. Somewhere in heaven, a pantheon is ashamed, and you are kinder for not knowing which.

events.text: The four Elder Lineages keep an archive of every promise heaven ever made. They have found one, from before your time, made by the first Arbiter, Jang Murae, to them: that the scales would never weigh an Elder Lineage. They want to know if it binds you.

choices.text: Rule that it binds

effects.log: The Elder Lineages are beyond your scales by an old promise. It is strange, and it is precedent.

choices.text: Rule that a promise to be above the law is no law

effects.log: The Lineages are shocked, then thoughtful. They come under the scales like everyone.

events.text: Two of your disciples have quarrelled, badly, over a young god of the Green Assembly whom both admire, and want a Trial of Judgement. The young god in question has written to you separately to say they would rather like to be asked.

choices.text: Ask the young god

effects.log: You ask. They choose neither. Both disciples are crushed, then friends again, which seems to have been the idea.

choices.text: Refuse the trial: hearts are not clashes

effects.log: Your disciples sulk. The young god of the Assembly writes to thank you.

events.text: Sweeping the empty space at dawn, Seo Gyeol finds footprints worn into the stone, very faint, leading from the chair to the edge of heaven and back. They are not yours. They are older than the pantheons. Seo Gyeol thinks they are Jang Murae's, the first Arbiter.

choices.text: Walk in them

effects.log: You set your feet in the hollows and walk where the first Arbiter walked. At the edge of heaven they stop, facing out.

choices.text: Have them preserved

effects.log: Masons of the Mountains seal the prints in clear stone. Litigants stop to look at them before they come in.

events.text: At the edge of heaven, where Jang Murae's footprints stop, you find what the first Arbiter was facing: the world below, all of it, spread out in one view as it can be seen from nowhere else. Every quarrel of gods lands somewhere down there.

choices.text: Come here every year

effects.log: You stand where they stood, once a year, and look at what your judgements fall on. It changes how you write them.

choices.text: Bring the four envoys to see

effects.log: Four envoys stand at the edge, silent. Cheon Ugeun weeps a small rain on the world below. It is a good harvest.

events.text: A second set of footprints has appeared beside Jang Murae's, worn into the stone from the chair to the edge: yours. You did not know you had walked it so often. Seo Gyeol says nothing, and seals them in clear stone beside the first.

choices.text: Look at the two together

effects.log: Two paths, an age apart, to the same place. Yours wander a little more. You find you do not mind.

choices.text: Walk them once with Seo Gyeol

effects.log: You walk it together. At the edge, Seo Gyeol says, "Someone will walk it after you." It is a comfort.

events.text: At night, when the hall is empty and you have gone to rest, Seo Gyeol has heard a voice from your chair: dry, patient, reciting judgements nobody alive remembers. Tonight you stay to listen. It is reciting one of yours.
events.arc: A Voice in the Empty Chair

choices.text: Answer it

effects.log: You speak into the dark. The voice stops. Then it says, quite clearly, "Not bad," and goes on reciting.

choices.text: Write down what it recites

effects.log: Seo Gyeol fills a scroll by morning: a hundred lost judgements of Jang Murae. Some of them contradict yours.

events.text: The voice of Jang Murae, the first Arbiter, talks with you now on the nights you stay. It is not a ghost, Mok Dami says. It is the chair remembering. It asks about the pantheons as an old relative asks about the children.
events.arc: A Voice in the Empty Chair

choices.text: Tell it everything

effects.log: You tell the chair the history of heaven since it was empty. It listens all night, and at the end it sighs.

choices.text: Ask it how it ended

effects.log: The voice is quiet for a long time. "Ask me when you are ready to hear it," it says.

events.text: You have a hard case, harder than any, and nobody to ask. Late at night you put it to the chair. The voice of Jang Murae listens to the whole case and then asks you, very gently, what you would have wanted, if you were the one who would lose.
events.arc: A Voice in the Empty Chair

choices.text: Answer honestly

ok.log: You answer. The judgement writes itself after that, and it is the best you have given.

fail.log: You cannot answer. You give the judgement anyway, and it is only fair.

choices.text: Tell the chair it is not its case

effects.log: The voice laughs, very drily. "It never was," it says. "That is the trouble with chairs."

events.text: The voice in the chair has grown fainter every year. Tonight it barely reaches you. Jang Murae, or what the chair keeps of them, says it is tired of remembering, and asks you to let it rest: to sit in the chair one night and think of nothing at all.
events.arc: A Voice in the Empty Chair

choices.text: Do it

effects.log: You sit all night and empty yourself. At dawn the chair is only wood. You miss the voice for a thousand years.

choices.text: Ask for one more night

effects.log: The voice gives you one more. It tells you a joke from before the Calendar. Then it rests.

events.text: In the archive behind the nameless door, Seo Gyeol's student finds the last page Jang Murae ever wrote. It is not a judgement. It is a letter to whoever would sit in the chair next, and it begins: "You will be asked to take a side. Here is what happened when I did."

choices.text: Read it

effects.log: Jang Murae took a side once, for a pantheon that was right. It won. Then it became the pantheon everyone needed protecting from.

choices.text: Seal it unread

effects.log: You seal it. Some warnings should be learned, not read. Seo Gyeol's student is deeply disappointed.

events.text: The rest of the letter: after the side they chose won, no pantheon trusted the first Arbiter again, and heaven stopped bringing its quarrels to the empty space, and a judge nobody comes to fades. "Neutrality is not a virtue," Jang Murae wrote. "It is the price of being asked."

choices.text: Carve the last line over your door

effects.log: It stands over the door for the rest of your life. Every envoy reads it coming in.

choices.text: Write your own answer under it

effects.log: You write: "And it is worth it." Seo Gyeol adds the date. Neither of you is sure it is true.

events.text: The pantheon Jang Murae helped, long ago, still exists. It is one of the four, and it does not know. You could tell it. It would change how it sees itself, and how it sees the empty space.

choices.text: Tell it

effects.log: The pantheon is silent for an age. Then its envoys come to your bench more humbly than before.

choices.text: Let it not know

effects.log: The secret stays between you and a dead Arbiter. Heaven goes on, a little unbalanced, a little kinder for not knowing.

events.text: Heaven is calm. No pantheon is at war; no god is selling their domain; the Calamity Stars keep their distance. Your bench has been empty for a month. Seo Gyeol has started reorganising the shelves, twice.

choices.text: Rest

effects.log: You rest for the first time in an age. It is strange, and good, and you sleep for a year.

choices.text: Go and look for the quarrels nobody is bringing

effects.log: You walk heaven for a decade. You find several, small, festering in corners. You hear them.

events.text: In a calm heaven, the young gods have begun to say that the Arbiter is no longer needed. They say it in the festivals, laughing, and in the halls of the Court, not laughing. A petition circulates to turn the empty space into a garden.

choices.text: Let them say it

effects.log: You let them. That they can say it is the measure of what you have done. You do not say so.

choices.text: Hold a hearing on the petition, fairly

effects.log: You hear the case for your own abolition. It is well argued. You rule, at length, that a chair is cheap and a war is not.

events.text: The young gods who wanted a garden have their first real quarrel: two of them, over a domain. They come to your bench, sheepishly, because there is nowhere else to go.

choices.text: Hear them without a word about the petition

effects.log: You hear them. Neither mentions the garden. Afterwards one of them plants a tree outside your door.

choices.text: Mention the garden, once, lightly

effects.log: They blush. You judge them fairly anyway. The story goes round heaven and ends the petition.

events.text: Heaven is shaking. Every pantheon has a grievance; the Court cannot keep up with its warrants; below the clouds, the seasons have started to come in the wrong order. Envoys stand three deep at your bench and none of them will wait.

choices.text: Hear the gravest first, and only the gravest

effects.log: You sort the cases like a field surgeon. Many are angry. The worst are heard.

choices.text: Close the bench for a day, and think

effects.log: A day of silence while heaven shakes. Envoys are furious. At dawn you have a plan.

choices.text: Hear every case as it comes, all of them

effects.log: You do not sleep for a year. Heaven sees the Arbiter work. It helps a little.

events.text: In the shaking, a god of the Throne of Storms has let loose a gale that has torn a hall of the Will of Heaven off its foundations. Both pantheons have their armies out. The gale is still blowing. Cheon Ugeun and Hwang Seonjae both stand at your bench.

choices.text: Step into the gale and stop it

ok.log: You stand in the wind until it breaks around you. Both armies see it, and lower their weapons.

fail.log: The gale throws you back. You get up. You go back in. The second time it stops, and you are hurt.

choices.text: Bring the two envoys into the same room and lock it

effects.log: Hwang Seonjae and Cheon Ugeun, locked in, find a way. The gale dies at midnight.

events.text: Below, the seasons have come wrong for ten years: snow at harvest, drought in the floods' months. The mortals do not know which god to blame and blame them all. Their prayers arrive at your chair with no god's name on them, only "whoever is responsible."

choices.text: Take the prayers as yours

effects.log: You answer them, a little each night. It is not your domain. It steadies them, and you.

choices.text: Send them to the twelve gods of the domains, by name

effects.log: Each god of each domain receives a sack of prayers marked "whoever is responsible". Most are ashamed.

events.text: The shaking is passing. Not because of any one judgement, but because heaven has seen the Arbiter at work every day of it, and has begun, in small ways, to imitate. Gods settle little things themselves now, in the way they have watched you do.

choices.text: Write it in the Book

effects.log: Seo Gyeol writes: "The shaking ended." There is no judgement attached. It is the only such page.

choices.text: Rest, at last

effects.log: You sleep a decade. Nobody wakes you. When you open your eyes the bench is quiet and the seasons are right.

events.text: Heaven has been stable long enough that the four pantheons want to hold a festival for it. The Festival of the Level Scales, they call it. They want the Arbiter to open it. You have never opened a festival.
events.arc: The Festival of the Level Scales

choices.text: Open it

effects.log: You stand before all four pantheons and say a few words. They are short. The pantheons cheer as if you had said something.

choices.text: Ask them to open it themselves

effects.log: Four envoys open it together, a word each. It is the best opening in the Calendar.

events.text: At the festival, a game has grown up: young gods of rival pantheons try to balance a set of scales by putting things in each other's pans. It is noisy and silly and they are all laughing. Seo Gyeol watches it with tears in their eyes.
events.arc: The Festival of the Level Scales

choices.text: Join in

effects.log: You put a hailstone in one pan and a seed in the other. They balance. The young gods are amazed and want to know how.

choices.text: Watch with Seo Gyeol

effects.log: You stand with your clerk and watch. "This is what it was for," Seo Gyeol says.

events.text: The Festival of the Level Scales has become part of the Heavenly Calendar. The keepers ask what should happen to it in an age when heaven is not stable. Should it be held anyway, or skipped, so that it means something?
events.arc: The Festival of the Level Scales

choices.text: Hold it always

effects.log: It is held in good ages and bad. In bad ones, it is a promise.

choices.text: Hold it only when it is earned

effects.log: It is skipped in the bad ages. Gods work to bring it back. It means a great deal.

events.text: When heaven is unsteady, the world below feels it first. A great river below has split in two, each half running to a different god's sea. The people on its banks pray that the gods will stop fighting over their river.

choices.text: Go down and stand in the river

effects.log: You stand where it splits. The two halves curl round your ankles and, after a day, run together again.

choices.text: Summon the two sea-gods

effects.log: They come, both certain the river is theirs. You hear them. The river waits, split.

events.text: The people of the river below have built a statue of a figure standing in the water, arms out, a hand to each bank. It does not look like you. They do not know what you look like. It is the most accurate statue of you in any world.

choices.text: Visit it once

effects.log: You stand beside it in disguise. A child tells you who it is. They get most of it right.

choices.text: Leave it be

effects.log: You never see it. Seo Gyeol does, and describes it to you, and you are moved.

events.text: Heaven settles, and the river below runs whole. The people still keep the statue. Every year they hold a day when two quarrelling families must each stand on one bank and shout their case across the water until one of them laughs.

choices.text: Send a blessing on the day

effects.log: A soft wind carries both families' words across. More of them laugh. More of them settle.

choices.text: Write the custom into the Book

effects.log: A mortal custom of settling, in the Book of heaven. Gods begin to try it, on rivers of their own.

events.text: Your chair has worn to the shape of you. The arms have two smooth places where your hands rest; the seat has sunk; the back leans a little to the left. Seo Gyeol asks, carefully, whether you would like a new one.

choices.text: Keep this one

effects.log: You keep it. It leans. You lean with it. Litigants find the lean reassuring.

choices.text: Have it straightened, not replaced

effects.log: A carpenter of the Mountains straightens it. It creaks for a year and then is quiet.

events.text: In the unsteady years, the four envoys have stopped dining together. Hwang Seonjae eats alone in the Will of Heaven; Mok Dami does not eat; Na Puleum is ill; Cheon Ugeun rains on everyone. Someone has to invite them.

choices.text: Invite them, yourself, all four

effects.log: They come. Nobody speaks. By the end, Mok Dami has passed Hwang Seonjae the salt.

choices.text: Invite them one at a time

effects.log: Four dinners, four confessions. Each envoy tells you what they will not tell the others.

events.text: Heaven is so calm that dust has settled on the pans of your scales. Seo Gyeol wants to wipe them. You find yourself wanting to see how long the dust can lie there undisturbed.

choices.text: Let it lie

effects.log: The dust lies for a century. It is a kind of record. When it is finally disturbed, by a small case about a fence, you are almost glad.

choices.text: Wipe the scales yourself

effects.log: You polish them until they shine. They are ready for anything. It comes, eventually.

events.text: Seo Gyeol's student has counted: you have given more judgements than there are stars in the sky of heaven. They want to make a star for each one. Cheonho, Who Hangs the Stars, is willing.

choices.text: Let them

effects.log: A whole new constellation, vast and faint, of every judgement. Below, sailors cannot use it; it is too crowded.

choices.text: Ask for one star only: for the first case

effects.log: One small star for Gu Hyeon's well. It hangs just above the horizon.

events.text: In the worst year of the shaking, you catch yourself thinking that if you chose a side, just once, the shaking would stop. It is probably true. Jang Murae's letter is in the drawer.

choices.text: Read the letter again

effects.log: You read the first Arbiter's warning by lamplight. In the morning you judge level, and it is harder than ever.

choices.text: Go and stand at the edge of heaven

effects.log: You look at the world below until the thought passes. It takes all night.

events.text: A god from a faded pantheon, the last of their line, comes to see the empty space because they have heard that heaven is at peace, and they want to see what peace looks like before they fade too.

choices.text: Show them the bench, the Book, the scales

effects.log: You show them everything. They sit on the bench a while. "Smaller than I thought," they say, and are content.

choices.text: Show them the four envoys at dinner

effects.log: They watch four pantheons share a meal. They fade a year later, smiling.

events.text: Your hands shake now, a little, when you hold the brush to sign a judgement. Nobody mentions it. Seo Gyeol's student has started, without being asked, to steady the paper.

choices.text: Thank them

effects.log: You thank them. They blush. From then on every judgement of yours has two hands in it.

choices.text: Sign anyway, shaking

effects.log: Your signature wavers. Heaven, oddly, trusts the wavering ones more.

events.text: The keepers of the Heavenly Calendar tell you that when your scales are level, the seasons below come exactly on time; when they tip, the seasons wander. They have kept the figures for an age. They show you the chart.

choices.text: Study it

effects.log: You learn to read the seasons below as a measure of your own work. It is humbling.

choices.text: Ask them to send the chart to all four pantheons

effects.log: The pantheons see how their quarrels fall on the harvest. Some are more careful.

events.text: Seo Gyeol has chosen a student without telling you: Han Byeol, a young god of no domain who came to your hall to deliver a letter and stayed to sweep. They have a terrible hand and a perfect memory. Seo Gyeol asks your leave to teach them the Book.

choices.text: Give it gladly

effects.log: Han Byeol bows so low they drop the broom. Seo Gyeol picks it up, and something in their face loosens.

choices.text: Ask to examine them first

effects.log: You ask Han Byeol to recite the first page of the Book. They recite it, and then the margin, and then the ink Seo Gyeol used.

events.text: Han Byeol has found an error in the Book of Precedent: a judgement in Seo Gyeol's own hand, centuries old, that cites a precedent that does not exist. They are frightened to say so. Seo Gyeol has seen them hesitating and asks what is wrong.

choices.text: Let Han Byeol tell them

effects.log: Han Byeol tells them. Seo Gyeol goes white, then laughs, then corrects it in front of both of you. It is a good morning.

choices.text: Tell Seo Gyeol yourself, privately

effects.log: You tell them. Seo Gyeol corrects it at night. Han Byeol never knows it was mended.

events.text: Seo Gyeol is fading. A clerk of heaven lives as long as their work does, and the first Book is closed. They spend their days now on the bench outside, in the sun, listening to Han Byeol read the morning's cases aloud, and correcting their pronunciation.

choices.text: Sit with them each morning

effects.log: You hear your own cases read aloud on the bench with your clerk. It is the slowest, best court of your life.

choices.text: Ask the four pantheons to keep them

ok.log: Four envoys lay their hands on Seo Gyeol. The fading slows. They have a century more, and spend it teaching.

fail.log: The pantheons try. Nothing holds a clerk whose Book is closed.

events.text: Seo Gyeol has faded, on the bench, in the sun, mid-sentence while correcting Han Byeol. Han Byeol finishes the sentence for them. On the first page of the second Book, under the copy of the first case, they write one line in their terrible hand.

choices.text: Read the line

effects.log: It says: "Seo Gyeol kept this. Now I do." You read it many times over the years.

choices.text: Ask Han Byeol to grind the last of the sliver ink

effects.log: The last of the ink from your chair writes Seo Gyeol's name on the cover of the first Book, in a hand that is theirs.

events.text: Gu Hyeon has gone down to the world below to the town of the first case. They write to you from it: the well is full; the town is small and stubborn; its children throw pebbles in the well and make wishes, and Gu Hyeon grants the small ones.

choices.text: Write back every year

effects.log: Your letters and theirs cross for a century. Gu Hyeon's are full of the town. Yours, you notice, are full of cases.

choices.text: Visit, in disguise

effects.log: You drink from the well. It is cold and good. Gu Hyeon sees you, and pretends not to.

events.text: A child of the town below has wished, at the well, to become a judge. Gu Hyeon has never granted a wish so large. They ask you, by letter, whether they should, and whether it is their place.

choices.text: "Grant the learning, not the office"

effects.log: The child grows up clever and fair. Whether they become a judge is their own doing. They do.

choices.text: "Not your place, nor mine"

effects.log: Gu Hyeon grants nothing. The child becomes a judge anyway, by sheer stubbornness, which is the town's gift.

events.text: The child of the well became a judge below, and a good one, and on the day they died they climbed into heaven as a newly risen god, and came straight to your chair. It is the young god who once accused a god of springs before you, a long time ago.

choices.text: Tell them where they came from

effects.log: They listen, astonished, and go down to the well, and sit with Gu Hyeon for a year.

choices.text: Let Gu Hyeon tell them

effects.log: Gu Hyeon tells them. The young god comes back up with a pebble from the well, and gives it to you.

events.text: Na Puleum has faded, as the eldest of the Green Assembly do, into a grove. Their successor as envoy is very young: Na Saeum, a sapling-god barely a century old, who has never been to your hall and is terrified of the hailstone.

choices.text: Show them the shelf, gently

effects.log: You show them the seed, the hailstone, the feather. Na Saeum touches the seed and says, "That was mine. Before."

choices.text: Hear their first petition as if they were Na Puleum

effects.log: You hear them gravely. Their petition is about a hedge. They are so relieved they cry.

events.text: Na Saeum brings the Green Assembly's first hard case: the war between two of their own gods, Saengmo's line and Horang's, has broken out again after ten thousand years. The young envoy asks how Na Puleum would have handled it.

choices.text: Tell them what you remember

effects.log: You tell them about the stags and the fence. Na Saeum goes home and finds a stag, and asks it.

choices.text: Tell them to handle it as they would

effects.log: Na Saeum handles it badly, then well. The Assembly is surprised by them.

events.text: At the envoys' dinner, Na Saeum sits in Na Puleum's old place for the first time. The other three envoys wait to see what they will say. They say nothing. They put a sapling in a pot on the table, the way Na Puleum used to.

choices.text: Water it

effects.log: You water it. The other envoys look at each other. The dinners go on.

choices.text: Leave it for the envoys

effects.log: Hwang Seonjae waters it. Cheon Ugeun rains on it a little. It grows.

events.text: Mok Dami of the Silent Hall has spoken aloud in your hall for the first time in a thousand years of visits: one word, "No," at a ruling you gave. The whole Silent Hall heard it, from across heaven. They are horrified. Mok Dami is quietly pleased.

choices.text: Ask them what was wrong

effects.log: They tell you, in a whisper that takes an hour. It was a ruling on a dream. They were right. You change it.

choices.text: Stand by the ruling

effects.log: Mok Dami bows. They have said their word. The Silent Hall forgives them, slowly.

events.text: The Silent Hall has called Mok Dami home to answer for speaking. Mok Dami asks if you will come and listen, not to judge. In the Silent Hall, a trial is held in silence, and the verdict is whether anyone speaks at the end.

choices.text: Go, and keep the silence

effects.log: You sit through a day of silence. At the end, Unmyeong the Weaver says one word: "Enough." Mok Dami is free.

choices.text: Go, and speak for them at the end

ok.log: You say: "They were right." The Silent Hall is shocked, and agrees, silently.

fail.log: Your word falls into the silence and is not picked up. Mok Dami is sent to the archives for a century.

events.text: Mok Dami has begun to speak at your dinners. Very little, very quietly. The other envoys lean in. It is as if a new pantheon had joined the table.

choices.text: Ask them to say grace

effects.log: Mok Dami says one sentence over the food, about the dead. Nobody forgets it.

choices.text: Say nothing, and listen

effects.log: You listen. Mok Dami says, eventually, that this is the only place in heaven they are not afraid to talk.

events.text: The Will of Heaven has put Hwang Seonjae on trial in their own hall, under their own law, for the shadow that spreads from them. Your precedent says doubt is no crime under the scales. Their hall says the scales do not reach inside it.

choices.text: Go to the trial as a witness

effects.log: You stand in the shadowless hall and testify. Every god there sees that the Arbiter has a shadow too.

choices.text: Rule that your precedent reaches every hall

effects.log: It is a large claim. The Will of Heaven rejects it. The other three pantheons watch closely.

events.text: The Will of Heaven's verdict: Hwang Seonjae is guilty of doubt and stripped of their herald's rank. Then Mujin of the Thousand Banners, who prosecuted, stands up in the noon light, and everyone sees that Mujin's shadow has grown too.

choices.text: Say nothing

effects.log: The hall sees it without you. The verdict stands, and is quietly never enforced.

choices.text: Point it out, gently

effects.log: Mujin looks down at their own shadow a long time. "Then I am guilty too," they say, and sit down.

events.text: Hwang Seonjae, a herald no longer, has come to live in the empty space, in a little room beside your hall, and keeps your door. Envoys of the Will of Heaven still bow to them on the way in. Their shadow falls across your threshold every morning.

choices.text: Give them a new title: keeper of the door

effects.log: They take it with a laugh. They are the best doorkeeper heaven has had.

choices.text: Let them keep it without title

effects.log: They keep the door because they want to. Titles, they say, were the trouble.

events.text: Cheon Ugeun brings their last forecast before they retire as herald: a quarrel coming from the Throne of Storms itself, a century off, against the empty space. The Throne will say the Arbiter has stopped reading the weather. They are sorry to bring it.

choices.text: Ask what you have missed

effects.log: They tell you: a slow drought in the Throne's mountains, that you ruled on once and forgot. It is still going on.

choices.text: Thank them and wait for it

effects.log: You wait. The quarrel comes exactly when forecast. You are ready for it.

events.text: The drought in the mountains of the Throne of Storms: Daeak of the Unmoving Peak has been holding back the rain, unknowing, for three centuries, out of grief for a mountain they lost. Cheon Ugeun weeps over the forecast. It does not rain.

choices.text: Go and sit with Daeak

effects.log: You sit with the mountain-god a decade. They grieve aloud for the first time. The rain comes.

choices.text: Rule that the rain must fall

effects.log: The rain falls by law. The grief stays where it was. Daeak is very quiet for an age.

events.text: Cheon Ugeun's last day as herald. They come to your hall in a light, warm rain, and stand by the shelf where the hailstone sits, and tell you their successor will be a storm-god who has never once agreed with them.

choices.text: Promise to read the new one's weather too

effects.log: Cheon Ugeun laughs in thunder and goes out into the sun.

choices.text: Give them the hailstone at last

effects.log: They take it home and set it in the floor of the Throne's hall. It still does not melt.

events.text: Pyo Ara has been asked by the Court to do the unthinkable: audit the Court itself, its ladder, its warrants and its seals. They come to you because there is nobody on the ladder they can safely ask for advice.

choices.text: Advise them to start at the top

effects.log: They start at the top rung. The highest judges are outraged. Pyo Ara keeps going.

choices.text: Advise them to start at the bottom

effects.log: They start with the clerks. What they find there leads, slowly and inevitably, upward.

events.text: Pyo Ara's audit of the Court has found that one rung of the ladder has been selling warrants: a warrant against a rival for a price. The rung is held by a god very high and very old. Pyo Ara is afraid.

choices.text: Hear the case at your own chair

effects.log: You take it from the Court. The god on that rung is sealed. The Court thanks you with its teeth.

choices.text: Return it to the Court with your protection for Pyo Ara

effects.log: The Court judges its own. Pyo Ara is under the Arbiter's seal, and nobody touches them.

events.text: Every warrant the corrupt rung sold must now be reviewed. There are nine thousand. Pyo Ara and Han Byeol sit in your hall for a century, beads clicking, pages turning, and one by one the wrongly accused are told they are free.

choices.text: Help them

effects.log: You take a thousand of the warrants yourself. You do not finish first. Han Byeol does.

choices.text: Let them work, and judge the hard ones

effects.log: Forty of the warrants come to your bench. You judge each slowly. Heaven sees.

events.text: Hyeolsa keeps the domain of Thresholds now, or waits for it, and the comet that raided heaven for nine thousand years has a visitor's bench outside its door. The first visitor, it tells you, was a god it once raided. They came to talk.

choices.text: Ask what they spoke of

effects.log: "The night I burned their hall," Hyeolsa says. "They wanted to know if I remembered. I did."

choices.text: Leave the comet its visitors

effects.log: You do not ask. Others come after. Hyeolsa's bench is never empty for long.

events.text: A young god has come to Hyeolsa's door, cast out by their own pantheon for a crime they did not do, and asked the comet what to do with their anger. Hyeolsa brings them to you instead of answering.

choices.text: Hear their case

effects.log: You hear it. They were wronged. You set it right, with Hyeolsa watching from the door, red and quiet.

choices.text: Ask Hyeolsa to answer them first

effects.log: The comet tells them: do not wait nine thousand years. Then you hear the case.

events.text: Hyeolsa has asked for one more hearing: its own, again, from the start. Not to change the sentence, it says. To hear itself told by a court that will listen, now that it can sit still long enough to be heard.

choices.text: Hear it

effects.log: You hear the whole case of the Red Comet again. At the end, Hyeolsa thanks you, and goes back to its door, and closes it gently.

choices.text: Tell it the Book already holds it

effects.log: Hyeolsa reads its own page in the Book. It is enough. It was always enough.

events.text: Han Byeol's handwriting is so bad that litigants have started to bring their own clerks to read the Arbiter's judgements aloud. Han Byeol is mortified and practising at night. The ink has run out twice this month.

choices.text: Have them read every judgement aloud

effects.log: Han Byeol becomes the voice of the Arbiter's chair. Their reading is perfect. Nobody minds the hand.

choices.text: Teach them yourself, stroke by stroke

effects.log: A century of lessons. Their hand improves. Yours, oddly, gets worse.

events.text: The pebble from Gu Hyeon's well sits on your shelf of evidence beside the hailstone and the seed. On dry days, it is damp. On the day of any case about water, it is wet through.

choices.text: Keep it where it is

effects.log: It becomes a quiet witness. You never rule on water without looking at it.

choices.text: Take it with you to every hearing on water

effects.log: You carry it in your sleeve. The gods of water notice, and are careful.

events.text: All four of the first envoys are gone now, faded or retired, and their successors have never known a heaven without the empty space. They take your chair for granted, the way mortals take the sky. You find you are glad.

choices.text: Tell them about the first envoys

effects.log: You tell them. The new envoys listen politely and do not quite believe it.

choices.text: Let them take it for granted

effects.log: It is the best thing that could have happened to it.

events.text: You catch Pyo Ara counting on their black abacus during one of your hearings. Afterwards they show you what they counted: how many times each party was allowed to speak. It is level, to the bead.

choices.text: Ask them to count every hearing

effects.log: They count for a century. Nothing changes. It is reassuring to know.

choices.text: Ask what they would have done if it were not

effects.log: "Told you," they say, surprised you needed to ask.

events.text: The young champion who took Ok Saebyeok's blade has fought their first trial with it, and lost. They come to apologise to the blade, which hangs, or used to hang, in your hall.

choices.text: Tell them the blade has lost too

effects.log: They did not know Ok Saebyeok ever lost. They go away lighter.

choices.text: Let them sit with it

effects.log: They sit beside it an hour. Then they bow to it and go back to train.

events.text: Han Byeol and Baek Narae, the grey clerk who once brought the true book, have become friends. They argue over the precise meaning of every word of every judgement, loudly, at lunch. It is the most useful noise in your hall.

choices.text: Join them at lunch

effects.log: You eat with your clerks and are corrected twice before the soup. You enjoy it.

choices.text: Have their arguments written down

effects.log: The arguments of two clerks become a commentary on the Book. Heaven studies it.

events.text: A god of lanterns has faded, the last of their mortal worshippers gone, and left a small domain: the light of lamps in windows at night. Three gods claim it as heirs. One is the faded god's child, one their student, and one the god of Fire, who says all light is theirs.

choices.text: Hear the child first

effects.log: The child has kept one lamp burning for a century, in the faded god's empty hall. It is very small.

choices.text: Hear the god of Fire first

effects.log: Hwarin of the First Hearth argues well: a lamp is a fire. It is true. It is not the whole truth.

events.text: Below the clouds, the lamps in windows have begun to flicker, because nobody holds their domain. Mortals put lamps in their windows for travellers coming home. Tonight, many travellers will not find their way.

choices.text: Hold the domain yourself until judgement

effects.log: You hold the lamps of the world below for a season. It is not your domain. They burn steady.

choices.text: Give it to the child at once, on trial

effects.log: The child takes the lamps. They flicker, then steady. The other heirs object, and the lamps stay lit.

events.text: Your ruling on the lamps of windows: it goes to the one who kept a lamp burning when nobody was watching. The child bows. The student is hurt. Hwarin of the First Hearth, to everyone's surprise, gives the child a coal from the first fire as a gift.

choices.text: Write it as precedent: a domain goes to its keeper

effects.log: Seo Gyeol writes it. Every faded domain after is decided by who kept it.

choices.text: Give the student a lamp of their own

effects.log: One window, one lamp, the student's alone. They keep it the rest of their life.

events.text: Gang Dohee, a god of the Harvest's orchards, has petitioned to stop being a god. They want to go below and live one mortal life, and grow old, and die, as the orchard-keepers they watched for ten thousand years have done.

choices.text: Hear why

effects.log: "Because I have never been afraid," Gang Dohee says. "And every mortal I loved was. I want to know what they knew."

choices.text: Rule that no law lets a god resign

effects.log: Gang Dohee bows. They go back to their orchards and tend them worse.

events.text: Pungnyeon of the Golden Field objects: if gods may resign, heaven will empty in an age of the tired ones. Saengmo, Mother of Seeds, supports Gang Dohee: life is for living. Both are right. Gang Dohee waits.

choices.text: Allow it, once, as an exception

effects.log: Gang Dohee goes below as a newborn. Their orchards are given to their student. Heaven watches what becomes of them.

choices.text: Find a middle way: one life, then return

ok.log: One mortal life, then the domain again if they wish. Both gods accept. Gang Dohee goes, weeping with joy.

fail.log: There is no such law and you cannot make one. You must refuse. Gang Dohee understands, and is broken a little.

events.text: Gang Dohee lived one mortal life below: an orchard-keeper, poor, much loved, afraid of many things. They died old. Now they stand before your chair again, a god, and say they would like to keep their domain, and that they are frightened all the time now, and glad.

choices.text: Welcome them home

effects.log: The orchards of heaven are tended better than they have ever been. Gang Dohee is gentler with every mortal who prays.

choices.text: Ask what the fear taught them

effects.log: "That it is what makes a promise worth keeping," they say. You write it down.

events.text: Twin gods, Seol and Ha of the east wind, have shared their domain since the beginning, blowing turn and turn about. Now they want it split: the east wind in two, one half for each. Nobody knows what half a wind is.

choices.text: Ask each what they want their half to do

effects.log: Seol wants a wind for ships. Ha wants a wind for kites. They have wanted it for an age, and never said.

choices.text: Refuse: a wind cannot be split

effects.log: The twins go home and quarrel in the air. Below, the east wind is erratic for a century.

events.text: The split you ruled: the east wind over water for Seol, over land for Ha. It works for a decade, and then a ship tries to fly a kite, and both twins claim the wind that carries it.

choices.text: Rule that the kite decides

effects.log: A kite is Ha's. A ship is Seol's. A ship with a kite is a festival. The twins laugh, together, for the first time in an age.

choices.text: Reunite the domain

effects.log: One east wind again. The twins accept it, relieved; it turns out they missed each other.

events.text: A god of a small river borrowed faith from a god of a great one in a drought, a thousand years ago: a share of the great river's worship, to keep their own flowing. The great god now wants it back, with interest. The small river would run dry.

choices.text: Hear the loan's terms

effects.log: The loan was made by a handshake on a riverbank. There were no terms. That is the problem.

choices.text: Rule that faith cannot be lent

effects.log: A bold precedent. The great god is furious. Every loan of worship in heaven is suddenly in doubt.

events.text: The mortals of the small river do not know their prayers were borrowed. They pray to their own god, as always. If the debt is repaid, their prayers will go elsewhere without their knowing. Yun Haesol, or someone like them, would call it theft.

choices.text: Rule that the mortals must be asked

effects.log: The question goes down in a dream. The mortals of the small river choose their own god. The debt is void.

choices.text: Rule for repayment, over a thousand years

effects.log: Slowly, prayers drift to the great river. The small river shrinks. Its god does not complain.

events.text: The great river-god comes back, not to appeal. They have watched the small river for an age and are ashamed. They forgive the debt, and ask to be judged for having asked for it.

choices.text: Judge them: a season of the small river's work

effects.log: The great god keeps a small river for a season. They come back humbled and much kinder.

choices.text: Rule there is nothing to judge

effects.log: Shame is its own sentence. The great god nods and goes, lighter.

events.text: In a case of murder below the clouds, a god is accused of drowning a mortal in a river. The only witness is the river itself, which is very old, and very slow, and has never testified before.

choices.text: Call the river

effects.log: It takes a month for the river to arrive in your hall, as a slow cold mist. It wants to tell everything it ever saw.

choices.text: Judge on the other evidence

effects.log: The other evidence is weak. The god walks free. The river, below, runs a little darker.

events.text: The river has testified for a year. It has told you about ten thousand years of drownings, rescues, washing and love. At the end of the year it reaches the night of the case, and stops, and says it does not want to say it.

choices.text: Ask it gently, again

ok.log: The river tells it. The god did not drown the mortal; they tried to save them, and failed. They have never forgiven themselves.

fail.log: The river will not. It goes back below. The god is judged on doubt, and acquitted, and does not believe it.

choices.text: Release the river from its oath

effects.log: The river goes home. The god is acquitted. You never know what the river saw.

events.text: The god who failed to save the mortal from the river has asked to become a keeper of that river, so that nobody drowns in it again. The river has agreed, which rivers rarely do.

choices.text: Grant it

effects.log: Nobody drowns in that river again for ten thousand years. The god keeps it, and is quiet, and is mostly at peace.

choices.text: Grant it, for a thousand years only

effects.log: A sentence of mercy, with an end. The god keeps it, and at the end, asks to keep it longer.

events.text: A god of the Silent Hall has had their true name stolen. Without it they cannot be prayed to; their worshippers below pray into silence, and the god is fading by the day. They suspect a god of the Will of Heaven, who has been heard using it.

choices.text: Summon the suspect

effects.log: The god of the Will of Heaven comes, wearing the stolen name like a borrowed cloak. They say they found it lying in the road.

choices.text: First give the fading god a name to live on

effects.log: You lend them a name, temporary, from the Book. They stop fading. Their worshippers below are confused, and pray anyway.

events.text: The god who took the name says names are not property: you cannot steal what was never owned. They have a precedent, an old one of Jang Murae's, which says exactly that. Han Byeol finds it in the drawer. It is real.

choices.text: Uphold Jang Murae: names are not property

effects.log: The thief keeps the name. The robbed god keeps the lent name. It is lawful, and it is wrong, and you know it.

choices.text: Overturn Jang Murae

ok.log: You overturn the first Arbiter. A name is not property; it is a person. The thief must give it back.

fail.log: You cannot find the words to overturn it. The precedent stands. The robbed god looks at you a long time.

events.text: The name is returned. The god of the Silent Hall speaks it aloud in your hall, and below, all at once, the prayers into silence are heard. The thief, unnamed now, has nothing to be called by, and asks you for something.

choices.text: Give them a name from the Book

effects.log: You give them a plain name, an honest one. They take it. They are better company under it.

choices.text: Let them find their own

effects.log: They walk heaven nameless for a century and come back with one they chose. It suits them.

events.text: The robbed god lives on the lent name now, and has decided to keep it. The old name is still worn by the thief. Their worshippers below have two gods, one wearing each name, and are unsure which to pray to.

choices.text: Let the mortals choose

effects.log: Most go to the lent name, because it answers kindly. The thief fades a little, deservedly.

choices.text: Rule the old name retired

effects.log: Nobody may use it. It goes in the drawer. Heaven has one name fewer.

events.text: A whole kingdom below has filed a suit against heaven, by prayer, all of it at once: a million voices on the same night, with a list. Heaven, they say, has sent them three plagues, two famines and a war in one generation, and has never said why.

choices.text: Hear it

effects.log: You hear a mortal kingdom's case against heaven. The gods of the domains involved are summoned. Several are very uncomfortable.

choices.text: Rule that heaven need not explain

effects.log: The prayers stop. The kingdom goes on. Something in it closes, towards heaven, for an age.

events.text: The gods summoned to answer the kingdom's suit have answers: the plague was a god of Death's error; the famines were weather from a quarrel of the Throne of Storms; the war was nobody's, the mortals' own. The kingdom wants an apology for the first two.

choices.text: Order the apologies

effects.log: Two gods apologise to a mortal kingdom, in dreams. The kingdom is astonished. It rebuilds faster.

choices.text: Order repair, not apology

effects.log: Harvests are doubled for a decade, and no plague touches the kingdom for a century. They are grateful and still angry.

events.text: Saengmo, Mother of Seeds, and Baekun the Pale Ferryman are arguing about one tree below, very old, that should have died a century ago and has not. Life says it is theirs. Death says it is overdue.

choices.text: Rule the tree may choose its hour

effects.log: The tree goes on another century, then falls in a storm on a quiet night. Both gods attend.

choices.text: Rule for Death: everything has an hour

effects.log: The tree falls that winter. Saengmo plants its seed in your garden.

events.text: A minor god has asked the Arbiter to name them, because nobody ever did: they were made in a hurry during a war, to hold a bridge, and the war ended before anyone had time. They have held the bridge for nine thousand years.

choices.text: Name them after the bridge

effects.log: They are delighted. Below, the bridge is renamed to match. Travellers greet it by name.

choices.text: Ask them what they would like

effects.log: They have thought about it for nine thousand years. They have a list. You help them choose.

events.text: The smallest case ever brought to your chair: two gods of neighbouring gardens and a single plum that fell on the line between them. Both have hired champions for a Trial of Judgement. The champions are embarrassed.

choices.text: Cut the plum in half

effects.log: You cut it. Each god gets half. The champions go home unbloodied and laughing.

choices.text: Eat the plum yourself

effects.log: You eat it. "Case dismissed for lack of evidence," you say. Both gods are outraged and delighted.

events.text: A mortal judge has climbed to heaven after death, not as a god, only as a soul passing through, and asked to see the Arbiter on the way to the Ferryman. They have one question: were their judgements in life any good?

choices.text: Read their record in the Book of Fates

effects.log: You read it. Most were good. A few were not. You tell them both. They go to the boat at peace.

choices.text: Ask them which ones they doubt

effects.log: They name three. You look at them. Two were right. They go to the boat grateful for one.

events.text: Cheonho, Who Hangs the Stars, and Hwarin of the First Hearth both claim the sun. The Sky holds it up; Fire makes it burn. They have argued about it since before the Calendar, and want, after all this time, to be told.

choices.text: Rule it shared, by day and night

effects.log: The sun is Fire's when it burns and the Sky's when it sets. Both gods sulk, and keep the ruling.

choices.text: Rule it belongs to those who see by it

effects.log: The sun is the mortals'. The gods are scandalised. Below, nothing changes, and everything is a little warmer.

events.text: A god has set up as an advocate in the empty space, arguing cases for any side for a fee in faith. They are very good. Litigants who hire them win more. Han Byeol thinks it is unfair. The advocate thinks it is the point.

choices.text: Allow it, and give every litigant an advocate

effects.log: Every side gets one, paid by the empty space. Your hall becomes a place of arguments, and fairer.

choices.text: Forbid it: litigants speak for themselves

effects.log: The advocate goes to the Heavenly Court, which welcomes them. Your hall stays plain.

events.text: A litigant brings a feather from the boat of Baekun the Pale Ferryman as evidence, and sets it on the left pan of your scales. It tips the pan to the floor. Everyone looks at the feather. It weighs exactly what one death weighs.

choices.text: Hear the case with the feather in the pan

effects.log: The case is about a death. The feather stays. Your judgement is slower and heavier.

choices.text: Remove the feather and judge on evidence

effects.log: You take it out. The pans come level. Some evidence is too heavy to be fair.

events.text: The last worshipper of a faded god below has died, and their soul, on the way to the Ferryman, asks to pass through the empty space and leave a prayer for their god, who is gone, on your chair, because there is nowhere else.

choices.text: Accept the prayer

effects.log: It lies on your chair overnight. In the morning it is gone. Mok Dami says, gently, that something heard it.

choices.text: Carry it to the Silent Hall's archive of faded gods

effects.log: It is filed with the god's dust. The archivist weeps; it is the first prayer filed in an age.

events.text: Two crises at once, and Han Byeol has found the thread between them: {sov_corrupt}, whom heaven is judging for selling their domain, has been selling to both sides of the war as well. Every battle raises their prices.

choices.text: Join the two cases

effects.log: One hearing for a war and a corruption. The envoys of both armies sit beside {sov_corrupt} on the bench.

choices.text: Keep them apart, and tell the armies

effects.log: The armies learn who has been profiting. Both cut off {sov_corrupt}. The war slows, for lack of supply.

events.text: With the two armies and {sov_corrupt} on one bench, it emerges that both sides knew. Each bought from the corrupt god because the other did. Nobody can be judged for the war without being judged for the trade.

choices.text: Judge all three together

effects.log: One sentence for three parties. It is long and it holds. Heaven is quiet for a decade, ashamed.

choices.text: Find the one who bought first

ok.log: It was the side that is now losing. You judge them for it. It tips the war; you know it, and do it.

fail.log: The records are burned. You cannot tell. The case collapses into three angry parties.

events.text: The war is over, the corrupt god sealed or stripped. Han Byeol has found one more thread: a mortal city below that supplied {sov_corrupt}'s weapons of heaven, not knowing what they were. Its people ask, by prayer, whether they are guilty.

choices.text: "No."

effects.log: One word, in a dream, to a whole city. Its people sleep for the first time in years.

choices.text: "You did not know. Now you do."

effects.log: The city stops making the strange metal. It makes ploughs instead, and grows rich on them.

events.text: The Calamity Star raids every pantheon but one: {sov_pantheon}, which stands over half of heaven. Na Saeum of the Green Assembly brings you a map of every raid. The only safe ground in heaven is under {sov_pantheon}'s roof.
events.arc: The Pantheon That Fed a Star

choices.text: Ask {sov_pantheon} why

effects.log: Their envoy says the Star fears them. Their envoy is lying, and does it badly.

choices.text: Watch the next raid yourself

effects.log: You follow the Star in the dark. It meets a herald of {sov_pantheon} at the edge of heaven, and they talk.

events.text: {sov_pantheon} has been feeding the Calamity Star the locations of its rivals' weakest domains. The other pantheons grow poorer, and come to {sov_pantheon} for protection, and it grows. It is the most elegant crime you have ever seen.
events.arc: The Pantheon That Fed a Star

choices.text: Expose it before all four pantheons

effects.log: Heaven erupts. {sov_pantheon} loses three domains in a year to their own former allies.

choices.text: Judge it quietly, and bind {sov_pantheon} to repair

effects.log: {sov_pantheon} must rebuild every raided domain, unseen. It does, grimly. Nobody else knows why.

events.text: The Calamity Star, cut off from its informant, has come to your chair of its own accord. It wants to testify against {sov_pantheon}, in exchange for nothing at all. "They used me," it says. "I would like that written somewhere."
events.arc: The Pantheon That Fed a Star

choices.text: Write it in the Book

effects.log: Han Byeol writes it in their terrible hand. The Star reads it and goes, and raids nothing for a year.

choices.text: Judge the Star too

effects.log: You hear its testimony and then its case. It accepts its sentence. It wanted to be judged, it turns out, more than it wanted revenge.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has declared for one claimant to the throne of {sov_realm}, and sent warrants for the others. You hold a rung on its ladder. The other claimants come to the empty space and ask whether the Arbiter is the Court.

choices.text: Say plainly: the Arbiter is not the Court

effects.log: You say it in your hall and on the ladder. The Court is furious. The claimants trust the empty space.

choices.text: Resign your rung

effects.log: You step off the ladder. The Court is shamed by it, and quietly withdraws the warrants.

events.text: The Court's claimant to {sov_realm}, it turns out, owes the Court's high rungs a great deal of faith. Pyo Ara or someone very like them has left the accounts on your bench without a word.

choices.text: Hear the case against the Court

effects.log: The Arbiter judges the Court. It has never been done. You do it slowly and plainly. Two rungs fall.

choices.text: Send the accounts to the Court, and wait

effects.log: The Court has a month to act before you do. It acts. It is very sorry.

events.text: The throne of {sov_realm} has been decided, without the Court's claimant, by the war itself. The Court comes to you, through its highest judge, to ask how it may be trusted again.

choices.text: "Be audited."

effects.log: The Court accepts an audit every age, by an auditor it does not choose. Pyo Ara would have been glad.

choices.text: "Judge one case against yourselves, honestly."

effects.log: The Court does. It loses. Heaven trusts it a little more for that.

events.text: The War in Heaven between {sov_war_a} and {sov_war_b} has made orphans: young gods whose parents fell on both sides, too young to hold the domains they inherit. Both pantheons claim them. Some of them have a parent on each side.

choices.text: Take them into the empty space for now

effects.log: Forty young gods in your hall. It is very loud. Han Byeol teaches them to read the Book.

choices.text: Rule each goes to the side of the parent who fell first

effects.log: It is a rule. It is clean. It sends some children to strangers.
