events.text: Your forty war-orphans have begun to fight among themselves along the lines of the war: {sov_war_a}'s children against {sov_war_b}'s. The ones with a parent on each side are caught in the middle and beaten by both.

choices.text: Put the ones with two sides in charge

effects.log: The children of both sides become the orphans' judges. They are fair, because they have to be.

choices.text: Separate them

effects.log: Two halls, two sides. The fighting stops. So does something else.

events.text: The war-orphans of your hall are grown, and hold their domains, on both sides of the old war. They meet once a year, in your hall, all forty, and have never once fought. Both pantheons have noticed that their wars go worse when the forty are on opposite sides.

choices.text: Let the forty be heaven's peace

effects.log: They become a sort of quiet council. No war since has lasted a decade.

choices.text: Tell them nothing; let it be theirs

effects.log: They never learn what they are. They simply keep meeting.

events.text: A case has come to your chair against one of your own: a disciple of your hall, now a minor god, who used your name to frighten a god of the Lesser Hall into giving up a domain. The evidence is clear. Everyone is watching to see what the Arbiter does to their own.

choices.text: Judge them as any other

effects.log: You judge your own disciple more strictly than you would a stranger, and you know it, and do not stop.

choices.text: Recuse yourself and send it to the Court

effects.log: The Court judges your disciple lightly. Heaven thinks it knows why.

choices.text: Judge them as any other, exactly

effects.log: Not more, not less. It is the hardest thing you have done in a century.

events.text: Your disciple has served their sentence and come back to your door. They do not ask to be a disciple again. They ask only whether you were harder on them than on a stranger.

choices.text: Tell them the truth

effects.log: You were. You say it. They nod, and say they would have been too, in your chair.

choices.text: Tell them the Book will say

effects.log: They read the Book for a year and compare. Then they come back and thank you.

events.text: Ryu Jaeon, a junior envoy of the Throne of Storms, has been caught carrying the words of your private hearings to their pantheon. Cheon Ugeun, or Cheon Ugeun's successor, is mortified and brings them to you in the rain.
events.arc: The Envoy Who Listened at Doors

choices.text: Hear why

effects.log: The Throne threatened their family. Ryu Jaeon wept the whole time they listened. They are the second victim.

choices.text: Ban them from the empty space

effects.log: Ryu Jaeon is banned. The Throne sends a new envoy, and a new listener, eventually.

events.text: Ryu Jaeon's family is under the Throne of Storms's threat. If you judge the Throne, they will suffer. If you do not, the Throne will keep listening at your doors through someone else.
events.arc: The Envoy Who Listened at Doors

choices.text: Bring the family into the empty space first

ok.log: The family arrives in a single night, soaked and safe. Then you judge the Throne.

fail.log: The Throne learns of it first. The family is held. You must bargain.

choices.text: Judge the Throne at once, openly

effects.log: All of heaven hears the charge. The Throne cannot touch the family now without confessing.

events.text: A soldier of the war writes to the Arbiter from the front: the weapons of heaven they were given break on the third blow, and everyone at the front knows who sold them. The letter is signed by forty soldiers of both sides.

choices.text: Bring the letter into {sov_corrupt}'s hearing

effects.log: Forty soldiers' names, read aloud. {sov_corrupt} stops arguing.

choices.text: Send the soldiers better weapons yourself

effects.log: Both sides get shields from the empty space. Neither knows the other did.

events.text: A clerk of the Heavenly Court has come to the empty space to defect: they are afraid of what the high rungs will do now that the Arbiter has judged the Court. They want sanctuary in your hall.

choices.text: Grant it

effects.log: They stay. They know where every file of the Court is kept. You do not ask.

choices.text: Send them back with your seal

effects.log: Your seal on a clerk's sleeve. Nobody on the ladder touches them.

events.text: Mortals below have been drafted into the War in Heaven: their prayers are gathered as weapons by {sov_war_a}. They do not know it. They only feel tired when they pray.

choices.text: Rule it forbidden at once

effects.log: No prayer may be a weapon. {sov_war_a} protests and obeys. Below, people wake rested.

choices.text: Rule it forbidden for both sides

effects.log: Both sides had done it. Both stop. The war is smaller, and slower.

events.text: The Calamity Star has a nest: a dead domain at the edge of heaven where it rests between raids. Han Byeol has found it on an old map. You could go there while it sleeps.

choices.text: Go, and leave a summons beside it

effects.log: The Star wakes to find the Arbiter's summons on its pillow. It comes, out of sheer astonishment.

choices.text: Leave it its rest

effects.log: Even a Calamity Star must sleep somewhere. You mark the map and leave it.

events.text: {sov_pantheon} has petitioned the Arbiter to dissolve the Concord of Domains, on the grounds that a pantheon as large as they are cannot be governed by rules made for small ones.

choices.text: Rule that rules are made for the large

effects.log: The petition is refused. {sov_pantheon} is furious. The small pantheons quote you for an age.

choices.text: Hear it, fully

effects.log: You hear their whole case. It is well made. You refuse it anyway, and explain.

events.text: A bard of heaven has written a lament for the war of the throne of {sov_realm}, and in it the Arbiter is a cold figure who watched and did nothing. It is being sung everywhere. Han Byeol is furious.

choices.text: Let them sing it

effects.log: You let them. The bard, hearing you let them, adds a verse in which the Arbiter is cold, and listening.

choices.text: Invite the bard to a hearing

effects.log: They watch you judge for a week. The lament gets longer and kinder.

events.text: Han Byeol has found, rereading old files, that {sov_accused} was accused by the Court on evidence that a clerk of the Court later confessed to forging. The confession was filed and forgotten.

choices.text: Bring the confession to the Court

effects.log: The Court reads it, white-faced. {sov_accused} is cleared in a day, after a century of being accused.

choices.text: Take the case yourself

effects.log: You clear {sov_accused} in your own hall. The Court is shamed in public. It deserved to be.

events.text: A crisis is alive in heaven and another is beginning, and your decree can only answer one before the clerks tire. Han Byeol lays both drafts on your desk side by side and waits.

choices.text: Answer the one that hurts mortals most

effects.log: The decree goes out for the world below first. The other crisis waits. Heaven grumbles.

choices.text: Answer the one that will spread fastest

effects.log: You stop the fire before it reaches the forest. The other crisis waits, smouldering.

events.text: Bae Onyu was your friend before you were the Arbiter: a god of the Green Assembly's orchards, who shared wine with you on the night you chose the path. They have not visited since. Today they are at your door, unsure if they are allowed in.

choices.text: Welcome them as a friend

effects.log: You sit together on the steps with a pot of tea. It is like the old days, almost. Envoys of the other pantheons notice.

choices.text: Welcome them as a visitor of the Assembly

effects.log: You are courteous. Bae Onyu understands at once, and is hurt, and stays only an hour.

events.text: Bae Onyu has a case before your chair. They did not bring it; their pantheon did, and named them a party. Now the other side says the Arbiter drinks with them, and cannot judge.

choices.text: Recuse yourself

effects.log: The case goes to the Court. Bae Onyu loses it there. They write you one line: "You were right to."

choices.text: Judge it, and judge it against them if the law says

ok.log: The law is against them. You rule it. Bae Onyu stands, bows, and does not visit for a century.

fail.log: You rule for them, fairly. Nobody in heaven believes it was fair.

events.text: A century of silence, and then Bae Onyu comes back with a jar of the same wine. "I have decided," they say, "that a judge who rules against a friend is the only judge worth having as a friend." They pour two cups.

choices.text: Raise the cup

effects.log: You raise the cup and set it down. It is the best wine in heaven, they say. The envoys see you, and say nothing.

choices.text: Raise the cup, and keep the jar on the shelf of evidence

effects.log: The empty jar sits by the hailstone. Bae Onyu laughs every time they see it.

events.text: Bae Onyu stopped coming after your formal welcome. You hear from Na Saeum that they have faded into one of the Assembly's orchards, and left a tree that bears your name on a small tag at its foot.

choices.text: Go and see the tree

effects.log: You stand under it. It bears one fruit a year. You eat it, alone.

choices.text: Send a gardener to tend it

effects.log: The tree is tended for the rest of your life. You never go.

events.text: Someone has set a second chair in heaven: in the shadow of the Throne of Storms's hall, a god named Jin Gyeoul sits and offers judgements to anyone who comes, faster than yours, and simpler. Litigants have started to go there first.

choices.text: Go and watch them judge

effects.log: You sit in the gallery. Jin Gyeoul is quick and clever and decides everything in an hour. Some of it is right.

choices.text: Rule their chair unlawful

effects.log: Your ruling goes out. Jin Gyeoul ignores it. Litigants keep going.

events.text: Jin Gyeoul's judgements are fast, and a third of them come back to your chair on appeal, worse for having been rushed. Jin Gyeoul comes to your hall to complain that you are reversing them.

choices.text: Invite them to sit beside you a season

effects.log: Jin Gyeoul sits at your side for a season, impatient. By the end they ask to stay a year.

choices.text: Tell them speed is not justice

effects.log: They leave angry. Their chair goes on. So do the appeals.

events.text: Jin Gyeoul has learned to judge slowly, and their chair under the Throne of Storms now hears the small cases you do not have time for. Heaven has two chairs, and one of them sends you the hard ones.

choices.text: Recognise their chair as a lesser court

effects.log: Han Byeol writes it into the Book: the Chair of the Storm's Shadow. Jin Gyeoul is very proud.

choices.text: Leave it unrecognised, and trusted

effects.log: Jin Gyeoul prefers it that way. Their chair has no law behind it, only results.

events.text: Seok Ieum, a young god of no pantheon, has sat in your gallery every day for forty years. They have never brought a case. Today they ask if they may be considered, one day, for your chair. They are trembling.
events.arc: The One Who Would Sit After

choices.text: Ask them why

effects.log: "Because nobody else wants it," they say, "and someone should." It is the right answer.

choices.text: Tell them the chair is not given

effects.log: They nod. "Then I will wait until it is taken," they say, and go back to the gallery.

events.text: You set Seok Ieum a test: a real case, small, between two gods of the Lesser Hall. You watch from the gallery. They hear both sides for a week, and then rule for the side you would have ruled against.
events.arc: The One Who Would Sit After

choices.text: Ask them why

effects.log: Their reason is one you had not seen. It is good. It might be better.

choices.text: Overrule them

effects.log: You overrule. Seok Ieum accepts it, and you see them thinking about it for years.

events.text: Seok Ieum has been offered a seat by {sov_pantheon}: a great domain, a hall, everything a young god could want. All they must do is stop sitting in the Arbiter's gallery. They have come to tell you they refused, and to ask whether that was foolish.
events.arc: The One Who Would Sit After

choices.text: "It was the first price. There will be more."

effects.log: They nod slowly. You see them understand what the chair costs.

choices.text: "Take it, if you want it. The chair will wait."

effects.log: They do not take it. But they are glad you said it.

events.text: Seok Ieum has heard a hundred cases at your side. Han Byeol keeps their judgements in a book of their own. When you are absent, litigants have started to ask for Seok Ieum by name.
events.arc: The One Who Would Sit After

choices.text: Name them your successor before the four

effects.log: Four envoys hear it. They do not object. Seok Ieum goes very pale and does not sleep for a week.

choices.text: Name no one: the chair chooses

effects.log: Seok Ieum understands. They go on sitting at your side, unnamed, which is harder.

events.text: Your own sect, the house of your disciples below, has sent up a petition: a rival house has wronged them, and they would like the Arbiter of heaven, who is after all their founder, to say so.

choices.text: Refuse: you judge no case of your own house

effects.log: Your disciples are hurt. Their rivals are astonished. The quarrel is heard by a mortal court, and settled.

choices.text: Send it to your clerks to judge

effects.log: Your clerk judges it, scrupulously, against your own house on one point. Your disciples sulk for a decade.

events.text: Your disciples below have taken your refusal to heart. The house now has a rule: no member may ask a favour of heaven in a quarrel. Other houses have begun to copy it. Below, quarrels are settled by people for the first time in an age.

choices.text: Bless the rule

effects.log: You send a quiet blessing. The house grows, slowly, by reputation for fairness.

choices.text: Say nothing; it is theirs

effects.log: They keep it without your blessing, which they say is the point.

events.text: A painter of heaven, Moon Gaon, asks to paint the Arbiter. All four pantheons have commissioned the portrait together, to hang in each of their halls, and they have agreed, for once, on the painter.

choices.text: Sit for it

effects.log: You sit for a year. Moon Gaon paints slowly and talks a great deal about light.

choices.text: Refuse: let them hang an empty chair

effects.log: Moon Gaon paints your chair, empty, with the crooked scales on it. All four pantheons hang it.

events.text: Moon Gaon has finished, and will not show you. They say the four pantheons must see it first. You hear, from Han Byeol, that each pantheon saw something different in your face, and each was sure it was a lean towards them.

choices.text: Ask to see it at last

effects.log: It is your face, listening. Nothing else. You understand why they each saw what they wanted.

choices.text: Never look

effects.log: You never see it. The portraits hang in four halls. Each pantheon is quietly sure you favour them.

events.text: You have not been to a feast in a pantheon's hall for a thousand years, because going would be a side. Han Byeol has noticed and has made dinner, a bad one, and set two places on the bench outside.

choices.text: Eat it, all of it

effects.log: It is terrible. You eat it all. Han Byeol is so pleased that you will eat it again.

choices.text: Cook the next one yourself

effects.log: You have not cooked in an age. It is worse. You both laugh.

events.text: No case today. Not one. The bench is empty, the envoys are home, and the light in the empty space falls on nothing but the chair.

choices.text: Sit in the light

effects.log: You sit. It is warm. For a whole day nobody needs anything of you.

choices.text: Read the Book from the start

effects.log: You read your own judgements. Some make you wince. You are glad there was no case.

events.text: The bronze pans of your scales have gone green at the edges. A smith of the Mountains offers to recast them. You would have new scales, perfect, and nothing of the old ones.

choices.text: Keep them green

effects.log: They stay green. The smith shrugs. Litigants say the green ones look older, and trust them.

choices.text: Have them cleaned, not recast

effects.log: The smith cleans them for a month. They shine. The weight in the left pan is still there.

events.text: Your hands are always cold now. It is the chair, Mok Dami says: a judge who sits between gives up a little of the warmth of every side. You did not know there was a price written into the wood.

choices.text: Accept it

effects.log: You accept it. Litigants who shake your hand remember the cold.

choices.text: Warm them at Hwarin's first coal

effects.log: The coal warms them, a little, for a day. You go back to it often.

events.text: Four kinds of tea arrive on the same morning, one from each pantheon, each the finest of its hall, each with a note hoping the Arbiter will find it the best.

choices.text: Blend them

effects.log: You drink all four at once. It is awful. You send each pantheon the same note: "Remarkable."

choices.text: Drink water

effects.log: You drink water, plainly, and send the teas to the litigants' bench.

events.text: The child who once brought a case about a kite is grown now, a god of a small domain, and has brought a kite to your hall, a very good one, to fly from the steps with you, as you did once.

choices.text: Fly it

effects.log: You fly it together from the steps of the empty space. Four pantheons watch from their windows, as before.

choices.text: Let them fly it, and watch

effects.log: You watch from the chair. The kite goes very high. Your judgement that day is very kind.

events.text: The pile of petitions waiting for your chair is taller than you are. Han Byeol has sorted it by urgency, by pantheon and by colour of ink. They want to know which order you would like.

choices.text: By how long they have waited

effects.log: The oldest first. It is slow and fair. Nobody can complain, and everybody does.

choices.text: By how much harm they could prevent

effects.log: You go through the pile like a healer. The worst wounds are closed first.

events.text: Once a century, you count yourself. The figure this time: you have judged the Will of Heaven a little more harshly than the others. Not much. Enough to show on the beads.

choices.text: Correct it

effects.log: You judge the Will of Heaven more gently for a century. They notice and are suspicious.

choices.text: Look for why

effects.log: You find it: a judgement long ago that you were never sure of. You reopen it. The figure comes level.

events.text: A second forger has copied your new seal, the plain one. They are not very good. Han Byeol spots the forgery at once and is very pleased with themselves.

choices.text: Let Han Byeol judge the forger

effects.log: Han Byeol sentences them to copy the first page of the Book a thousand times. They are rather good by the end.

choices.text: Thank the forger for the compliment

effects.log: The forger is so startled they confess to three other forgeries.

events.text: Today a litigant came to your chair and, halfway through their case, stopped and said they no longer needed a judgement. Hearing themselves say it aloud before the Arbiter had been enough.

choices.text: Let them go

effects.log: They go, lighter. Han Byeol writes it in the Book under a new heading: cases that judged themselves.

choices.text: Give them a judgement anyway

effects.log: You give a short one. They take it home and frame it, beside their own words.

events.text: A young immortal on their way up the Dao has come to ask the Arbiter what balance is, as a Dao. You have been asked this before. You have never answered the same way twice.

choices.text: Answer with a question

effects.log: You ask them what they would put in each pan. They are still thinking about it when they leave.

choices.text: Show them the crooked scales

effects.log: You show them the weight in the left pan. They look at it a long time, and bow, and go.

events.text: A god you once judged harshly has died, faded, in their sealed hall. Their pantheon mourns them. You are not invited to the mourning, of course. Nobody would expect you.

choices.text: Go anyway, and stand at the back

effects.log: You stand at the back in grey. Nobody turns. At the end, one of the mourners nods to you.

choices.text: Mourn them alone at your chair

effects.log: You sit with the Book open at their page all night. Han Byeol brings you tea and says nothing.

events.text: The two sides of the war you ended by decree want to raise a monument to the peace in the empty space: a tall stone carved with your decree, word for word. Each side has already designed it. The designs do not match.

choices.text: Allow one stone, designed by both

effects.log: It takes a decade of meetings. The stone, when it rises, is plain and odd and nobody likes it. It is perfect.

choices.text: Refuse: no monument in the empty space

effects.log: They raise it on the old front instead, half on each side. Soldiers of both armies tend it.

events.text: Someone has chipped a word out of the peace monument in the night: the word "both". Each side accuses the other. The old generals are at your bench before breakfast.

choices.text: Find who did it

ok.log: A young god of neither side, who thought the peace unfair to a third pantheon nobody had asked. They were not wrong.

fail.log: Nobody is found. Each side keeps its suspicion. The word is carved back in, deeper.

choices.text: Carve it back yourself

effects.log: You carve "both" back into the stone with your own hand. It is the only word on it in your writing.

events.text: The third pantheon that nobody asked comes to your chair at last. Your decree ended a war between two, and it paid for the peace with a border it was never consulted on. It is a small claim, and old, and true.

choices.text: Reopen the decree on that point

effects.log: One clause is rewritten. The third pantheon gets its border back. The monument gets a new line.

choices.text: Compensate them, and keep the decree

effects.log: The decree stands. The third pantheon is paid in domains. It is less than right and more than nothing.

events.text: The god you sealed held a domain, and nobody holds it now. Its worshippers below pray into an empty hall, and its work goes undone. Every pantheon has sent a candidate to take it, with flattering letters to the Arbiter.

choices.text: Hold an open hearing for the candidates

effects.log: Eight gods argue for an empty domain. The best of them is the one who argued least.

choices.text: Ask the worshippers below whom they would have

effects.log: They answer in a dream, a million of them. They want someone who will answer without a price.

events.text: The candidate the worshippers chose is Baek Narae, the grey clerk who once brought you the true book. They are horrified. They have never held a domain. They have never wanted anything but accounts that add up.

choices.text: Persuade them

effects.log: Baek Narae takes the domain, shaking. The accounts of it are the cleanest in heaven within a century.

choices.text: Let them refuse, and choose the next

effects.log: Baek Narae refuses with relief. The next candidate is good, if a little proud.

events.text: Whoever holds the sealed god's old domain has found, in its hall, a letter from the sealed god, left the night before the seal: instructions for the domain's work, careful and kind, in the hand of the god you sealed for selling it.

choices.text: Read it

effects.log: It is the work of a god who once loved their domain. You keep it in the drawer with Jang Murae's scroll.

choices.text: Take it to the seal and read it aloud

effects.log: You read the god's own letter to them through the seal. They are silent for a long time, and then say "thank you".

events.text: A hero of {sov_world}, the Pocket World you made, has climbed up into heaven to stand before your chair. They are not a litigant. They have come to accuse their maker: {sov_world} has a famine, and its maker sits judging gods.
events.arc: A Hero of the Pocket World

choices.text: Hear them as a litigant

effects.log: You hear the case against yourself. They are right. You were busy.

choices.text: Go down with them at once

effects.log: You go down into {sov_world} with the hero and see the famine. It is real and you are ashamed.

events.text: The famine of {sov_world} is the fault of no god: it was a quarrel of two kingdoms there, who burned each other's fields. The hero wants you to punish them. The kingdoms want you to tell them who started it.
events.arc: A Hero of the Pocket World

choices.text: Judge them, as you judge pantheons

effects.log: Two mortal kingdoms before the Arbiter of heaven. They are terrified, and listen, and the burning stops.

choices.text: Feed {sov_world} and let them settle it

effects.log: You send rain and seed. The kingdoms make peace on their own, grudgingly.

events.text: The hero of {sov_world} has stayed in heaven, in your gallery, to learn how pantheons are judged. They want to take it back down. Han Byeol has given them a copy of the first page of the Book.
events.arc: A Hero of the Pocket World

choices.text: Send them home with your blessing

effects.log: They go down and found a court in {sov_world}. It is the fairest thing there.

choices.text: Ask them to stay and judge with you a while

effects.log: They stay a decade. They make you think about mortals more than you have in an age.

events.text: The Heavenly Court keeps the margins of the Book of Fates, where small corrections are written. Han Byeol has noticed that the margins of one god's fate are much fuller than anyone else's: someone on the Court has been correcting it, again and again, in their favour.
events.arc: The Margins of the Book of Fates

choices.text: Read the corrections

effects.log: Every correction softens a fall, removes a debt, extends a life. The god is a high rung's child.

choices.text: Report it to the Court and wait

effects.log: The Court investigates slowly. The margins stop growing. Nothing else happens.

events.text: The high rung who corrected their child's fate comes to you before you can summon them. They are not sorry. Any parent would do the same, they say, who had a brush. They ask the Arbiter whether you would not.
events.arc: The Margins of the Book of Fates

choices.text: Rule the corrections void

effects.log: Every correction is erased. The child's fate is as it was written. Their parent leaves the Court.

choices.text: Rule them void, but let one stand: the first

effects.log: One mercy kept, the rest erased. The parent weeps. It is a judgement of a parent, by someone who understands.

events.text: The envoys of {sov_war_a} and {sov_war_b} have come to your hall for talks, and neither will sit, because the bench is one bench and neither will share it. They have been standing for three days.
events.arc: The Envoys Who Would Not Sit

choices.text: Remove the bench

effects.log: Everyone stands. Including you. The talks go faster standing.

choices.text: Bring a second bench

effects.log: Two benches, side by side. They sit. They move them apart, inch by inch, over a week.

events.text: Standing, the envoys talk for a month. At the end, exhausted, one of them sits down on the floor. After an hour, the other sits too, a pace away. They go on talking, on the floor of the empty space, like children.
events.arc: The Envoys Who Would Not Sit

choices.text: Sit on the floor with them

effects.log: Three on the floor. A truce is agreed by evening.

choices.text: Stay in the chair, and listen

effects.log: You let them have the floor. The truce takes another month, and is theirs.

events.text: The child of a god the Court has exiled has come to your hall. They have done nothing. But the Court's sentence named the exile's house, and the child cannot hold a domain, enter a festival or marry into a pantheon. They are nine hundred years old and have never been anything.

choices.text: Hear their case

effects.log: You hear it. The Court's sentence is lawful. It is also a sentence on someone who was not born when the crime was done.

choices.text: Send them to the Court

effects.log: They go up the ladder and are turned away at the second rung.

events.text: You can rule that no sentence falls on a child for a parent's crime. It would overturn a hundred sentences of the Court, and the Court would be shamed, and a great many children of exiles would be free.

choices.text: Rule it

effects.log: The precedent goes out. A hundred houses of exiles have children who can be something. The Court does not speak to you for a century.

choices.text: Ask the Court to amend it themselves first

effects.log: The Court amends it, grudgingly, a year later. They take the credit. The children do not care who.

events.text: The exile's child has a domain now: a small one, the domain of second chances, which nobody else wanted. They come once a year to your bench to report on it. It is busier than they expected.

choices.text: Ask who comes to them

effects.log: "Everyone," they say. "Everyone has been someone's child."

choices.text: Send them the cases you would have been harsh on

effects.log: They take your hardest cases and give them second chances. You learn from them.

events.text: Behind every raid of the Calamity Star, scavengers have come: lesser gods and immortals who pick through the ash of raided domains for relics, and sell them. There is a market in the ash now, at the edge of heaven, and the raided gods want it judged.

choices.text: Go and see the market

effects.log: It is busy and grim. A god is selling a raided god's child's toys. You stop at that stall.

choices.text: Close it by decree

effects.log: The market moves. It is harder to find, and the prices rise.

events.text: The stall-keeper selling the toys is a young god of the Lesser Hall, poor, who did not think about what they were selling until you stopped. Now they cannot stop thinking about it.

choices.text: Have them return everything they sold

effects.log: They track down every buyer for a decade. Most give the relics back. The raided gods are amazed.

choices.text: Rule: relics of the raided belong to the raided

effects.log: The market empties overnight. Relics flow back to their domains.

events.text: The children born in the first year of the peace you decreed are grown now, gods of both sides who have never known the war. They have sent you an invitation to their coming of age, signed by all of them.

choices.text: Go

effects.log: You stand among a hundred young gods of two pantheons. None of them know which side their parents fought on, and none of them care.

choices.text: Send a gift: the burnt beam from the first fire

effects.log: They hang it in their hall. They do not know what it is. They will ask, one day.

events.text: A hundred years since you sealed a god. Their pantheon sends a single white flower to the seal, every year, and this year, for the first time, they have sent one to your chair as well.

choices.text: Put it in water

effects.log: It lives a week. The next year there is another. You keep the vase on the shelf.

choices.text: Take it to the seal

effects.log: Two white flowers at the seal. Their pantheon sees, and understands, and is quieter towards you.

events.text: The weather of {sov_world} has been strange: rain on one valley only, every day, and none on the next. Your Pocket World's people say their maker is judging them. You are not. You check, and find that you have been, unawares, in your sleep.

choices.text: Stop

effects.log: You make yourself stop judging in your sleep. The rain evens out. The valleys are relieved.

choices.text: Find out what you were judging

effects.log: A quarrel you heard of and forgot. You hear it properly. The rain falls fair.

events.text: Your robes of a rung of the Heavenly Court hang beside your plain Arbiter's grey. Han Byeol wants to know which you will wear to today's hearing, which is about the Court.

choices.text: The grey

effects.log: You judge the Court in grey. The Court notices and approves, grudgingly.

choices.text: Neither: you take the robe off the rung for good

effects.log: You give up the Court post. You are lighter for it.

events.text: In the middle of the War in Heaven, the envoy of {sov_war_a} and the envoy of {sov_war_b} have started having tea together on your bench before the hearings. They do not speak during it. They each pour for the other.

choices.text: Leave them be

effects.log: You never mention it. The tea goes on all through the war, and after.

choices.text: Join them, once, silently

effects.log: Three cups. No words. It is the best hearing of the war.

events.text: The Calamity Star raiding heaven has written to you, in a fine, neat hand. It asks only one thing: whether the Arbiter judges a Star by its raids alone, or also by whatever made it a Star.

choices.text: "Both."

effects.log: The Star does not write again. But it raids a little less, as if waiting for its hearing.

choices.text: "By the raids. The rest is mercy."

effects.log: It writes back one line: "Then I will ask for mercy, when I come."

events.text: A student of {sov_corrupt} has come to your chair. They learned their domain's work from the corrupt god and want to know if what they learned is also corrupt, or only the way it was sold.

choices.text: "The work is good. The price was the crime."

effects.log: They go home and do the work, freely. They are the first good thing to come of the case.

choices.text: Ask them to show you the work

effects.log: They show you. Some of it is good. Some of it was made for selling. You help them tell which.

events.text: A small god of {sov_pantheon}, the pantheon that stands over half of heaven, has come to your chair secretly. They are afraid of their own pantheon. They want to know whether the Arbiter protects gods from their own side.

choices.text: "Yes."

effects.log: They go home braver. Within a decade, three more come, openly.

choices.text: "I protect the law. Bring me a case."

effects.log: They bring one. It is real. {sov_pantheon} is judged by its own.

events.text: A child of one of the claimants to the throne of {sov_realm} has run away from their parent's war-camp and arrived at your hall. They do not want any throne. They want to be allowed to study the stars.

choices.text: Send them to Cheonho, Who Hangs the Stars

effects.log: They study the stars. Their parent is furious, then, over a century, proud.

choices.text: Send them home, with a letter to their parent

effects.log: Your letter is short. The parent reads it, and lets the child go to the stars anyway.

events.text: Heaven is calm, and you use the quiet to hear a case that has waited three thousand years: two gods of the Mountains over a single stone. Both are long faded. Their heirs barely remember the stone.

choices.text: Hear it anyway

effects.log: You hear it fully. The stone goes to neither; it goes back to the mountain. The heirs are relieved to have it done.

choices.text: Rule it settled by time

effects.log: Han Byeol writes: settled by forgetting. A new heading. It is used often after.

events.text: In the shaking years, someone has slept on your litigant's bench every night: a god with no hall, no domain and no case, who says only that the empty space is the one place in heaven that does not shake.

choices.text: Let them stay

effects.log: They sleep there through the worst years. On the first calm morning they are gone, and the bench is warm.

choices.text: Give them work: sweeping the steps

effects.log: They sweep for a decade and leave with a domain of their own: doorsteps.

events.text: At the Festival of Masks in the Heavenly Calendar, every god goes masked and nobody may say which pantheon they serve. This year a hall of the Throne of Storms was robbed during it, and the thief wore a mask, and the Throne wants the Arbiter to unmask the whole festival.

choices.text: Refuse: the masks are the festival

effects.log: You will not unmask heaven. You will find the thief another way.

choices.text: Unmask only those near the hall

effects.log: Forty gods unmasked. Three pantheons are scandalised. The thief is not among them.

events.text: You go to the next Festival of Masks yourself, masked, unknown, as any god may. In the crowd near the Throne's hall, someone in a plain grey mask is watching the doors the way only a thief or a judge would.

choices.text: Follow them

ok.log: They lead you to the stolen goods, hidden under the festival stage. They take off their mask: it is a god of the Throne itself, in debt.

fail.log: You lose them in the crowd. The festival goes on. You enjoy it, despite yourself.

choices.text: Speak to them, masked to masked

effects.log: They talk to you as one stranger to another, and confess, not knowing who you are. Then they guess.

events.text: The thief of the Festival of Masks was a god of the Throne of Storms who robbed their own hall to pay a debt their pantheon would not forgive. The Throne wants them sealed. The festival wants its masks kept.

choices.text: Judge them, masked

effects.log: You let them keep their mask through the hearing. The sentence is fair. The festival is unharmed.

choices.text: Judge the debt first

effects.log: The debt was unjust. You judge it. Then the theft, lightly. The Throne is not pleased.

events.text: You arrive one morning and your chair is gone. Not broken: gone, taken in the night from the empty space. The scales are on the floor where it stood. Han Byeol is in tears. The envoys are already arriving to hear the day's cases.

choices.text: Judge standing

effects.log: You judge the whole day on your feet beside the scales. Nobody mentions the chair. The judgements are just as binding.

choices.text: Close the bench until it is found

effects.log: Heaven waits a month without its Arbiter. Some of it does not wait well.

events.text: The chair is found in the great hall of a pantheon, set at the head of its table. Its gods say they did not take it. They found it there, they say, one morning, and thought the Arbiter had come over to their side.

choices.text: Find who really moved it

ok.log: It was a god of a rival pantheon, who wanted the Arbiter to look partial. They are found and judged.

fail.log: You never learn. The pantheon that held it is suspected for an age.

choices.text: Carry it home yourself, publicly

effects.log: You walk the chair back across heaven on your own shoulders. Every god sees it go home to the empty space.

events.text: All twelve gods of the domains have come to your chair together, for the first time in your tenure: Mujin and Cheonho and Hwarin, Baekun and Unmyeong and Mongsa, Saengmo and Horang and Pungnyeon, Haeryong and Noegong and Daeak. They have one case, and it is against heaven itself.

choices.text: Hear it

effects.log: Their case: the domains are older than the pantheons, and the pantheons have made them servants. They want to be judged as domains, not as halls.

choices.text: Ask why now

effects.log: Mongsa the Sleeper, half awake, says: "Because you are here. Nobody was, before."

events.text: The four pantheons answer the twelve gods: the domains were wild and warring before the pantheons gathered them. Without the halls, Thunder and the Sea would drown the Harvest every spring. Both sides are right, again, as they always are.

choices.text: Rule that the domains are the pantheons' partners, not servants

effects.log: A new page in the Book. The twelve keep their halls and gain a seat at every pantheon's table.

choices.text: Rule for the pantheons, and record the twelve's grievance

effects.log: The halls hold. The grievance is in the Book. In an age, it will be cited.

events.text: The twelve gods of the domains hold a feast in the empty space to mark your ruling. They seat themselves at one long table, in no pantheon's order, and leave a thirteenth place empty at the end, for the domain of Thresholds.

choices.text: Fill the thirteenth place yourself

effects.log: You sit at the end. The twelve raise cups to the Arbiter. It is a long, loud, good night.

choices.text: Leave it empty

effects.log: The empty place stands for every domain that faded. The twelve drink to it in silence.

events.text: A god arrives at your hall claiming to be descended from Jang Murae, the first Arbiter, and therefore the chair's rightful heir. They have a genealogy. It is very good. They are very polite. They would like you to step down.
events.arc: The Heir of the First Arbiter

choices.text: Hear their claim

effects.log: You hear it. It is plausible. It is also irrelevant: the chair has never passed by blood.

choices.text: Ask the chair

effects.log: You put the claimant's question to the old wood at night. Nothing answers. That is, Mok Dami says, an answer.

events.text: The claimant has gathered supporters: gods who would like an Arbiter of their own choosing, and see in the heir a chance. Rule against them and they will say the Arbiter clings to the chair. Rule for them and the chair becomes a crown.
events.arc: The Heir of the First Arbiter

choices.text: Rule that the chair passes by no blood, and step aside for a day

effects.log: You rule it, and then sit in the gallery for a day while the chair stands empty. Nobody takes it.

choices.text: Rule against them, plainly

ok.log: Heaven accepts it. The claimant goes home. Their supporters scatter.

fail.log: Heaven mutters. The claimant's party lasts a century.

events.text: Heaven is shaking, and the gods are tired: they have not rested in a century of crises. Han Byeol suggests bending a small law: let one day a year be a day on which no quarrel of heaven can begin, by law.

choices.text: Bend it

effects.log: One day of rest a year, written into the laws of heaven. On the first, nobody believes it. On the second, everybody sleeps.

choices.text: Refuse: rest cannot be ordered

effects.log: Han Byeol is disappointed. Heaven goes on shaking, tired.

events.text: On the day of rest, a god has broken the law: they began a quarrel at dawn, deliberately, to see if it would hold. It did not begin. The words came out of their mouth and fell to the floor of heaven like dropped stones.

choices.text: Summon them, the next day

effects.log: They come, shaken. "It worked," they say. "I did not think it would." They are the law's greatest defender after.

choices.text: Let the law speak for itself

effects.log: Nobody tries again. The day of rest becomes the best day in the Calendar.

events.text: At the turning of the Heavenly Calendar, every god of heaven stands still for one breath, and by custom the Arbiter speaks the year's last word. You have done it many times. This time you cannot think of one.

choices.text: Say: "Again."

effects.log: The word goes round heaven. The new year begins. It feels like a promise.

choices.text: Say nothing

effects.log: The breath goes on longer than it should. Then someone laughs, and the year turns anyway.

events.text: A god brings two pieces of evidence: a feather and a stone, and says they weigh the same. They do not. The god insists the scales are wrong, not their evidence.

choices.text: Check the scales

effects.log: The scales are right. The god is embarrassed. You judge the case anyway, and they win it.

choices.text: Weigh the god's certainty

effects.log: You ask them to put their certainty in the pan. They laugh, and withdraw the claim.

events.text: Haeryong, Keeper of Tides, accuses the Moon of stealing tides. There is no god of the Moon. Haeryong knows this. They want it judged anyway, so that it is written somewhere who is to blame.

choices.text: Judge the Moon in absence

effects.log: The Moon is found guilty and sentenced to keep stealing. Haeryong is satisfied.

choices.text: Rule that some things have no one to blame

effects.log: Haeryong grumbles. It is the most often cited page in the Throne of Storms.

events.text: A litigant you ruled against comes back with a gift: a small carved scale, very well made. They lost, they say, but they were heard, and nobody had heard them before.

choices.text: Accept it

effects.log: It sits on the shelf. You look at it on hard days.

choices.text: Give it to Han Byeol

effects.log: Han Byeol keeps it on their desk. It is the first gift anyone has given them for the work.

events.text: You dream you are a litigant at your own bench, and the Arbiter in the chair is someone you do not know. They hear you out patiently. They rule against you. It is fair.

choices.text: Wake and write it down

effects.log: You write: "It was fair. It hurt." Han Byeol files it under the first page.

choices.text: Try to see the judge's face

effects.log: You dream it again for a year. You never see the face. You stop trying.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has issued a warrant for a wind. A wind cannot be served. The Court knows this. It wants the Arbiter to rule on what to do with warrants that cannot be served, of which there are, it turns out, four thousand.

choices.text: Rule them void

effects.log: Four thousand warrants voided. The Court's archive is lighter by a hall.

choices.text: Serve the wind yourself

effects.log: You stand in the wind and read the warrant aloud. The wind stops for a breath. The Court records it as served.

events.text: Two envoys of rival pantheons, who met on the bench outside your hall, want to marry, and want the Arbiter to marry them. Neither pantheon approves. Both envoys have resigned to do it.

choices.text: Marry them on the bench where they met

effects.log: The bench outside your hall has seen many things. This is the first wedding.

choices.text: Ask both pantheons to attend

effects.log: Both pantheons come, stiffly. By the end of the night they are drinking together.

events.text: For one moment this morning the crooked scales came level on their own. No one touched them. Han Byeol saw it and could not speak.

choices.text: Look for what changed

effects.log: You search heaven for a day. Somewhere, two old enemies made peace, quietly. It was enough.

choices.text: Let it be a mystery

effects.log: You never know why. The scales go crooked again by noon. You smile all day.

events.text: Han Byeol announces, very formally, that today's case is the ten-thousandth heard at your chair. It is about a hedge. The litigants are mortified to be the ten-thousandth.

choices.text: Judge it as gravely as the first

effects.log: The hedge is judged with full ceremony. The litigants frame the judgement.

choices.text: Give them a festival after

effects.log: Ten thousand cases, one hedge, a feast. Heaven comes.

events.text: Pungnyeon of the Golden Field asks the Arbiter to rule on whether a harvest god may refuse to feed a kingdom below that has burned their temple. The kingdom is hungry. The temple is ash.

choices.text: Rule: feed them

effects.log: Pungnyeon feeds them, resentfully. The kingdom rebuilds the temple, ashamed.

choices.text: Rule: the god may grieve one season, then feed

effects.log: One hungry season, then plenty. The kingdom learns, and so does Pungnyeon.

events.text: Every pantheon in heaven has, at one time or another, offered you a seat. Han Byeol has made a list of every offer, with dates. It is long. They want to know whether to keep it.

choices.text: Keep it

effects.log: The list of every seat refused. It is the most honest record of the office there is.

choices.text: Burn it

effects.log: You burn it together. Neither of you will forget a line of it.

events.text: Over the empty space one night, someone has written a single word in the stars, small enough that only you, looking up from the chair, would see it: "Fair." It fades by dawn. Cheonho, Who Hangs the Stars, denies everything.

choices.text: Write back in the stars

effects.log: You write "Thank you" in faint stars. Somewhere a god reads it and is happy.

choices.text: Leave it unanswered

effects.log: You keep it to yourself. It is the best review the office has ever had.

events.text: A champion sent to your Trial of Judgement refuses to fight. They say their side is wrong, and they will not win a wrong for it. Their pantheon is outraged.

choices.text: Rule the clash for the other side, on the champion's word

effects.log: An honest champion ends a clash without a blow. Their pantheon disowns them. You take them on as a clerk.

choices.text: Hear the clash on the law instead

effects.log: You hear it properly. The champion was right. Their pantheon, embarrassed, takes them back.

events.text: A young god touches the hailstone on the shelf of evidence, on a dare, and it does not melt under their hand, though it is warm. They run off. The hailstone, Han Byeol notes, has never been colder.

choices.text: Leave it

effects.log: The hailstone sits on, unmelted. Its legend grows.

choices.text: Find the young god and tell them what it means

effects.log: You tell them about Cheon Ugeun and the hailstone. They become an envoy, in time.

events.text: A mortal child from below has fallen asleep and dreamed their way into the empty space. They sit on the litigant's bench, swinging their feet, and ask what this place is for.

choices.text: Tell them

effects.log: "For when people disagree," you say. "Oh," says the child. "That is everybody." They wake, below, and do not forget it.

choices.text: Ask them what they think it is for

effects.log: "For sitting," says the child. They are not wrong.

events.text: Long after the Court's case against {sov_accused} ended, they have sent you a letter. Whatever came of it, they write, the Arbiter was the only god in heaven who asked them what had happened before asking what they had done.

choices.text: Keep the letter

effects.log: It goes on the shelf. You read it before hard cases.

choices.text: Send it to the Court

effects.log: The Court reads it. A rule of the Court changes, slowly: the accused are asked first.

events.text: Late at night, Han Byeol has gone, the envoys are home, the hall is dark but for one lamp by the chair. Outside, four pantheons sleep. Somewhere a war is not happening because of something you said a thousand years ago.

choices.text: Put out the lamp

effects.log: You sit in the dark of the empty space and listen to heaven sleep.

choices.text: Leave it lit for whoever comes

effects.log: Nobody comes. In the morning, there is a cup of tea beside it, still warm.

events.text: The Green Assembly has asked for the Book of Precedent to be read aloud in its hall, every page, so that its young gods know the law they live under. The other three pantheons, hearing of it, want the same. It would take a century in each.

choices.text: Read it in all four, in turn

effects.log: Four centuries of reading. Your voice goes hoarse in the second. Han Byeol or Seo Gyeol reads the rest.

choices.text: Have it copied for each instead

effects.log: Four copies go out. Each pantheon reads it its own way. The readings differ, a little.

events.text: In the Will of Heaven's hall, during the reading, a young god stands up at a judgement against their pantheon and shouts that it was unjust. The hall goes silent. Everyone waits for the Arbiter to answer.

choices.text: Stop and hear their objection

effects.log: You hear it there and then. They are half right. You say so. The hall is astonished.

choices.text: Finish the page, then hear them

effects.log: You finish. Then you hear them. They are calmer by then, and clearer.

events.text: The young god who shouted at the reading has become a scholar of the Book, the only one of their pantheon. They have written a commentary on every judgement against the Will of Heaven. It is fierce and fair, and they have sent it to you first.

choices.text: Read it, and answer every point

effects.log: It takes a decade. Your answers become part of the commentary. Both of you are better for it.

choices.text: Send it to the other three pantheons

effects.log: Three pantheons read a fierce, fair critique of the Arbiter by a god of the Will of Heaven. They trust you more.

events.text: The weight you lifted from the left pan of your scales sits on the floor beside your chair, cold, where you set it. Nobody can move it but you. Litigants step round it carefully. Han Byeol sweeps around it every morning, and once, absent-mindedly, talks to it.

choices.text: Leave it there

effects.log: It stays on the floor, the weight of every judgement you were not sure of, where anyone can see it.

choices.text: Carry it to the edge of heaven and set it down

effects.log: You carry it to where Jang Murae's footprints stop. It sits there, looking at the world below.

events.text: The weight has begun to grow, slowly, by a grain at a time: one grain for every judgement you give that you are not sure of. Han Byeol has been measuring it. They show you the figures, worried.

choices.text: Put it back in the pan

effects.log: The scales tip again. You judge with them crooked. You are, oddly, relieved.

choices.text: Be sure more often

effects.log: You take longer over every case. The weight stops growing. Litigants wait longer, and complain, and are better served.

events.text: A young god kneels at your bench: the grandchild of a god you sentenced a thousand years ago to give up a domain. The domain went to another. The grandchild has grown up in a small hall, poor, knowing only that the Arbiter took what was theirs.

choices.text: Hear what they want

effects.log: They do not want the domain. They want to know what their grandparent did. Nobody in their house will tell them.

choices.text: Tell them the sentence was just

effects.log: It was. They listen. They do not believe you, yet.

events.text: You read them the old case from the Book. Their grandparent let a river below run red with a quarrel, on purpose, to shame a rival. Mortals drowned. The grandchild listens to the end, and is quiet for a very long time.

choices.text: Ask what they will do with it

effects.log: "Be better," they say, "and make sure nobody in my house has to learn it from a judge."

choices.text: Offer them work at the empty space

effects.log: They take it. They are the most careful clerk you have ever had.

events.text: The grandchild of the god you sentenced has done something you did not expect: gone to the domain their grandparent lost, and to its new god, and offered to serve it. The new god, astonished, has accepted.

choices.text: Write it in the Book

effects.log: Under the old sentence, a new line: the house that lost the domain now serves it. A judgement, come back, finished.

choices.text: Go and see

effects.log: You see the grandchild at work in the domain. They are good at it. They do not see you.

events.text: In the shaking years, a small pantheon of the Lesser Hall's kind has fallen: its halls burned in a war between two greater ones, and it asked the Arbiter for protection, and the Arbiter stands with no side. Its last god stands before you in ash.
events.arc: The Hall That Fell While You Stood Between

choices.text: Hear them

effects.log: They do not ask for anything. They want you to know what neutrality cost them, exactly, name by name.

choices.text: Shelter them now

effects.log: You open your hall. It is late. It is something.

events.text: The last god of the fallen pantheon has read you the names of everyone lost. It took a whole day. Han Byeol has written every name in the Book, on a page with no judgement.
events.arc: The Hall That Fell While You Stood Between

choices.text: Judge the two greater pantheons for it

effects.log: You bring the war that burned them before the scales. Both greater pantheons pay. It does not bring anyone back.

choices.text: Leave the page without a judgement

effects.log: A page of names, no verdict. It is the heaviest page in the Book.

events.text: The last god of the fallen pantheon has founded a new domain in the empty space, with your leave: the domain of the Unprotected, whose god hears those whom no pantheon will shelter. They bring you their first case.
events.arc: The Hall That Fell While You Stood Between

choices.text: Hear it

effects.log: You hear it with them beside you. It is the first of many. Heaven has a new voice, and it is not quiet.

choices.text: Let them hear it alone

effects.log: They judge it alone. They are stern and fair. You learn from them.

events.text: Han Byeol has found a precedent in the Book that has never once been cited, in all your tenure: a small ruling about a fence. They want to know if it should be struck out.

choices.text: Keep it: someone will need it

effects.log: A century later, someone does. Han Byeol is unbearably pleased.

choices.text: Strike it out

effects.log: The Book is one page lighter. Nobody notices. You do.

events.text: Each of the four pantheons has its own season of festivals in the Heavenly Calendar, and each invites the Arbiter. You have refused them all for an age. This year they have combined them into one, so that going would favour no one.

choices.text: Go

effects.log: One festival of four pantheons. You attend. You favour no one. It is the best party in an age.

choices.text: Thank them and stay

effects.log: They hold it without you, together, which was perhaps the point.

events.text: A young god of the Lesser Hall, bringing a petition, does not know your name. They know only "the Arbiter". When you tell them, they write it carefully on the back of their hand, so as not to be rude.

choices.text: Tell them it does not matter

effects.log: "It matters to me," they say, and keep it on their hand all day.

choices.text: Ask theirs

effects.log: You write their name on the back of your own hand. They are delighted.

events.text: A god asks you to unbend a law you bent long ago, for them, at their request. They have changed their mind. The change helped them once; now it hurts their children.

choices.text: Unbend it

effects.log: The law goes back. Their children are spared. Han Byeol writes: bent and unbent.

choices.text: Rule that a bent law, once given, is the children's too

effects.log: You hear the children. They want it kept. It stays.

events.text: Children of the two pantheons at war play a game in the empty space: one side are the armies, and one child sits in the middle on an upturned bucket as the Arbiter. The child on the bucket always says, "Both of you, sit down."

choices.text: Watch them play

effects.log: You watch from the steps. The children's war always ends the same way. You envy them.

choices.text: Ask to play the army

effects.log: You play an army. The child on the bucket tells you to sit down. You sit down.

events.text: A warrant of the Heavenly Court has arrived at your bench nine hundred years late, delayed in a courier's bag. The god it names has since become a good one, and holds a domain well.

choices.text: Rule it lapsed

effects.log: The warrant lapses. The god never learns how close they came.

choices.text: Hear it anyway

effects.log: The god is found guilty of a small old wrong and sentenced to an apology. They give it gladly.

events.text: A case comes to your bench with every name removed: no pantheon, no god, no domain, only what was done. Han Byeol prepared it so on purpose. They want to see what you do with nothing to lean on.

choices.text: Judge it

effects.log: You judge it. When the names are read out afterwards, you find you ruled against your own sympathies. Good.

choices.text: Ask for the names first

effects.log: Han Byeol refuses, politely. You judge it anyway. It is the fairest judgement of the year.

events.text: Mongsa the Sleeper has dreamed so deeply this century that their dreams have spilled into the Will of Heaven's halls, where nobody sleeps. Gods of the noon are having dreams for the first time, and are very upset about it.

choices.text: Rule that Mongsa may dream as they like

effects.log: The Will of Heaven goes on dreaming. Some of its gods come to like it.

choices.text: Ask Mongsa to dream a little more quietly

effects.log: Mok Dami carries the message into the dream. Mongsa turns over. The spill stops.

events.text: Your grey robe has worn through at the elbows from leaning on the arms of the chair. Han Byeol has had a new one made, exactly the same grey. You find you do not want to give up the old one.

choices.text: Wear the new one

effects.log: The new robe is stiff. In a century it will lean like the old.

choices.text: Have the old one patched

effects.log: It is patched with cloth from four pantheons. Nobody planned it. It looks right.

events.text: A case before you is the exact mirror of one you judged a thousand years ago, only the sides are reversed: the pantheon that won then is the accused now. Both remember.

choices.text: Rule as precedent says, exactly

effects.log: The old winner loses now, by the same law. Both sides accept it. That is what precedent is for.

choices.text: Rule on its own weight

effects.log: You rule differently, carefully. The old loser says nothing. Its silence is loud.

events.text: Someone has built a tiny shrine to you on the edge of heaven where Jang Murae's footprints stop: a stone the size of a fist, with two pebbles balanced on it. Every day someone rebalances them.

choices.text: Find out who

effects.log: It is Han Byeol, every morning, before work. You never let them know you saw.

choices.text: Rebalance them yourself, one morning

effects.log: The next morning there is a third pebble, in the middle. You laugh aloud.

events.text: A god asks you, in the middle of a hearing, the old question: who judges the Arbiter? The hall goes quiet. You have been asked it a hundred times. This time you have an answer.

choices.text: "Everyone I have judged."

effects.log: The hall is silent a long while. Then the hearing goes on, and it is gentler.

choices.text: "The ones who come back."

effects.log: You mean the litigants who return, and keep returning. They understand, and nod.
